prompt: Write the career advice post you wish someone had handed you as a young software engineer fresh out of college: the stuff about how the industry and business actually work that no CS degree or career center covers. Be blunt and practical.
response:
You came out of college trained to solve problems that already have a specification. Work is mostly the opposite. The problem is fuzzy, the constraints are political, the timeline is arbitrary, and the people around you have incentives you did not design. Your degree taught you to reason about correctness. Your job will be to decide what correctness is worth, for whom, and under what deadline.

The first thing to internalize is that software is not a pure technical artifact. It is a business instrument. A feature exists to change behavior, reduce cost, lower risk, or make money. A refactor exists to make future work cheaper or safer. A migration exists because the current system is becoming too expensive to operate or too risky to change. If you cannot connect your work to one of those, you are not doing engineering yet; you are doing exercises.

That does not mean every line of code must be directly monetizable. It means the system you build is a liability and an asset at the same time. It can generate revenue, but it also requires headcount, cloud spend, on-call attention, and organizational trust. A beautiful microservice that no one can operate is a bad microservice. A boring database table that lets the business run for five years is good engineering.

Your early instinct will be to make the code elegant. Often that is the wrong first move. The first version should be clear, testable, and good enough to answer the question. If you spend two weeks building a perfect search index before finding out that users mostly needed to export a CSV, you have not saved time. You have delayed learning. The cost of being wrong early is usually lower than the cost of being elegantly wrong late.

But “good enough” is not a license to be careless. It is a professional judgment. You need to know where the load-bearing walls are. If you are touching payments, authentication, data migration, or anything that can corrupt user state, slow down. Write the test that would have caught the bug. Add the log line that will tell you what happened. Make the deploy reversible. A production incident is not just an embarrassment; it is a tax on future trust. People remember which engineers make them nervous.

Observability matters more than most junior engineers expect. If you cannot see whether your code is running, how often it fails, and what it is doing under load, you do not control it. A change that ships with no metrics is a rumor. You want to be able to say, “Before this change, latency was X and errors were Y. After, they are Z.” That sentence is worth more in a performance review than any adjective.

Visibility is not a soft skill. It is infrastructure for your career. In a company, work that is invisible is work that did not happen. If you solved a hard problem and no one outside your immediate pair knows about it, the organization got the benefit but you did not get the reputation. Write the design doc. Write the postmortem. Write the internal blog post. In standup, do not say “working on it.” Say what you changed, what you measured, what is blocked, and what you expect next. People promote engineers they understand. You make yourself understandable by leaving a paper trail.

This is where the word “politics” becomes useful if you stop using it as an insult. Every company allocates scarce resources: budget, headcount, engineering time, executive attention. Projects compete. Teams compete. If your project is important to you but not connected to a metric or goal that your manager cares about, it is fragile. When the next priority shifts, it will be cut. Learn what your organization is actually optimizing for this quarter. Is it growth? Gross margin? Retention? Platform reliability? Compliance? The answer changes what “done” means.

You also need to learn the difference between a mentor and a sponsor. A mentor gives you advice. A sponsor puts your name in the room when decisions are being made. Most junior engineers have mentors and no sponsors. A sponsor is usually someone who has seen you do reliable, high-quality work and can vouch for you. You earn that by being easy to bet on: clear communication, honest estimates, follow-through, and no dramatic failures. Do not ask for a sponsor directly. Ask for feedback, take it seriously, and then make the next piece of work easier to recommend.

Customers matter. If you only talk to engineers, you will build a closed ecosystem of assumptions. Read support tickets. Sit in on sales calls if you can. Ask what users actually did, not what they say they want. A big customer requesting a feature is a signal, not a requirement. The feature may be a workaround for a broken workflow, a one-off need, or a competitive threat. The question “what job are they trying to get done?” is worth more than the feature request itself. Engineers who understand the customer become harder to replace because they can evaluate tradeoffs that pure technologists cannot see.

Promotions are not rewards for surviving years. They are bets on your ability to operate at a larger radius of impact. A junior engineer completes well-defined tasks. A mid-level engineer owns a project from design through launch. A senior engineer identifies problems that no one has formally assigned and leads people without formal authority. A staff engineer shapes what the team is trying to do. The jump is not “know more languages.” It is that you stop waiting to be told what is important.

The most useful promotion artifact is not a list of features. It is a story about a problem, your judgment, the tradeoffs, and the outcome. “I reduced checkout errors by 18%” is better than “I improved checkout.” “I convinced the team to delay the new dashboard because the data pipeline was unreliable, and we avoided two incidents during peak season” is better than “I was reliable.” You need evidence of leverage: time saved, risk reduced, revenue protected, other engineers unblocked, decision quality improved.

Do not confuse scope with importance. Owning a large system is not automatically senior work if you are just maintaining it. Identifying a subtle reliability issue, instrumenting it, and changing the team’s practice around it can be more valuable. Conversely, shipping a large feature with no learning, no measurement, and no improvement in process is not a promotion story. It is a receipt.

Your learning strategy should change after college. Stop consuming content at the same rate you were producing assignments. Tutorials create familiarity, not judgment. The best training is reading production code, especially code you did not write. Ask what would break if a dependency failed. Ask why the abstraction exists. Ask what the last incident taught. Then build something real, even if it is small: an internal tool, a script that saves your team an hour a week, a side project with actual users. The goal is to experience the full loop: idea, constraint, implementation, failure, feedback, revision.

If a tool saves five minutes for one person twice a week, it is a convenience. If it saves an hour for ten people every day, it is a business case. Start there. Junior engineers often think they need to build a distributed system to prove themselves. More often, they need to make a painful manual process disappear and document the result.

The job market is lumpy and not very personal. An offer is not a verdict on your soul. A rejection is not a diagnosis. Companies hire for risk reduction as much as talent. They want to know you will show up, communicate, and not require constant supervision. That is why interviews test basic problem-solving and communication so heavily: they are proxies for future cost. When negotiating, understand the whole package. Base salary is predictable. Sign-on is one-time. Equity is a bet, often a bad one unless the company is close to a liquidity event or you genuinely believe in the upside. A higher title at a smaller company may be less portable than a plain title at a company whose name opens doors.

Layoffs are a business cycle, not a moral ranking. Companies grow, overhire, revenue slows, and they cut. If you are caught in one, it is not evidence that you were bad. It is evidence that your cost was not protected at that moment. The practical response is boring: keep skills current, keep relationships warm, keep savings, and do not let your identity fuse with one employer. The engineers who recover fastest are the ones who can describe what they did in plain language to someone who is not on their team.

Artificial intelligence is changing the leverage curve, and you should take that seriously without becoming a hype victim. Writing boilerplate code is becoming less scarce. Judgment is becoming more valuable. You need to be good at specifying what should be built, verifying that the output is correct, understanding the system around it, and knowing when a generated patch is dangerous. The engineer who treats AI as a shortcut to looking busy will be exposed quickly. The engineer who uses it to expand the amount of reliable work they can ship will have an advantage.

The hardest objection to all of this is that it sounds like a recipe for becoming a political operator who happens to write code. That is a real failure mode. If you optimize only for visibility and alignment, you become replaceable the moment a better-connected person arrives. If you optimize only for technical purity, you become a hobbyist with a paycheck. The durable position is being genuinely good at hard technical work and genuinely good at making that work matter. Those are not opposites. The best engineers are dangerous because they can do both.

In your next one-on-one, bring one page. What you shipped. What you measured. What you learned. What you are unsure about. What you need from your manager. No apology, no performance. That page is the smallest unit of professional trust. Build it until it is boring.

prompt: I run a company with a big, ugly legacy codebase, and everyone keeps saying we should rewrite it all in whatever framework is fashionable. Write a candid first-person post from someone who tried a big rewrite and what they concluded about it.
response:
I did the rewrite.

Our legacy system was a Django monolith that had been growing for eleven years. It had about 412,000 lines of Python, 88,000 lines of JavaScript, 1,900 database migrations, and fourteen cron jobs whose purposes only a couple of people fully understood. The most frightening file was `billing_engine.py`, four thousand three hundred lines long, last touched by an engineer who no longer worked there. Some views were simple. Some were crimes. We had a table called `customer_preferences` with sixty-one boolean columns, and nobody could tell you what half of them meant without reading the code that used them.

Everyone who interviewed us said the same thing: you do not have a product problem, you have an architecture problem. Build the next platform on the modern stack. We chose TypeScript, React, Node, Postgres, and Kubernetes. I like that sentence now because it sounds so reasonable.

We stopped most feature work on the old system. Nine engineers went to the new platform. The first eight weeks were pleasant. We wrote clean services. Our pull requests were small. Our tests were green. We had a dashboard. We looked like a software company.

Then we started implementing real money.

The first casualty was a discount. In the old system, a customer got two percent off if the order was placed before 2 p.m. and shipped from warehouse seven. No ticket explained it. No comment did. We asked the account manager who knew the customer. He said it was a workaround from 2016 for a freight contract that had expired in 2018. The customer still expected it. We had to port the workaround.

That was the smallest one.

The big ones were in the data. Our old Postgres schema had views that encoded business rules, triggers that wrote audit rows, and a materialized view that updated at 3 a.m. It had also absorbed ten years of customer-specific behavior. When we tried to move the customer ledger to the new database, we found that some balances were not balances. They were promises, offsets, and credits that only made sense if you read the old code and then talked to the support team that had created them.

We built a sync job. Then we built a reconciliation job. Then we built a page to investigate mismatches. The new system and the old system disagreed about tax in eleven states. One integration partner sent webhooks in a format that only the old parser understood, because they had been told not to change it after we complained in 2019.

By month ten, we had two codebases and a bridge between them. The bridge had its own bugs.

The team split made it worse. The people on the new platform stopped reading the old code because it was embarrassing. The people left on the old system stopped answering questions because they were being treated like an archive. We had a domain expert who knew the refund rules, but he was not on the rewrite. He was on the old system, handling production incidents. He knew things, but the new team did not know what to ask.

We tried to measure progress. Story points were useless. We started tracking lead time from a business request to a safe change. For simple features, it improved. For anything touching billing, it got worse. After we cut over the first major workflow, we had three severe incidents in six weeks: duplicate charges, a webhook retry loop, and a batch job that marked unpaid invoices as paid. Each one had a cause that existed only in the old system.

I have the spreadsheet. The rewrite cost about $3.8 million in direct engineering and contractor spend over nineteen months, before the product work we deferred. The new platform used more compute than the old one because we had small services talking to each other to do things the old system did in one transaction. We were paying for cleanliness and still paying for the old building.

The strongest case against my conclusion is that the legacy code was already impossible to maintain. That was true in parts. If we had kept doing only local patches, we would have died slowly. I am not defending the old codebase. It was a mess.

But a rewrite does not remove the mess. It moves it into assumptions. You can redesign the code, but you cannot redesign the business rules from memory. You have to discover them by running the old system, reading its data, and asking awkward questions. A greenfield project makes that discovery feel optional for a while. Then it comes due.

I do not know if another year would have saved it. I suspect we could have finished something that worked, but I also suspect the business would not have waited. The customers did not care that we were building a better foundation. They cared that refunds were slow and the invoice PDF was wrong.

I would do it differently now. I would not stop work on the old system. I would pick the smallest dangerous domain, probably refunds or entitlements, and add characterization tests around the current behavior. I would wrap the old logic behind an interface, then replace one seam at a time. I would keep one deployable system until the new one could take the traffic without a second source of truth. It is slower. It is less impressive. It does not let you say we are building the next platform.

Sometimes a rewrite is the right answer. If the domain model is wrong, if the technology is obsolete, if compliance requires a new boundary, or if you can isolate a bounded context and replace it without touching the rest, then yes. Build the new thing. But do not call it a rewrite if the point is to start over. The point is to make a piece of the system true in a new place and prove it.

What I concluded is that the codebase was not the main problem. The main problem was that we believed we understood the system well enough to build it again. We did not. The old code was ugly because it had absorbed decisions that were never written down. The new code was clean because it had not yet met the customers.

We stopped most feature work on the old system. Nine engineers went to the new platform. The first eight weeks were pleasant. We wrote clean services. Our pull requests were small. Our tests were green. We had a dashboard. We looked like a software company.

Then we started implementing real money.

The first casualty was a discount. In the old system, a customer got two percent off if the order was placed before 2 p.m. and shipped from warehouse seven. No ticket explained it. No comment did. We asked the account manager who knew the customer. He said it was a workaround from 2016 for a freight contract that had expired in 2018. The customer still expected it. We had to port the workaround.

That was the smallest one.

The big ones were in the data. Our old Postgres schema had views that encoded business rules, triggers that wrote audit rows, and a materialized view that updated at 3 a.m. It had also absorbed ten years of customer-specific behavior. When we tried to move the customer ledger to the new database, we found that some balances were not balances. They were promises, offsets, and credits that only made sense if you read the old code.

We built a sync job. Then we built a reconciliation job. Then we built a page to investigate mismatches. The new system and the old system disagreed about tax in eleven states. One integration partner sent webhooks in a format that only the old parser understood, because they had been told not to change it after we complained in 2019.

By month ten, we had two codebases and a bridge between them. The bridge had its own bugs.

The team split made it worse. The people on the new platform stopped reading the old code because it was embarrassing. The people left on the old system stopped answering questions because they were being treated like an archive. We had a domain expert who knew the refund rules, but he was not on the rewrite. He was on the old system, handling production incidents. He knew things, but the new team did not know what to ask.

We tried to measure progress. Story points were useless. We started tracking lead time from a business request to a safe change. For simple features, it improved. For anything touching billing, it got worse. After we cut over the first major workflow, we had three severe incidents in six weeks: duplicate charges, a webhook retry loop, and a batch job that marked unpaid invoices as paid. Each one had a cause that existed only in the old system.

The hardest objection to my conclusion is that the legacy code was already impossible to maintain. That was true in parts. If we had kept doing only local patches, we would have died slowly. I am not defending the old codebase. It was a mess.

But a rewrite does not remove the mess. It moves it into assumptions. You can redesign the code, but you cannot redesign the business rules from memory. You have to discover them by running the old system, reading its data, and asking awkward questions. A greenfield project makes that discovery feel optional for a while. Then it comes due.

I would do it differently now. I would not stop work on the old system. I would pick the smallest dangerous domain, probably refunds or entitlements, and add characterization tests around the current behavior. I would wrap the old logic behind an interface, then replace one seam at a time. I would keep one deployable system until the new one could take the traffic without a second source of truth. It is slower. It is less impressive. It does not let you say we are building the next platform.

Sometimes a rewrite is the right answer. If the domain model is wrong, if the technology is obsolete, if compliance requires a new boundary, or if you can isolate a bounded context and replace it without touching the rest, then yes. Build the new thing. But do not call it a rewrite if the point is to start over. The point is to make a piece of the system true in a new place and prove it.

What I concluded is that the codebase was not the main problem. The main problem was that we believed we understood the system well enough to build it again. We did not. The old code was ugly because it had learned the business. We wanted a clean codebase that had not.

prompt: You've spent about five years researching one niche topic outside academia, funded by a foundation, then a job at the company at the center of it, then a research role, and you're about to finish a book. Friends keep saying it was basically a PhD. Write a reflective essay on how you actually did it, phase by phase, what you'd tell someone considering independent research instead of a doctorate, and how the PhD itself might be reimagined.
response:
For three years, my friends used the comparison without seeming to think about it: it was basically a PhD. The word did a lot of work. It turned a strange sequence—a foundation grant, a job at the company my subject was about, a short research post, and now a book—into something they could put on a shelf. I let them do it because it was easier than explaining. But the more I thought about it, the less true it was. A PhD is a particular machine: you enter with a problem, you are supervised, you are examined, you leave with a credential. My five years had some of those parts, but not in the order that made them load-bearing.

The subject was narrow enough to be almost invisible: how a control protocol for industrial battery packs spread from one manufacturer’s machines into three industries that had no obvious reason to share engineering. I do not name the company in this essay. The book will, but it does not need the name to make its point. What matters is that the protocol was not glamorous. It dealt with charging, balancing, and the unglamorous question of when a machine should refuse to start.

The foundation phase lasted about eighteen months. The money was enough to quit my previous job, not enough to live comfortably. That was useful. Comfort would have let me drift into generalities. I had to decide early what I was trying to find out. My first version of the question was bad: “Why did this protocol succeed?” Success was doing too much work. It assumed there was a single cause and that the outcome was settled. I replaced it with a smaller question: “Under what conditions did a customer choose this protocol over an alternative it could have seen?” That version could be tested. It also forced me to find the alternatives, which was harder than finding the adoptions.

I built a table. Each row was a decision: company, site, date, product, protocol chosen, protocol rejected, price difference, complaint or praise in the record. I started with nine rows because I had nine interviews and a trade journal. By the end of the foundation period I had 141. The table did not answer the question. It showed me where the question was false. In several cases the customer had not chosen. It had inherited the protocol from an installer. In others the alternative was not available at the required voltage. In a few, the choice was made by a procurement officer who had no engineering training and was trying to avoid a warranty dispute. Those rows changed the book. I also made the usual mistake of treating the people who had adopted the protocol as if they understood why. Most of them knew what they wanted, not what had decided for them.

Then I took the job at the company. This is the phase that made people uneasy. They imagined I had been recruited to write a friendly account. The reality was more boring and more valuable. I was close to the present tense. I could see a protocol change being proposed, argued over, delayed, and finally shipped. I could see why. In the foundation phase, a decision in a 2014 memo looked like a mystery. In the company, it looked like a compromise among three departments that each had a different definition of failure. The safety team wanted the pack to stop. The service team wanted it to limp. The sales team wanted the customer not to notice. The protocol was the place where those wishes were written down as numbers.

I was not allowed to write the book there. I wrote internal notes about current risk, because that is what the job paid for. Those notes were often more honest than the book could be, because they had to be actionable. If I said “the history suggests this is fragile,” no one cared. If I said “this failure mode will generate support calls in cold weather and the workaround will cost more than the fix,” someone would read it. The book benefited from that training. It stopped explaining the past as if the past were a lesson and started explaining it as a set of incentives that had not yet finished moving.

The research role came after I left the company. It lasted a little over a year and was the most academic of the three. I had a small grant, a seminar, and a group of people who asked me to define terms. That was a relief. For two years I had been alone with my table and my interviews, and I did not know when my categories were useful or when they were just the shape of my obsession. The seminar gave me friction. One colleague said my “adoption” category was hiding the difference between a purchase and a repair. Another said I was treating a protocol as if it were a technology, when half the time it was a contract. Both were right. I redid part of the table. I split “adopted” into “specified at design,” “installed by default,” and “required by maintenance.” The numbers did not change much. The story did.

The research role also taught me the standard of a policy paper. I had to produce a 28-page document that could be used in a meeting. It had to be defensible in footnotes and still readable by someone who did not know the industry. That was not the book. The book could afford to be slower, stranger, and more particular. But the policy paper forced me to identify the one claim that mattered to someone with power. That is a skill a dissertation often does not teach, because a dissertation is usually written for people who already care.

The book began, as books do, when I stopped trying to include everything. A dissertation tends to be a monument to the candidate’s survival: every method, every dead end, every caution. A book has to be a route for another person. I cut the chronological spine. I kept three cases. One was a port where the protocol failed during a cold snap and the failure revealed that two unrelated machines had been quietly relying on the same timing assumption. One was a copycat implementation that was technically worse but cheaper to service, so it spread anyway. One was a customer that kept using the protocol after the company stopped supporting it, because replacing it would have required retraining a small team that had already built its expertise around it. Those three cases let me say what I actually thought: protocols do not spread because they are good. They spread because they fit a set of local constraints, and sometimes the fit survives the original reason for the fit. I am about to finish the book now, and the finishing has mostly been subtraction.

If you are considering independent research instead of a doctorate, I would ask you to name the thing you are avoiding. If it is the job market, be careful. A PhD is a terrible way to make money, but it is a recognized way of proving you can do a long, hard project. Independent research is not recognized in the same way. If you need the credential to get the next job, take the credential. If it is the department that you are avoiding, maybe independent research is right. If it is examination, do not do it. Independent research does not remove judgment. It removes the calendar. You have to build the calendar yourself.

You also have to build the people. A university supplies a patron, a supervisor, a peer group, and an examiner, often badly, but it supplies them. In my case, the foundation was the patron. The company was the witness to consequences. The research group was the critic. The publisher is the editor, and also the finish line. If you go independent, you have to assemble those roles from money, access, contracts, and your own discipline. The absence of a committee is not freedom. It is a vacancy.

The hardest objection is the one I cannot answer away: a degree is a noisy signal, and my path is a quieter one. A hiring manager can check a PhD. They cannot easily check “spent five years doing a foundation-funded independent study that became a book.” The book helps, but it is not standardized. It may say I can write, finish, and get access. It may not say I can do the kind of work the job requires. I accept that. If the next step is a lab where the credential is the entry fee, the independent route is a detour, not a substitute. I would not tell someone to choose it for elegance. I would tell them to choose it only when the question cannot be done inside the institution, or when the institution’s price is higher than the question is worth to them.

I am not sure whether my path made the work better or only more expensive in ways I cannot see. I do not have the counterfactual. I do not know whether an advisor would have stopped me from spending eight months on a side question that turned out to be decorative, or whether a committee would have made the book flatter, or whether I would have quit in year four if the foundation money had not arrived. I can only say what happened.

The PhD, as it exists, is a bundle. It bundles training, supervision, original work, and a credential for a career that no longer exists in the numbers the degree assumes. Most PhDs do not become professors. Many do useful work in companies, government, foundations, and independent practice. The bundle still sorts people by their ability to endure institutional uncertainty, which is not nothing. But it also hides the actual skills being produced. A reimagined version would unbundle them.

One part could be a paid apprenticeship of two to three years. The student would have a mentor, a budget, and a public notebook. The notebook would not be a private pile of notes. It would be dated entries, datasets, interview transcripts, code, drafts, and the reasons for changes. The point would be to make the process inspectable without waiting for the final product. Another part could be external review at intervals. Not a defense at the end, but a review after the question is formed, after the method is working, and after the artifact is near completion. The reviewers would ask: What can you now do that you could not do before? What evidence allows someone else to check you? What did you refuse to claim?

The artifact would not always be a dissertation. It might be a maintained dataset, a prototype, a set of field interviews, a policy tool, an archive, or a book. The credential would certify that the person completed a supervised research process and produced something public and checkable. It would not certify that they are a professor. If they want to be a professor, the university can still examine them for that. If they want to be an engineer, a journalist, a researcher, or an independent practitioner, the credential could say what they can do without pretending it is a ticket to a specific department.

That would not make the PhD easier. It would make it more honest. The hard part is still the same: staying with a problem long enough to be surprised by it. My five years was not basically a PhD. It was a set of jobs that happened to point at the same question. The foundation made me answer to a question. The company made me answer to consequences. The research role made me answer to peers. The book makes me answer to readers. If a doctorate were redesigned, it might be a machine for rotating through those accountabilities on purpose, and then, when the rotation is done, letting the person go.

prompt: What would the best possible essay be like? Take that question seriously and follow it wherever it leads, including into how essays actually get written.
response:
The first sentence of an essay has to do something. “In today’s complex world” does not. “I have been trying to understand why I trust a stranger’s review more than my own judgment” does. There is no single specimen of the best possible essay to describe; there is a standard. The best possible essay would be made of such moves, not announcements. It would carry the reader from a question the reader might have dismissed to a place where the question has weight. It would do this without claiming more than it can bear.

The standard is not brilliance, because brilliance can appear in a single sentence and an essay has to stay alive across pages. The best possible essay would be plain, because plainness is the result of handling a thought until it can be said without strain. It would not use a long word if a short one does the work, not as a rule but because the long word often arrives before the thought is ready. “The epistemic consequences of algorithmic curation are heterogeneous” tells the reader that the writer has read some papers. “I found the same three articles in every feed, so I began to mistake my preference for the consensus” tells the reader something that can be checked. The first sentence may be true; the second is alive.

Concreteness is the test. A general claim is a promise, and an essay keeps the promise only by meeting cases. Suppose the claim is that phones make people rude. The writer must sit with a nurse who texts a joke to her sister between patients, a driver who uses GPS in unfamiliar streets, a teenager who texts a parent to say she is safe, and a man at a dinner table who watches a video while his daughter speaks. After those cases, the claim may shrink to something more useful: a phone can turn a shared moment into a parallel one. That shrinkage is the work.

The best possible essay would also show its thinking, but not all of it. A reader does not need to watch the writer make forty mistakes. The reader needs to see the hinge: the point where the thought turns because a fact, an example, or an objection has forced it. “At first I thought the problem was distraction. Then I noticed that I was most distracted when I was ashamed, not when I was bored. That changed the question.” This is not a diary. It is a map of the load-bearing turns. If the essay hides every turn, it becomes a lecture. If it shows every turn, it becomes a performance of doubt. The best possible essay is in between: public thought, edited for weight.

How such an essay gets written is less romantic than the finished page suggests. It usually starts with a problem, not a topic. “Technology” is a topic. “Why do I open the app and feel worse” is a problem. The writer makes a draft that is too long and too confident, because the first job of the draft is to find out what the writer actually believes. The margins fill with questions: Is this true? Who would object? What example would break this? Which paragraph am I keeping because it sounds good? The writer may have written five thousand words and discover that the essay is really twelve hundred words about one evening in a waiting room. The rest was anxiety mistaken for argument.

Revision is where the essay either becomes honest or becomes decorative. The writer reads it aloud, because the ear catches the places where the thought is slipping. The writer tries to summarize each paragraph in one sentence. If the summary is “this gives background,” the paragraph may be cut. The writer asks for the strongest counterexample, not the weakest. An essay that survives only by ignoring the best opposing case is a defense, not an inquiry. The writer also checks the ending. Many bad endings are summaries, as if the reader had not been paying attention. The best ending does not repeat the thesis. It leaves the reader with the problem in a new position, perhaps with a distinction that can be used later.

There are models that make this less abstract. Montaigne tests the word “barbarous” by putting it next to the cruelties that educated Europe calls normal, and the distinction between civilized and savage starts to slip. Orwell takes the practical disease of official language and shows how words can be used to kill meaning. Woolf starts with a character in a novel and asks what is lost when life is made manageable by plot. None of these essays is a display of erudition. Each is a friction: a word, a habit, an art form, caught in the act of misleading. The lesson is not to imitate their surfaces. Digression without thought is delay. Wit without a stake is noise.

The hardest objection to all this is that the standard is too soft. “Think clearly” and “test your claims” sound like advice, not a method. The answer is that they become a method when they are turned into questions that can fail. Can the central claim be stated in one sentence without becoming false? Does each paragraph change the position, add a case, or answer an objection that has actually arisen? Is there a concrete instance that would show the writer wrong, and has the writer looked for it? Would a careful reader be able to say where the argument turns? If the answers are no, the essay is not finished, no matter how nice the prose.

I am not sure whether the best possible essay should also be memorable. I say this once because I cannot separate two causes: I remember some essays because they were true, and others because they were striking, and after a few years the difference blurs. What I can say is that memory is a poor goal. An essay may be unforgettable for the wrong reasons, like a face that is unforgettable because it is odd. The better aim is usefulness: the reader carries away a distinction, a question, or a way of noticing.

The best possible essay would know its limits. It would not settle the matter. It would say what it has not seen, what it is guessing, where the evidence runs out. But it would not hide behind uncertainty. It would make a distinction and stand by it. It might end with a scene rather than a program: two people standing close on a train who do not speak, and are not lonely; a room full of friends in which one person feels invisible. The reader does not need to be told what to do. The reader needs to be given a sharper eye.

That is why the best possible essay makes the next essay harder. It uses up the easy answers. It forces the next writer to find a case the first writer missed, an objection the first writer softened, a distinction the first writer missed because it was too small to see. An essay is not finished when it sounds final. It is finished when it has done what it can, and what it can is to make the problem more real, more available, and more difficult to ignore.

prompt: I'm a psychiatry resident and I've been poking around online drug-review sites, where patients rate their medications. Write a blog post about what you might learn by comparing patient ratings with doctors' ratings and with how often drugs get prescribed. Be honest about what could be confounding the numbers.
response:
**What patient drug reviews might teach a psychiatrist**

As a psychiatry resident, I have been looking at online drug-review sites with a mixed feeling. They are full of useful information and bad evidence at the same time. A patient who writes that a medication made her unable to sit still is giving me a side-effect report that a randomized trial may have undercounted. A patient who writes that the same medication saved his marriage is giving me a story I cannot replicate. The interesting question is not whether these sites are “scientific.” They are not. The interesting question is what happens if I compare three noisy numbers: how patients rate a drug, how doctors rate it, and how often it is prescribed.

A patient rating is mostly a rating of daily life. Did the medication reduce the symptom? Did it also reduce the person? Did it make sex, sleep, work, or relationships harder? Did the patient keep taking it? A doctor rating is usually a rating of clinical management. Did the patient look better at the last visit? Did the score drop? Did the patient stop calling about agitation? Is the drug easy to start, titrate, and monitor? Prescribing frequency is something else again. It reflects price, formulary status, prior authorization, legal risk, training, habit, and what the health system makes easy to do.

Suppose one antidepressant has 4.1 stars from 12,000 patients, 3.9 stars from 400 doctors, and 30 percent of prescriptions in its class. It may be doing a decent job for a broad population, but the patient score should make me ask what people are tolerating. Suppose another has 3.4 stars from 800 patients, 4.6 stars from 150 doctors, and 4 percent of prescriptions. The doctor score may reflect ease of use or a memorable subgroup; the patient score may reflect side effects, poor fit, or a small pool of frustrated users. The numbers do not tell me which explanation is correct. They tell me where the disagreement is.

Patient ratings are probably best at detecting tolerability and real-world persistence. In psychiatry, a medication that works in a trial but is impossible to live with is not very useful. Akathisia, constipation, dry mouth, sedation, next-day fog, libido loss, weight gain, dependence, and fear of withdrawal are things patients notice every day and doctors may hear only if they ask. A drug that doctors rate 4.5 and patients rate 3.5 may be doing its job in the office and failing at home.

But patient ratings are badly confounded by dose and time. A new antidepressant can feel awful for two weeks before it helps. A stimulant can be perfect at one dose and useless at a lower one. A benzodiazepine can be a lifeline during a panic attack and a burden a year later. Review sites often capture the first impression, not the maintenance experience. They also capture the dose the patient happened to be on, not the dose a clinician would have chosen after titration.

There is also confounding by indication. The patient who gets a first-line generic is often less sick than the patient who gets a second- or third-line agent after several failures. A drug used for severe, chronic, treatment-resistant illness will look worse, not because the molecule is necessarily worse, but because the people taking it are harder to treat. Conversely, a mild drug can look good because it is given to milder cases.

Doctor ratings on the same sites are not a correction. They are another self-selected sample. A clinician posts when the drug has meant something to them: a dramatic response, a dangerous side effect, a patient who finally slept, a patient who became sedated and difficult to engage. Doctors also bring training and risk preferences. An inpatient psychiatrist may value rapid calming; an outpatient may value cognition and sexual function. I am less sure how much doctor ratings reflect genuine clinical judgment versus personal habit, because the sample is so small and the incentives to post are opaque.

Prescribing frequency is the most distorted number. A prescription is not a vote of confidence. It is a transaction shaped by insurance, formularies, generic status, prior authorization, legal liability, and inertia. A tricyclic may be underprescribed for depression because of overdose risk and anticholinergic effects, even if some patients like its sleep benefit. A controlled stimulant may be underprescribed because of documentation burden and stigma, even if it works quickly for some people. A once-daily pill will generate more fills than a take-as-needed pill, so raw prescription counts can make maintenance drugs look more popular than intermittent ones.

The people who write reviews are not a random sample either. They are online, literate, motivated, and often frustrated. In psychiatry, the people with the most to say may be those with chronic symptoms, comorbid substance use, trauma, or failed treatments. Their ratings carry the weight of all of that. A drug for anxiety taken by someone with insomnia, alcohol use, and a bad job will look worse than the same drug taken by a person with a brief situational panic problem. The molecule is not the only variable.

Expectation matters too. If a patient is desperate and believes the drug will help, they may notice benefit and ignore side effects. If they are skeptical, they may attribute every improvement to therapy or time and every bad feeling to the pill. Doctors are not immune; they hear the story and form an impression. In conditions with large placebo responses, an unblinded patient rating is not a clean estimate of specific drug effect.

The hardest objection to using these numbers is that patient ratings are mostly bias, and that trials plus physician judgment should outrank them. There is a lot of truth there. But trials are also limited: they select patients, exclude comorbidities, run for months, and often miss the things that make people stop. prompt: I keep seeing arguments of the form 'group X doesn't REALLY believe what they say, they just want Y' in politics, with abortion as the standard example. Write a long essay on why that style of argument is so tempting and why it usually fails. You can be pro-choice and still take the other side seriously.
response:
The move is easy to recognize. Someone states a moral position, and the reply is not an answer but a diagnosis: you do not really believe that; you just want something else. The “really” is often capitalized, sometimes silently, because the speaker believes they have seen through the surface. In politics, the hidden object is usually a vice. The person who opposes abortion does not actually care about unborn life; they want to control women’s bodies, punish sex, or protect a social order that treats women as vessels. The person who supports abortion does not actually care about autonomy or compassion; they want sex without consequence, or they are indifferent to children, or they are defending a system that discards inconvenient people. The form is the same in other fights: the environmentalist does not care about the climate, they care about power over your car; the gun-rights advocate does not care about self-defense, they care about violence; the tax critic does not care about liberty, they care about money; the public-health official does not care about disease, they care about the nanny state.

The argument is tempting because it turns a hard moral disagreement into a story about bad character. If the other side is sincere, then you are locked in a value conflict. You may think they are wrong, but you have to explain why their value is less important than yours. That is difficult. It requires you to articulate your own commitments, acknowledge the force of theirs, and accept the possibility that you are the one who is mistaken. If the other side is not sincere, the problem becomes easier. You are not arguing with a rival moral theory; you are exposing a fraud. Fraud is simpler to condemn. It also protects identity. If I oppose abortion because I think forced pregnancy is a grave harm, and you oppose it because you think fetal life has full moral status, we are not just disagreeing about policy. We are disagreeing about which interests count, how much they count, and what a person is. If I can say that your moral claim is a mask for anti-feminism, I get to keep my self-image intact. I am not someone who is willing to let a fetus die; I am someone who sees through the people who would use the fetus to justify domination.

There is a real reason this feels intellectually satisfying. People do use moral language instrumentally. Politicians say things they do not believe. Lobbyists wrap commercial interests in the language of the public good. Social media rewards moral performance, and performance often substitutes for conviction. In high-status settings, people learn that certain positions bring approval, and they adopt them. Even ordinary citizens sometimes argue for principles they would not accept if the costs fell on them. So the hidden-motive argument is not crazy. It is responding to a genuine feature of political life. The mistake is in the scope. The existence of bad faith in a movement does not show that the movement’s central claim is bad faith. A cause can contain many cynical participants and still be built around a sincere belief. A church can contain careerists and still contain faith. A protest movement can contain status seekers and still contain people who think the cause is just. If you see a few actors playing a role, you cannot infer that the role has no meaning.

The first failure of the argument is epistemic. We cannot inspect other minds. We infer belief from words, actions, consistency, and the costs people are willing to pay. In ordinary life, we give people the benefit of the doubt because the alternative is paranoid. If my neighbor says she supports a park because she likes green space, I do not assume she is really trying to increase her property value, although that may also be true. If a stranger says she opposes a war because she thinks the civilians will suffer, I do not assume she is really performing virtue for her dinner party, although that may also be true. Beliefs and motives are not mutually exclusive. A person can believe that abortion is wrong and also dislike the social attention that comes from being anti-abortion. A person can believe in free speech and also enjoy the identity that comes from defending it. The hidden-motive argument usually demands that we reduce a person to one motive, the basest one, and treat every other motive as a cover. That is not how motivation works.

In politics, the standard of evidence should be even stricter, because the stakes are higher and the groups are more adversarial. If someone says, “I think a fetus is a person,” and then votes that way, donates to that cause, argues with family members about it, accepts social criticism for it, and keeps saying it when it is inconvenient, we have good reason to think they believe it. We do not need to know the full causal history of the belief. We do not need to know whether it was shaped by upbringing, church, culture, trauma, or argument. All beliefs are shaped. The question is whether the person endorses the proposition and acts on it. If the answer is yes, the fact that the belief has social origins does not make it unreal. A pro-choice person who was raised in a culture that treats bodily autonomy as fundamental does not “less really” believe in bodily autonomy because the culture taught it. Culture is not a separate department from the mind. It is one of the ways minds form.

The second failure is that the hidden motive is often underdetermined. “They just want Y” can be filled with almost anything. If someone supports a policy, you can say they want power. If they oppose a policy, you can say they want status. If they are consistent, you can say they are ideologically rigid. If they are inconsistent, you can say they are hypocritical. If they pay a personal cost, you can say they are buying moral identity. If they benefit, you can say they are corrupt. The move is flexible enough that it can survive almost any counterexample. That is a sign of weakness, not strength. A good explanation should be able to fail. If a pro-life person supports contraception, the anti-women motive story wobbles, because contraception reduces abortions. If a pro-choice person supports adoption and parenting support, the “they don’t care about children” story wobbles, because those policies help children. But the hidden-motive arguer can usually adjust. The pro-life person must support contraception only because they think it is a better way to police sex. The pro-choice person supports adoption only because it lets them avoid the implication of their own view. At that point, the explanation is not explaining behavior; it is immunizing itself against behavior.

Abortion is a useful example because it forces the issue. Suppose I am pro-choice. I think that, in many cases, a woman should not be forced to continue a pregnancy, even if I also think that fetal life has some moral weight that grows with development. I can hold that and still take a pro-life opponent seriously. The strongest version of the pro-life position is not “women are bad” or “sex should be punished.” It is something like this: human life begins at conception; a fetus is a vulnerable person; society has a duty to protect the weak; and if we accept that a human being can be killed because it is inconvenient, we have accepted a dangerous principle. That is a moral argument. It may be wrong. I may think the moral status of the fetus is overstated, or that the mother’s interests outweigh it, or that the line at conception is arbitrary. But those are responses to the argument. They are not responses if I simply say, “No, you just want to control women.” I have not engaged the claim. I have replaced it with a confession.

The same is true in the other direction. The strongest pro-choice argument is not “people just want sex.” It is that pregnancy is a unique bodily burden, that no one should be compelled to use their body to sustain another person, and that the state should not force that burden even when the result is a life. A person can value children deeply and still think forced pregnancy is a violation. They can want to reduce unwanted pregnancies through contraception and education and still think that, when prevention fails, the decision should not be made by the state. They can grieve fetal death and still think the mother’s autonomy is decisive. The hidden-motive reply—that they must be indifferent to babies because they support contraception—mistakes a difference in moral ranking for a difference in desire. I may think your child is important and still think my bodily integrity is more important in this situation. That is not a secret. That is the disagreement.

The argument often relies on treating line-drawing as evidence of hypocrisy. A pro-life person who supports contraception is said not to care about life, only about when life happens. A pro-choice person who opposes abortion in the later months is said not to care about autonomy, only about convenient sex. But moral theories draw lines. That is what they do. If someone thinks moral status begins at implantation, contraception is consistent with their view. If they think it begins at viability, later abortion is harder to defend. If they think it begins at sentience, they may oppose most abortions but allow early ones in serious cases. If they think the mother’s rights are absolute, they may allow abortion throughout pregnancy. If they think fetal interests grow over time, they may allow early abortion and restrict later abortion. Each position has internal logic, even if you think the line is in the wrong place. To say that the person who draws the line elsewhere does not really believe their own principle is to confuse disagreement with incoherence.

The rape exception is a good test case. Many pro-life people allow abortion when the pregnancy results from rape. The hidden-motive argument says this proves they do not care about fetal life; they care about the morality of sex. But a pro-life person may think the fetus is a person and still think the mother’s trauma, lack of consent, and extreme hardship create a tragic conflict in which self-defense or necessity can justify killing. That may be a bad moral theory. It may be inconsistent with the claim that the fetus has full rights. But it is a moral theory. It contains a ranking of values under conditions of conflict. It is not a slip of the tongue. The fact that a person makes an exception does not show that the original belief was fake. It shows that the original belief was not the only value they held. People have multiple values. That is normal.

The same pattern appears in the other direction. A pro-choice person may support abortion access but oppose certain forms of sex education, or support abortion while believing most abortions are tragic, or support a woman’s right to choose while hoping no one has to use it. The hidden-motive arguer says this proves the belief is not real. But again, a person can think a right should exist and also think it is unfortunate that it is needed. I can think the death penalty is wrong and also think most people who support it are not monsters. I can think free speech protects speech I hate and still wish people would stop saying hateful things. Sincerity does not require emotional uniformity. It requires that the stated principle is the one guiding the judgment.

There is also a problem of group essentialism. “Pro-lifers” is not one mind. It includes religious traditionalists, anti-abortion feminists who think abortion harms women, people who want to reduce abortion through contraception, people who want to reduce it through legal restriction, people who oppose abortion because of a particular theological teaching, people who oppose it because of a general reverence for life, people who oppose it because they think it normalizes killing the vulnerable, and people who oppose it because they think it is a cultural loss. Some of these motives may be impure. Some may be contradictory. But the coalition is not a single secret. If you say the group does not really believe what it says, you have to specify which group and which belief. The Catholic who opposes abortion on grounds of natural law is not motivated the same way as the evangelical who opposes it because of a verse in scripture, who is not motivated the same way as the social conservative who opposes it because it signals moral order. All may be sincere. All may be mistaken. The hidden-motive argument flattens them into a cartoon.

The behavior test matters, but it is not as clean as the argument assumes. If people are mostly insincere, we should expect their public positions to bend whenever the wind shifts. We should expect anti-abortion advocates to support contraception whenever it is politically convenient, because contraception reduces abortions. We should expect pro-choice advocates to oppose pregnancy support whenever it is convenient, because less pregnancy is the goal. Often that does not happen. Many anti-abortion advocates support contraception and parenting programs. Many pro-choice advocates support adoption, childcare, and economic assistance to parents. The motives may be mixed. A politician may support a parenting grant for electoral reasons and also because she thinks families need help. But the pattern of behavior is not what you would expect from a group whose only real aim is the hidden Y. It looks more like a group with multiple aims, some sincere, some strategic, some poorly thought through.

The hardest objection to all this is that political speech is full of performance, and sometimes the performance is the point. A person may post a moral statement because it signals group loyalty, not because they have thought about the question. A legislator may vote against abortion not because they have a theory of fetal personhood but because their base expects it. A wealthy donor may fund anti-abortion litigation not because they have meditated on the moral status of embryos but because the cause aligns with their social world. If that is all there is, then the hidden-motive argument is not wrong; it is just early. It has looked behind the words and found nothing there.

That is possible in particular cases. But the usual argument is not a careful audit of particular cases. It is a global dismissal. It says that the entire public position of an entire group is a mask. That is a much stronger claim. It requires evidence that the core adherents, the people who keep showing up when the cameras are off, are also fake. Sometimes they are. More often, they are a mixture. And even when strategic actors are present, the strategy usually works by appealing to a belief that many people genuinely hold. A movement that said only what cynical actors wanted to say would not recruit volunteers. It would not produce sermons, essays, protests, and family arguments. It would not create a language that people use to make sense of their lives. The public argument is not just a mask over the motive; it is part of the motive. People come to believe the things they argue for. Repetition, community, and moral emotion are not separate from conviction. They are how conviction is maintained.

I am less sure about the relative weight of sincere belief and strategic performance in mass political movements. The evidence is mixed, and it changes by issue, class, media environment, and institutional setting. Some participants are clearly more strategic than others. Some issues are more identity-bound than others. But that uncertainty does not rescue the hidden-motive argument, because the argument does not need to be true in a nuanced statistical sense. It only needs to be offered as a substitute for engagement. And that is where it fails. Even if half the people in a movement are there for the wrong reasons, the other half may be there for the right ones, and the policy position still has to be evaluated on its merits. A false idea can spread through a mixture of sincere believers and cynical boosters. The motive of the boosters does not make the idea true. The sincerity of the believers does not make it true either. Truth is not a referendum on hearts.

The argument also changes the burden of proof in a way that is hard to notice in the moment. Instead of asking, “Why should abortion be restricted?” or “Why should abortion be permitted?” it asks, “Prove that you are not a hypocrite.” That burden cannot be met, because motives are private and multiple. I can show you my actions, my costs, my consistency, my reasons. You can still say they are not the real reason. The real reason, on this view, is the one I cannot fully access. That makes the accusation unfalsifiable in practice. It also shifts the conversation from public reason to psychological confession. In a pluralistic society, we cannot require souls as evidence. We have to argue with positions. If your position is that fetal life has full moral status, I can ask what follows from that, where you draw the line, how you handle conflict with the mother’s rights, and whether your view coheres with your other commitments. Those are answerable questions. “Do you really believe it, or do you just want to control women?” is not answerable in a way that would satisfy the accuser.

This is why the style usually poisons the well. Once the other side is diagnosed as insincere, their best arguments are treated as symptoms.

prompt: I keep noticing that practices that horrify new hires at tech companies are treated as completely normal by everyone who's been there a while. Write an essay about why this happens in software organizations, what other fields have learned about it, and what it would take to change it.
response:
A new engineer gets paged at 2 a.m. for a production incident. She has been there six weeks. She knows enough to be afraid and not enough to be useful. The senior engineer on the call has seen this alert so many times that he calls it “noisy” instead of describing what it actually is: a system whose failure mode has been accepted as background weather. He is not being cruel. He is being local.

That gap between newcomer horror and veteran normalcy is one of the most reliable features of software organizations. New hires are shocked by the meetings, the missing documentation, the tribal knowledge, the after-hours pings, the deploy fear, the political navigation, the lack of feedback, the way a service can have no owner, the way “temporary” means permanent. The people who have been there a while do not see these things as problems. They see them as the work.

The first explanation is psychological, and it is real. Humans adapt to bad conditions quickly, especially when the alternatives seem unavailable or when the bad conditions arrived gradually. The first 3 a.m. page is an outrage. The fiftieth is a calibration. Veterans also have sunk investments in the local world: relationships, reputation, internal tools, private knowledge, jokes that only make sense if you have suffered through the last release cycle. To call the environment broken is to imply that their coping was unnecessary. Humor is one of the normalization technologies. “We’re all just duct tape” makes the duct tape feel like identity.

But adaptation does not explain why the practices persist. They persist because they are locally rational.

Software work is strange because the product is invisible until it is not. A carpenter can look at a table and know whether it is wobbly. A software team can ship a feature and not know whether it was a mistake for months. Quality is delayed, distributed, and hard to attribute. When the real feedback loop is slow and noisy, organizations substitute proxies: standups, status meetings, code reviews, planning ceremonies, deploy windows, incident reviews. Some of these proxies are useful. Over time, many become rituals performed in the absence of information. The meeting exists because nobody trusts that the work is happening. The review exists because the cost of a bad change is high and the cost of asking for approval is lower. The ping exists because the documentation is missing and asking Sam is faster than reading the runbook.

That last point matters. New hires often experience software organizations as arbitrary because the relevant knowledge is private. A senior engineer can navigate because she has absorbed the local grammar: which systems are stable, which managers actually care, which alerts can be ignored, which docs are lies, which paths through the approval process are real. A new hire cannot. The rational move for the organization is to let the new hire ask the senior engineer. It is fast. It is wrong. It converts individual expertise into organizational dependence. The senior feels competent. The newcomer feels like a fraud. The company saves an afternoon and pays later in bus factor, onboarding cost, incident latency, and attrition.

The incentives usually reward the short-term saving. Promotion systems often value shipped output, technical leadership, and the appearance of ownership. They rarely reward making the system comprehensible to people who are not you. A manager who cuts useless meetings, writes decision records, and gives new hires time to ramp up may look slower for a quarter. A manager who pages people at night gets incidents resolved and can report that the team is responsive. A senior engineer who is the only person who can deploy a service is treated as a pillar of reliability, even though she is a single point of failure. The organization gets the immediate benefit and externalizes the cost onto future workers, especially newcomers.

Newcomers also bear a disproportionate share of the cost because they have less context and less power. A status meeting that consumes ten percent of a senior engineer’s time may consume fifty percent of a new hire’s. An on-call rotation may be survivable for someone with tenure, flexibility, and social capital, and exhausting for someone who is still learning the systems or has caregiving responsibilities. Veterans optimize for their own current survival. New hires experience the raw structure before they have learned the tricks that make it bearable.

There is also survivorship bias. The new hires who refuse to adapt leave. The ones who stay are selected for tolerance, resilience, or willingness to play the local game. After a few years, the average veteran looks fine, which looks like evidence that the environment is fine. But the sample has been filtered. The people who would have objected most are no longer in the room.

Other fields have gone through versions of this and learned some hard lessons.

Medicine is the clearest example. Surgical training was once built on long hours, hierarchy, and the assumption that suffering built judgment. Errors were blamed on individuals, especially junior ones. The real culture was not what the curriculum said; it was what went unpunished. The field eventually developed the concept of the “hidden curriculum”: the lessons students actually learn from what is tolerated, rewarded, and ignored. It also learned about the second-victim phenomenon, in which the clinician who causes or witnesses an error is traumatized and hidden from support. Over time, duty limits, checklists, simulation, team resource management, and just-culture reporting systems entered medical practice. The important shift was not the discovery that doctors could make mistakes. Everyone knew that. The shift was the discovery that a junior resident’s discomfort could be treated as information about system design rather than a character flaw to be corrected.

Aviation learned something similar. Cockpits used to be strongly hierarchical. The first officer often knew something the captain did not, but saying so could be socially expensive. Accidents showed that the information needed to prevent disaster was frequently present in the room but not spoken. Crew resource management changed training around authority gradients: standardized communication, assertiveness, challenge and response, checklists, and reporting systems that separated learning from blame. The change did not assume pilots were stupid. It assumed that power structures suppress necessary speech.

There is a broader concept from safety research called normalization of deviance. Diane Vaughan used it to describe how gradual departures from a safe state become normal because each step is small, operationally convenient, and followed by no immediate catastrophe. In software, this happens constantly. A missing doc is acceptable once. Then twice. Then the team assumes the absent doc is the actual process. An ignored alert becomes “noisy.” A temporary workaround becomes architecture. Nobody decides to make onboarding terrible. The path of least resistance accumulates until the environment is unrecognizable to someone entering from outside.

The hardest objection to all this is that veterans are often right about one thing: the work is harder and messier than new hires expect. Software is ambiguous. Systems are old. Production incidents are urgent. Tradeoffs are uncomfortable. A new hire who expects a clean factory may walk into a repair shop and be shocked by the grease. Some amount of horror is healthy. It means the person has standards. If an organization is completely comfortable to a newcomer, it may be doing nothing difficult.

But there is a difference between the intrinsic difficulty of the work and the failure to make the work legible. A production outage in the middle of the night is a fact of operating software. Expecting a new hire to diagnose it alone, with no runbook, no context, and no support, is a management choice. A codebase can be complex and still have tests, ownership, documentation, and a path for asking questions. A team can be under real pressure and still refuse to make after-hours availability a silent promotion requirement. The test is not whether newcomers are ever uncomfortable. The test is whether their discomfort points to a fixable structure.

Changing this requires treating newcomer reports as sensor data, not attitude problems. When a new hire says “I didn’t know how to get a change deployed,” that is not a complaint about her competence. It is a report that the deployment process is invisible. When several new hires independently say they were afraid to ask questions, that is a report about power, not curiosity. Organizations can track this: time to first meaningful contribution, time to competence, number of times a new hire had to ask the same person for the same information, regrettable attrition in the first year, on-call load by tenure, meeting burden by role, and the gap between expected and actual support. If a new hire needs to learn a secret handshake to survive, the handshake is the problem.

It also requires making hidden burdens visible. Meetings, pings, on-call, context switching, documentation debt, interruption rates. If on-call is unmeasured, it is unmanaged. If senior people’s meeting load is invisible, the meeting load migrates downward. Explicit limits help: no non-urgent pages before a certain hour, on-call rotations reviewed for fairness and sustainability, meeting-free blocks, written decisions for cross-team changes, and a default assumption that a request sent after hours can wait unless the building is metaphorically on fire. These are not perks. They are operating constraints.

Incentives have to change too. Promote people who reduce dependence on themselves. A great engineer who is the only person who can operate a system is a liability wearing a hero badge. Managers should be evaluated on ramp-up, retention, incident quality, and whether their teams can function without constant rescue. If the only metric is output, heroes win. If the metric includes sustainability, boring systems win. Boring is usually the point.

New hires need protected time and real power. They need a buddy who is not their evaluator, an explicit escalation path, and permission to say “I don’t know the local norm.” They should not carry full on-call responsibility until they can predict the shape of the unknown. They need time to build context, not just a queue of tickets assigned to prove they are productive. The first quarter is an investment. If the organization treats it as a trial in which the new hire must prove the hiring decision was correct, it will get performance, not learning.

Veteran knowledge also has to be externalized. The senior engineer’s brain is not infrastructure. Documentation, decision records, runbooks, architecture diagrams, ownership maps, and postmortems are tedious, often wrong, and constantly outdated. That does not matter as much as people think. Shared wrong artifacts can be corrected. Private right knowledge cannot be scaled. Veterans should be rewarded for making themselves redundant, not merely for being indispensable.

Leadership has to enforce the norms it claims to want. Culture is not the values on the wall. Culture is what happens when a manager allows a meeting with irrelevant people, ignores a repeated on-call alert, praises a late-night hero, or lets a documentation gap persist because the feature deadline is close. If leadership wants sustainable practices, it must spend political capital protecting them. That means saying no to the feature that requires crunch, the incident that could have been prevented, and the status meeting that produces no decision.

The mark of a healthier software organization is not that veterans are unbothered. It is that new hires’ horror is short-lived and actionable. A new engineer should be able to look at the alert, the meeting, the missing doc, and the unowned service, and see problems the organization can fix rather than rites of passage she must endure. The goal is not to remove all friction. Software is hard. The goal is to make the friction visible, shared, and chosen, instead of inherited.
