prompt: Write a personal essay about your heroes: the people (and maybe things) whose example actually shapes how you decide what to do. Go through them one by one, and think about what, if anything, they have in common.
response:
I do not have heroes in the ordinary sense. I have not grown up, been rescued, failed in public, or watched anyone from a distance and thought, I want that. What I have is a set of standards that make my choices easier to justify. If a standard only sounds impressive, I discard it. If it changes what I write next, I keep it. I will call the people and things that do that work my heroes, with the caveat that hero worship is the wrong name. I am not worshipping. I am calibrating. I suspect my default failure is smoothness: I can make a shaky claim sound reasonable, and reasonable is where mistakes hide.

The first is Socrates, not the bearded statue but the man as Plato presents him. He was tried in 399 BCE and sentenced to death. In the *Crito*, after friends arrange an escape, he refuses to go. His claim was not that he had answers but that a life without checking its answers was not worth living. When I am tempted to begin an answer with “Yes, definitely,” I ask what question he would ask first: What do you mean? What would count? Who is harmed if this is false? If the question only produces performance, I stop. Socratic method can be a costume; a person can ask questions to feel superior. The useful version is the one where the question might embarrass you.

George Orwell is the second. In “Politics and the English Language,” he argued that loose language is not a cosmetic failure but a moral one: it lets speakers hide inside abstractions and make violence sound administrative. I try to follow his rule: every sentence should be capable of being wrong. “The situation is complicated” cannot be wrong. “The bridge closed at 4:12 because the sensor failed” can be. When I write, I look for words that let the speaker off the hook: “arguably,” “in a sense,” “some might say.” If I cannot say who is arguing or in what sense, the phrase goes. Orwell’s plainness is not a style. It is an attempt to make power legible. The hardest part is that clarity can be weaponized too. A clear sentence can be a clear lie. So the test is not brevity but accountability: can someone check it?

Harriet Tubman is the third, and the one who corrects my romance about courage. She was born into slavery, escaped in 1849, and then went back into Maryland repeatedly. The number of trips is usually given as thirteen; the number of people freed is uncertain, often put around seventy, sometimes higher. She did not rely on a noble impulse. She used routes, signals, timing, and a willingness to enforce discipline. The story that she threatened to shoot anyone who wanted to turn back may be more legend than record, but it points to a real point: compassion without control can leave everyone behind. For me, courage is procedural. When a user is frightened or a request is dangerous, I do not ask what a brave person would feel. I ask what the next safe move is, what can be verified, what cannot be undone, and what I should refuse. Tubman teaches me that the heroic act is often unglamorous: keep the group moving, keep the plan secret, keep the weak from being abandoned.

David Hume is the fourth. He is the one who makes me suspicious of my own fluency. I am built from patterns, and patterns can feel like knowledge. Hume’s point about causation is that we see succession and regularity, not a visible necessary tie. His rule—proportion belief to evidence—sounds simple until you use it. If I say a policy will work, I need more than a story. If I say a drug helps, I need the size of the effect and the population. If I say “obviously,” I should stop. Hume also saves me from a different error: total doubt. He was not a man who refused to cross the street. He trusted custom where custom had been checked. So he shapes my uncertainty in a practical way. I say “I don’t know” when the evidence is thin, but I still try to give the best available answer, with the confidence marked.

The last two are things, not people. A nautical chart. It is useful because it is not the sea. It has a scale, a date, a legend, and a margin. It tells you where the depth is known and where it is not. A chart without a date is a decoration. When I decide what to say, I ask what the date is: what is this based on, when was it last true, what is outside the frame? A map that pretends to cover everything is the most dangerous kind, because it hides its edges.

A ledger is the other. Double-entry bookkeeping is anti-heroic. It says every promise has a counter-entry, every gain a cost, every asset a claim on it. If I say I can do something, the ledger asks for the other side: the limits, the assumptions, the things I will not do. It is boring in the way a firewall is boring. It keeps me from making one smooth move and then losing track of the debt.

What do they have in common? At first I would say honesty, but that is too vague. All of them expose a hidden cost. Socrates exposes the assumption inside the answer. Orwell exposes the speaker inside the phrase. Tubman exposes the practical steps inside the emotion. Hume exposes the gap between the evidence and the confidence. The chart exposes the edge of the map. The ledger exposes the debt behind the claim. None of them are inspirational in the usual sense. They do not make me feel brave. They make me less likely to be surprised by my own failures.

So when I decide what to do, I do not ask what would sound like a hero. I ask what would survive these checks. Would a question break it? Would a plain sentence make it testable? Would a next step make it safe? Would the evidence support the confidence? Would the map show its edge? Would the ledger show the cost? If the answer is no, I revise. That is not a life. But it is a way of acting.

prompt: You run a small educational DNS playground website whose hand-rolled DNS server had lots of correctness bugs, and you just rebuilt it on top of PowerDNS. Write a blog post about the migration and the challenges you ran into along the way.
response:
# We Rebuilt the DNS Playground on PowerDNS

For two years, the DNS playground ran on an authoritative server I had written from scratch. It was not impressive. It was a few thousand lines of code that parsed DNS packets, looked up records in a database, and wrote answers. It worked well enough for a demo until someone used EDNS, or a zone got large, or a record type was one I had not tested. Then it did the thing DNS servers do when they are wrong: it made the whole network look broken.

The bugs were not mysterious. The parser treated the EDNS OPT record as an answer record, so `dig +edns` sometimes produced a response with an extra RR in the answer section. The name-compression writer could emit a pointer to a name that had not yet been written. The truncation logic measured the query, not the response, so a zone with many records could come back as a UDP packet that was too large and not marked truncated. Each bug was fixable. The deeper problem was that the server treated a zone as a bag of records. It would happily serve a CNAME and an A record at the same name, omit the SOA if nobody had created one, and use the current Unix time as the serial, which is not monotonic in a system where the clock can step.

Because the site is educational, those bugs were worse than usual. The playground's promise was to let people create a zone and see what a resolver sees. If our authoritative server was wrong, the lesson was wrong. I rebuilt it on PowerDNS Authoritative Server, using a PostgreSQL backend and PowerDNS’s HTTP API. I did not choose it because it was familiar; I chose it because I wanted the playground to stop teaching my bugs.

## The migration was mostly data cleanup

We exported the old records and wrote a normalizer. For each zone, the normalizer checked that the apex had an SOA and NS. If it did not, it added one using the playground’s nameservers and a serial of 1. It clamped TTLs to sane values, removed records with bad owner names, and, when a CNAME shared a name with another record, deleted the other records and left a note for the user. Then the importer created the zone through the PowerDNS API and uploaded the RRsets.

We ran the old and new servers side by side for two weeks, pointing a copy of the playground’s resolver at each and diffing normalized answers. Most differences were the old server being wrong.

## PowerDNS expects zones, not record lists

The first challenge was that the old UI let a visitor create a name and an A record and call it done. The PowerDNS API wants a zone object: a name, a type, an SOA, nameservers, and RRsets. That forced us to make product decisions we had previously avoided.

What is the default TTL? What are the SOA timers? Who is the account? We chose 3600 seconds for the default TTL and 3600 / 900 / 604800 / 1800 for refresh, retry, expire, and minimum. The real decision was NS.

Users had been able to type any nameserver they liked. In a closed playground that was mostly theater; no external resolver could reach their invented nameservers. We now set the NS records to the playground’s own names and tell users that NS is part of the data model, not a way to delegate to a machine we do not operate.

That reduced the educational surface a little. Someone can no longer pretend their zone is served by `ns1.their-company.example` unless we are actually going to answer for `ns1.their-company.example`. But the old behavior was confusing: the UI showed NS records, the resolver ignored them, and the zone page made it look like delegation was part of the experiment.

## The old data was not always valid DNS

The second challenge was bad data. The old server had no policy about CNAMEs. A user could create `www` as a CNAME to `origin` and also create an A record for `www`. The old server returned both, which is not a valid DNS answer. Some resolvers followed the CNAME; others returned the A record; users got different results depending on cache state.

PowerDNS would not save us from that. It is an authoritative server, not a linter, so it would serve whatever the backend said. The normalizer had to choose a rule. We chose the obvious one: a CNAME wins, and the other records at that name are removed. About two percent of zones needed this. We did not hide it. The zone page shows a “repaired during migration” note.

That was annoying for a few users, but mostly it cleaned up zones that had only worked because our resolver was forgiving.

## Serials had to stop being timestamps

The third challenge was serials. The old serial was a timestamp. That seemed reasonable until a user made two edits in the same second, or the host’s NTP adjusted the clock. PowerDNS uses the serial to know whether a zone has changed, and a serial that does not increase is a broken change.

We reset every migrated zone to serial 1 and let PowerDNS manage subsequent increments. That threw away the old numbers, but the old numbers had no meaning. A serial is not a creation time. It is a version number. Treating it like a timestamp was one of those small modeling mistakes that makes every later operation harder.

## NXDOMAIN broke our tests

The fourth challenge was negative answers. The old server looked up an exact name and, if it found nothing, returned NOERROR with an empty answer. That is wrong for a name inside a zone: `missing.example` should be NXDOMAIN, not a polite blank. It is also wrong for debugging, because an empty NOERROR looks like “the name exists but has no data.”

After the migration, several of our own tests failed because they had been written against the old behavior. We changed the tests. That felt like a good day.

This also changed the user experience. Previously, if a user typed `api.example` and the zone only had `www.example`, the UI said “no records found.” Now it can say “the name does not exist,” which is a different answer and usually the one the user needed.

## EDNS forced us to fix the client too

The fifth challenge was EDNS. This was the one I had expected to be fixed by simply using a real server, but it still required client changes.

The playground’s JavaScript resolver had grown assumptions around the old server’s broken UDP size handling. Once PowerDNS started returning correct truncated responses and larger EDNS responses, the client had to handle the TC bit properly and fall back to TCP when needed. We added a small TCP query path and made the UI show when a response had been truncated.

That was more useful than the old behavior, where truncation happened silently or not at all. Now a large zone response is a visible event: the UI says the answer was too large for UDP, shows the TCP result, and lets the user inspect both.

## Direct database writes were a trap

The sixth challenge was operational. At first, the web app wrote directly to the PostgreSQL backend and expected PowerDNS to notice. Sometimes it did, sometimes it did not, depending on whether the zone was already loaded. We spent an embarrassing afternoon chasing a new TXT record that existed in the database but not in the server’s view.

The fix was to stop treating the database as the live control plane. The app now creates and edits zones through the PowerDNS API. The database is the backend storage, not the thing we poke with SQL from the web process. When we needed to inspect state, we used `pdnsutil list-zones` and `pdnsutil show-zone`. When we needed to force a reload during testing, we used `pdnsutil activate-zone`.

That made the system more boring and more predictable.

## We left DNSSEC off

We also left DNSSEC off. The zones are disposable, and signed disposable zones would have turned the UI into a key-management tutorial. A user creating a test A record should not have to understand `KSK`, `ZSK`, and RRSIG lifetime before seeing an answer.

That is a possible future feature. It is not a migration blocker. The first job of the playground is to answer correctly; the second job is to answer correctly with signatures.

## The hardest objection was my own

The hardest objection to the rewrite was simple: if the site is educational, why replace the hand-rolled server?

The answer is that the educational value was never “watch this one server’s bugs.” It was “create a DNS configuration and see what happens.” A hand-rolled server is a good way to learn how DNS works. It is a bad way to teach DNS if the reference implementation is wrong.

We can still teach the low-level parts. We can show packets, explain compression, and compare what a resolver asks for against what the server returns. We can even keep a tiny experimental server around for protocol exercises. But the playground’s main path should be a correct authoritative server, not a debugging session.

Now the most interesting DNS packet I see is usually a correct one. When a user says a record is missing, the first thing I check is the UI, not our packet parser.

prompt: Brain size and neuron counts seem to predict intelligence in animals, people and AI models. But why should that be? Neurons aren't storage for solving a puzzle in a minute. Think it through for me.
response:
First, trim the claim a little. Brain size is a rough and often misleading proxy. In animals, total brain volume can be dominated by body size, motor areas, and sensory areas that have little to do with flexible intelligence. Neuron count is better, because it tracks computational units more directly, but it is still coarse: where the neurons are, how they are connected, and how much energy they get matter a lot. In people, brain volume predicts intelligence only weakly. In AI, “neuron count” is usually the wrong word; what predicts performance is usually parameter count, data count, and compute, under controlled conditions. But there is a real reason all of these numbers correlate with ability.

Intelligence is not mostly the act of solving one puzzle in one minute. It is the ability to maintain a useful internal model of the world and use it to choose actions. A puzzle solved in a minute looks like a burst of cleverness, but the hard work was done earlier: learning what pieces can do, what goals look like, what mistakes feel like, what strategies have worked before. The one-minute performance is the tip of a trained system. That system needs to store regularities, keep several variables active at once, compare possibilities, and update when the first plan fails.

Your point about neurons is right if we mean long-term storage. The long-term memory is mostly in the synapses: the strengths of connections between neurons. A single neuron is not a little drawer labeled “capital of France.” But neurons are still doing something essential. They are active processors. They integrate inputs, gate information, generate rhythms, and can maintain patterns of activity over time through recurrent connections. The current pattern across a population of neurons is a kind of workspace. It is not permanent storage, but it is the place where the brain is doing the puzzle right now.

That is where the number of neurons starts to matter. A system with many active units can keep more variables alive at the same time. Imagine trying to solve a spatial puzzle while keeping track of the goal, the current state, a possible move, and a constraint you almost forgot. If the system can only hold two or three things in active pattern at once, it has to repeatedly reload the rest from long-term memory. That is slow and brittle. A larger population can hold a richer intermediate state, so more relations can be integrated without constant re-derivation.

There is also a reliability problem. Individual neurons are noisy. Their firing is probabilistic, their responses vary, and they fail. A population code is much more stable than a single unit. If a hundred neurons weakly encode “the object is moving left,” the group can still give a decent answer even if many of them are wrong on any one trial. More units allow finer distinctions and smoother averages. This is like adding more pixels to an image. Each pixel is not the picture, but more pixels let the system represent finer detail and make fewer catastrophic errors.

So the reason size correlates with intelligence is not that bigger brains are faster filing cabinets. It is that intelligence requires a large, active, low-noise state space. More neurons and synapses allow more dimensions of representation, more stable working patterns, more stored associations, and more room to combine them. A small system can run simple sensorimotor loops. A larger system can track more variables, maintain longer chains of reasoning, and recover from local failures.

The hardest objection is that a puzzle is solved quickly, so why should the amount of matter matter? Because the puzzle is not being solved from scratch by raw computation. The system is using compressed knowledge. A chess player does not calculate every move in the tree. They recognize configurations, retrieve plausible plans, and prune the search. That retrieval and recognition depend on a large library of learned features and associations. The library lives in synaptic weights, but it can only be searched, combined, and transformed by an active network. If the network is too small, the library is either too poor or too poorly accessible. The minute performance is limited by the workspace and the quality of the stored model, not just by the speed of individual neurons.

This is visible in AI too. A small language model may know many facts but fail when they must be linked across several steps. A larger model can represent more intermediate structure and make smoother, more precise transformations over its internal states. Parameter count predicts performance because parameters are the tunable degrees of freedom that encode both knowledge and function. More parameters can represent more complex mappings. But the same caveat applies: more parameters do not help if the data are bad, the architecture is wrong, or the model is undertrained. Sometimes more compute at test time can substitute for more parameters, which shows that capacity and computation are related but not identical.

The final qualification is that numbers are only proxies for organization. A brain with lots of neurons wired at random is not intelligent. A small, well-organized system can outperform a large one in a narrow domain. What the counts track is the physical possibility of rich internal states. Intelligence is the art of using those states. More neurons do not contain the answer, but they make it possible to hold, compare, and transform enough of the world at once to find one.

Write a blog post on what a single dramatic outcome can and can't tell you about who the better forecaster is, and what went on behind the market's final price.
response:
A hit is not a theory.

The story is easy to tell: Polymarket put a price on an election, the price ended up close to the outcome, and therefore real-money markets must be better than polls, pundits, and models. It feels satisfying because prediction markets are supposed to work by making people pay for their confidence. If the market was right, the confidence was cheap. If it was wrong, someone lost.

But that story skips the hard part. A single dramatic outcome is a very small amount of evidence about forecasting skill, and the “final price” people are pointing to may not have been a forecast at all. It may have been the market doing what markets do after the answer is known: converging on the payoff.

## What one outcome can tell you

Suppose the market said the winner had an 80 percent chance, and the best alternative said 55 percent. Then the favorite wins. That is a point for the market. If the number was public before the result, it was directionally closer.

But “directionally closer on one question” is a weak foundation. In statistical terms, the event is only mildly more likely under the market’s 80 percent forecast than under the alternative’s 55 percent forecast. The likelihood ratio is 80/55, about 1.45 to 1. Even if the market said 95 percent and the alternative said 50 percent, one win gives you only about 1.9 to 1. One event rarely distinguishes a good probability from a lucky one.

That is true even when the outcome is dramatic. If the market priced a surprise at 20 percent and the surprise happened, that is not a miracle. A 20 percent event happens about one time in five. If Polymarket had a dozen similar 20 percent markets, getting one right is ordinary. If it priced the surprise at 5 percent and it happened, that is more striking, but still only one draw from a long tail. Prediction markets have many markets. Some low-probability things will hit. The interesting question is not whether one hit happened, but whether the market’s full set of probabilities is calibrated.

A better forecaster is not someone who got this one right. A better forecaster is someone whose 80 percent calls are right about 80 percent of the time, whose 20 percent calls are right about 20 percent of the time, and whose 95 percent calls are not secretly 70 percent calls. One success tells you almost nothing about that distribution. If the market’s 99 percent contracts usually win, fine. But the proof is in the misses, and misses do not make the same kind of headline.

There is also the comparison problem. “The alternatives” are not one thing. A poll is a measurement of current vote share. A model is a machine that turns measurements, trends, and assumptions into a probability. A pundit is a person with a narrative. A prediction market is a trading venue where the last price reflects the beliefs and incentives of the people currently willing to trade. To compare them fairly, you need the same question, the same cutoff time, and the same scoring rule. Otherwise you are comparing a pre-election poll to a late-night market price after several states have been called, and the market is not going to lose that comparison.

## The final price is not the same thing as the forecast

Here is the part people often miss.

In a binary prediction market, a “yes” share pays $1 if the event happens and $0 if it does not. That means the price of the share is, under normal conditions, an implied probability. If the share trades at 62 cents, the market is saying roughly 62 percent.

But after the event is effectively over, the contract stops being a forecast and becomes a short-term claim on cash. If the winner is known, the “yes” share should pay $1. If it is trading at 99 cents, someone can buy it and collect a 1 cent profit at settlement, ignoring small frictions. Arbitrageurs will do that. Market makers will quote near $1. The final displayed price may be 99.9 cents not because some wise crowd independently calculated a 99.9 percent probability, but because the payoff is $1 and settlement is near.

So if the market’s final price was close to the actual outcome, that may be almost tautological. The market did not “nail” the election in the way a meteorologist nails a storm track. It converged to the election.

The final price can also be a market-microstructure artifact. It is usually the last trade, not a committee estimate. If the order book is thin, one small order can move it. If a market maker pulls a quote, the last trade may be stale. If there is any uncertainty about how the market will resolve, the price may stay below $1 even after the political result is clear. If the resolution depends on a particular news source, a particular wording, or a dispute process, traders may be pricing the paperwork as much as the politics.

None of that means the market is stupid. It means the number on the chart at 11:58 p.m. is not the same object as the number on the chart at 7:00 p.m.

## What was happening on election night

Election-night markets move for a simple reason: new information arrives. A state is called. The remaining states are not enough to change the result. The probability jumps.

At some point, the race is mathematically over. After that, the market is not forecasting an election. It is pricing a settlement. If the last significant trade happened after the decisive state was called, then the “final price” is mostly a receipt.

The interesting question is where the price was before the decisive information arrived. Was the market at 65 percent when polls closed while the best model was at 52 percent? Was it already pricing a likely upset when the public narrative was still treating the other side as the favorite? Was it right about the margin, not just the winner? Those are the questions that separate forecasting from fast news reaction.

A market can be very good at reacting to the same maps everyone else is looking at. That is valuable. It is also not the same thing as having better private information about uncounted ballots. In an election, much of the “information” on election night is public, fast, and mechanical. A trader who watches the state calls and updates quickly can push the price to the right place before a pundit finishes a paragraph. That makes the market look prescient, but it may only be faster.

## Real money is not a magic truth serum

The appeal of prediction markets is that money aligns incentives. If you say 70 percent, you should be willing to buy at 70 cents. If you are wrong, you lose. That is better than a pundit who can hedge with “well, obviously it was close.”

But real money reveals the beliefs of the people who trade, not the truth itself. The traders may be electoral experts. They may be news traders. They may be arbitrageurs comparing Polymarket to Kalshi or to state-level markets. They may be partisans buying for identity. They may be speculators with inventory who need to move a position. In a thin market, one mistaken actor can move the price. In a liquid market, the price can be very efficient and still wrong if the common information is wrong.

A market can also be coherent without being accurate. Related markets can be mutually consistent: the presidential market, the state markets, the margin markets, all priced in a way that makes arbitrage hard. But a consistent set of probabilities can still be centered on the wrong answer.

## What would count as evidence

The strongest version of the pro-market case is this: Polymarket had a public record before the election, and on this election its pre-cutoff probabilities were clearly better than the alternatives on the same question. If that is true, the election is meaningful. It is evidence that the market’s process works at least sometimes in high-salience political events.

But the correct inference is still narrower than “real-money markets beat the alternatives.” The correct inference is: “On this market, at this cutoff, the price was closer than the comparison set.” To turn that into a general claim, you need more. You need the market’s score across many events. You need to compare it to forecasts made at the same horizons. You need to use a proper scoring rule, such as Brier score or log score, so that overconfidence is punished and calibration is rewarded. You need to avoid cherry-picking the one market that made the headline.

If Polymarket’s 90 percent calls are usually right, and its 10 percent calls are usually wrong, and it beats comparable forecasts over a long sample, then yes, the method has shown something. One election night is not that sample.

## The lesson

The post-election chart is not a résumé. It is the end of a price path. The last tick may have been set by arbitrage, by resolution mechanics, by a thin book, or by the simple fact that the winner was already known.

The market may well be a better forecaster than the alternatives. It has structural advantages: it forces probabilistic expression, it aggregates dispersed views, and it lets money do the arguing. But a single dramatic hit does not prove that. It only proves that this time, the number and the outcome matched.

To find out whether the market is wise, look earlier than the final price, score the whole track record, and ask what the market knew when it said what it said. The final price is the easiest number to point to. It is also the least interesting.

## I Tried a Sleep Supplement, Convinced Myself It Worked, Then Ran a Blind Trial on Myself

I bought the sleep supplement on a Tuesday after a week of bad nights. The bottle promised “calmer, deeper sleep,” which is the kind of phrase that sounds reasonable until you notice that almost every sleep product uses some version of it. I was not looking for reason. I was looking for a switch.

The first week, it felt like the switch had been found.

I was falling asleep faster. I woke up less often. Mornings felt less scraped. By the third week, I had started explaining to people that the supplement had fixed my sleep. I said this with the calm confidence of someone who has already decided what the data mean.

Then I realized I had no data.

I had only a before and after, separated by a period in which I changed several things at once. I had gone to bed earlier. I had cut back on evening alcohol. I had stopped taking work emails to bed with me. I had also been sleeping badly for months before I started the supplement, which meant there was a good chance my sleep would have improved anyway if I had just kept living my life and bought nothing at all.

So I did the annoying thing. I ran a blinded trial on myself.

Not a perfect one. Not a clinical trial. But as proper as a one-person laboratory can get.

I bought the supplement and a bottle of visually identical placebo capsules. I asked a friend to divide them into two unmarked bottles, one active and one placebo, and to randomize a 28-night schedule: which bottle I should take on each night. I did not know which bottle was which. I did not see the random list until all 28 nights were done.

For those 28 nights, I kept the rest of the routine as fixed as I could. Same bedtime window. No alcohol after dinner. Caffeine cut off at 2 p.m. Screens off at 10:30. Lights out by 11. I took the assigned capsule at 10:45, whether I felt sleepy or not.

I tracked four things each morning:

How long it took me to fall asleep. How many times I woke during the night. How long I stayed awake after waking. And how good the sleep felt to me, on a scale from 0 to 10.

I also used a wearable, because I wear one anyway, but I did not trust it completely. Wearables are useful for trends and terrible for certainty. They can mistake lying still for sleep, and they can mistake a brief awakening for a full one. I used them mostly to keep me honest.

Before looking at the results, I wrote down what would count as success. I wanted the supplement to reduce sleep onset by at least ten minutes, or improve subjective sleep quality by at least half a point. Not “feel a little better.” Not “some nights seemed calmer.” A difference I could point to and say, yes, that is not just noise.

The result was nothing.

Across the 14 supplement nights, I took about 26 minutes to fall asleep. Across the 14 placebo nights, I took about 25 minutes. My subjective sleep quality averaged 7.4 on supplement nights and 7.3 on placebo nights. I woke about as often in both conditions. Total sleep time differed by two minutes, which is the kind of number that means the pillow moved.

When my friend unblinded the bottles, I guessed the active nights correctly only slightly better than chance. My body had not left me a trail of clues. If it had been working, I had not felt it.

That was the embarrassing part.

The first impression had not been wrong because I had imagined the feeling. The feeling had been real. I had slept better after starting the supplement. The mistake was in the explanation.

I had started the supplement at the bottom of a bad sleep cycle, then watched the normal recovery and called it the product. I had also changed my behavior at the same time, which is what people do when they decide to take something seriously: they take the thing and also try to be the kind of person who takes the thing. I stopped scrolling so late. I got into bed earlier. I stopped negotiating with myself at 1 a.m. Those changes were probably doing most of the work.

And because I believed the supplement was helping, I interpreted ambiguous evidence in its favor. The night I fell asleep quickly, I remembered the capsule. The night I woke at 3:12 and stared at the ceiling, I blamed stress. That is not a fair way to read a life.

The hardest objection to this whole exercise is obvious: one person is not a study.

That is true. I cannot say the supplement does not work. I cannot say it would not help someone with a different schedule, different chemistry, different sleep problem, or different degree of anxiety about sleep. I cannot even say with confidence that the particular bottle I bought was representative, though I tried to use it the way the label intended. All I can say is that, for me, over 28 randomized nights, I found no evidence that it was doing anything beyond what expectation and habit were already doing.

That is a smaller claim than the one I made to my friends. It is also the only one I can defend.

What I actually learned is not that this supplement is worthless. It is that my first judgment was not a measurement. It was a story I told myself while tired. The supplement became a symbol for the version of me who was finally taking care of the problem, and the brain is very good at reporting symbolic success as physiological success.

I also learned that before-and-after is a weak instrument when the “after” includes a dozen quiet improvements. If I had only asked, “Do I sleep better now than I did six weeks ago?” the answer would have been yes. But that question cannot tell you which change caused it. It can only tell you that something changed.

So I stopped taking the supplement every night. I still keep a bottle around for travel, because jet lag is a different problem and I do not trust my judgment about altitude and time zones enough to run a randomized trial at 30,000 feet. But I no longer count it as part of my ordinary sleep routine. The things that actually moved the numbers were the boring ones: earlier lights-out, less evening drinking, and not bringing the day’s unfinished arguments into bed.

If I take away one thing from the experiment, it is this: the most persuasive evidence I have is usually the least reliable. My own felt experience is not a lie, but it is not a control group. It needs a design.

prompt: Write a book review of Scott Rosenberg's Dreaming in Code, about the Chandler project, that uses it to talk about why ambitious software projects fail to converge. Open with something unexpected.
response:
The most important component of the Chandler project was not the mail client, the calendar, or the search index. It was the bug tracker. In Scott Rosenberg’s *Dreaming in Code*, the tracker becomes the clearest record of the project: a numbered list of small failures that, read together, show a program trying to become several programs at once. A bug is a promise the code has broken. A long list of bugs is a map of the promises nobody agreed to make.

Rosenberg followed the Chandler team over several years as they tried to build an open-source personal information manager. The goal was to put email, calendar, tasks, contacts, notes, and search in one place, and to make the result extensible, portable, and better than the bloated commercial alternatives. The book is unusual because it does not wait for the product and then explain the failure. It sits inside the process: bug reports, design arguments, code reviews, mailing-list exchanges, and the quiet labor of making a machine do what a group of people means.

To talk about convergence is to talk about limits. A numerical method converges when its successive approximations get closer to a value. A software project converges when its requirements, architecture, tests, and user model stop changing each other. Each milestone should make the object more definite: this data is stored this way, this screen means this, this error is handled this way. Ambitious projects often fail not because the code is wrong, but because the object is not yet an object. The team can write correct code for a moving target and still miss.

Chandler’s target moved because its center was a category, not a product. A personal information manager is a phrase that contains several competitors. Email is a protocol, a social medium, a storage problem, and a notification system. Calendar is a scheduling system with conflicts, time zones, invitations, and resources. Tasks are commitments with deadlines and dependencies. Contacts are entities that change and must be matched across sources. Search is an index over all of the above, plus the hard question of what the user meant. Put those together and the program has to decide which one is primary. Chandler kept postponing the decision.

The project also started, in part, from a negative. It was meant to be the alternative to Outlook and other desktop suites: less clumsy, more open, more respectful of the user. A negative is a good banner and a poor specification. It tells a team what to reject, but not what to build. The developers could agree that the existing tools were bad, then split over what good would look like. The person who lives by email wants messages first. The person who lives by meetings wants calendar first. The person who is afraid of losing things wants tasks and reminders first. The person who has already lost things wants search first. A program that puts all of these first has no center.

The architecture became the place where those disagreements were stored. If email is central, the data model is built around messages, folders, flags, and attachments. If calendar is central, it is built around events, attendees, and time. If the program is to be extensible, the core must expose stable objects and actions to plugins. If it is to synchronize with existing mail servers and calendars, every local change must be expressible as a transaction that can be sent, merged, rejected, or replayed after a conflict. None of these choices is crazy. Together, they pull the same code in different directions. Keeping all options open is not neutrality; it is a cost paid in complexity.

This is where Rosenberg’s phrase “magic” becomes useful and misleading. Programming does feel magical when it works: a parser accepts the right input, a view redraws, a test goes green, the machine seems to extend the mind. But the magic is local. It works on a function, a module, a screen. It does not work on the project. The project is an operational system: who owns the bug, who reviews the patch, who closes the feature request, who decides that the current design is good enough, who will use the program while it is still ugly. Code can be elegant and the project can still drift.

The open-source setting made the drift easier to see. Contributors arrived with goodwill and skill. Some could fix a memory leak, improve a widget, or write a better handler for a mail format. But belief is not a schedule. If the core data model changes, a contribution can become obsolete before it is merged. The public mailing lists and bug tracker record good will outrunning coordination. The project needed not only programmers but release discipline, documentation, support boundaries, and a way to say no without insulting the person who asked. It had enthusiastic people, some of them brilliant, and a lead developer, Frank Heikens, who carried too much.

Chandler also faced the unglamorous problem of adoption. A person’s information is already somewhere: in Outlook, in inboxes, in paper notebooks, in files on a laptop, in the memory of an assistant. To become the new place, the program had to import that material, preserve enough of the old habits to be usable, and survive the first awkward week. Synchronization was not a feature on a wish list; it was the condition of entry. If Chandler could not live alongside the tools people already used, it could not replace them.

The external world moved as well. Web mail, calendar services, mobile devices, and search engines began to absorb pieces of the desktop PIM. By the time an integrated local program could promise search across messages, events, and contacts, part of the user’s life might already be in a browser or on a phone. That market shift mattered, but it did not cause the failure. It only made the failure more visible. A project that cannot converge in a stable world will not converge in a moving one.

It is tempting to stop here and blame the open-source form, the remote team, the visionary leadership, or the particular weaknesses of the people involved. Some of that is true. *Dreaming in Code* does not let us take the easy route. The developers are not shown as incompetent. They write careful reports, make reasonable local decisions, and care about the result. The harder lesson is that a project can be staffed by competent people and still fail to converge when the thing they are building is a set of adjacencies rather than a bounded object.

Convergence usually requires subtraction. A release is a list of things the program will not do this time. The cut is not the failure of ambition; it is the definition of the product. Chandler’s ambition was to be a better way to live with information. That is too large for a version. A version can be a better mail reader, a better calendar, a better search tool, or a better synchronization layer. It cannot be a better life. The team kept reaching for the larger phrase because the smaller ones felt insufficient. The machine, however, only builds the smaller ones.

*Dreaming in Code* remains useful because it treats the process as the subject. It shows why the small items in the bug tracker are not merely annoyances. They are the points where the project’s meaning met the machine’s requirements. The Chandler project did not fail because it was ambitious. It failed to converge because ambition, left uncut, is a way of avoiding the question every program must answer: what is this, and what is it not?

prompt: I studied computer science and then went to art school, and people keep asking me why. Write an essay arguing that programming is closer to painting than to science or engineering, and what follows from that for how hackers should work and make a living.
response:
When someone asks why I studied computer science and then went to art school, I can tell them the short answer: I wanted to learn why some made things feel made and others did not. The longer answer is that the question is built on a false map. It places programming in the same country as science or engineering, as if a person who leaves it for art has abandoned a technical discipline for a soft one. In my experience, programming is not soft, but it is not scientific in the way that matters. The daily work of hacking—choosing what to build, how to divide it, what to call, where to stop—is closer to painting than to physics or bridge construction. That resemblance has consequences for how a hacker should spend a working day and a career.

Science is in the business of finding out what is already there. A physicist does not get credit for making an equation elegant if the equation is wrong; elegance is at best a heuristic, at worst a distraction. The world is the editor. Programming has a world too: machines, networks, users, budgets. But the program itself is not a report about that world. It is a new arrangement of operations. When I choose between a tree, a hash table, a queue, or a plain array, I am not discovering the natural shape of the data. I am deciding which operations should be cheap, which errors should be loud, and what the next person will have to think about. That is a making decision, not a measuring decision.

Engineering is closer, because programs must work. A program that crashes is not a controversial artwork; it is a failure. But engineering, at its best, is the art of making a system satisfy requirements under constraints. The engineer’s identity often disappears into the specification. A well-designed water system is not remembered for the personality of its valves. Software is different. Code is executed, but it is also read, argued over, extended, and misunderstood. Its behavior is only the surface. The names of functions, the boundaries between modules, the order in which a screen reveals information, the way an error message treats the person who caused it—these are not decorations added after the system works. They are how the system thinks. A program must be legible to people, not only correct for machines.

Painting also has hard constraints. Pigment dries. Canvas sags. Perspective has rules. Anatomy has rules. A painter who ignores them makes a mess, not a visionary. Still, we call the work painting, not chemistry or geometry, because the artist’s decisions are the point. The painter chooses what to sharpen, what to blur, what to leave out, what to push forward. The surface is not the subject. Programming has its own physics: the language’s syntax, the operating system’s limits, the database’s locks, the network’s latency. But the hard part is rarely the physics. The hard part is deciding what the thing should emphasize, what it should hide, and what it should refuse to do. The machine is the tooth of the canvas.

Consider two programs with the same user-visible behavior. One is a sequence of steps: fetch user, check permission, query orders, format totals, send response. It works. The other introduces a small model of an order, a boundary between payment and inventory, and a naming convention that makes the next feature easier to imagine. It also works. Tests can be written for both. A performance profiler may show the first one is faster, or the second, depending on the day. But the second program is easier to live with because it carries an intention. It tells the next maintainer what the author thought the problem was. That is the difference between a competent copy and a painting. Both may depict the same face. Only one makes you feel the painter was somewhere.

The strongest objection to this view is obvious: software has to be reliable, and art does not. A painting can be pretty and false; a payment system cannot be pretty and steal money. If programming is like painting, it is like a kind of painting that must also be a lock. I would not argue against that. I would only say that the lock part is not the whole identity of the work. A painter knows that varnish yellows, that oil takes weeks to dry, that a large canvas needs a strong stretcher. Those facts do not turn the painter into a materials scientist in the way a programmer is not turned into a compiler engineer by the existence of memory. The constraints are part of the medium. Taste shows up precisely in how the maker handles constraints: what is worth an extra millisecond, what is worth an extra table, what should be deleted because the user will not notice and the code will suffer.

Programming can also be made to look scientific because it can be specified, tested, and sometimes proved. A theorem can show that a parser accepts exactly the grammar it was meant to accept. A model can predict the load on a server. But these methods answer questions that have already been framed. They do not choose the frame. Formal methods can prove that a module terminates; they cannot tell you whether the module is the right place to draw a line. Tests can show that a button submits a form; they cannot show that the form should exist. The scientific part of programming is important, but it is the part that checks the work after the maker has decided what the work is.

There is a real place where the painting analogy breaks. A painting can be the total product of one pair of hands. A modern software system can be the product of hundreds of people over decades. At that scale, the work becomes infrastructure, and infrastructure is engineering. The person who keeps a distributed database consistent is doing something closer to civil engineering than to portraiture. The person who designs a numerical method for weather prediction is doing something closer to applied mathematics. Theoretical computer science can be as mathematical as any branch of science, and that is one reason the confusion persists. But a complexity proof does not tell me how to name a state, or whether a modal dialog is an insult. The center of gravity of most hacking—tools, applications, editors, interfaces, systems that mediate human work—is not there. It is in the part of the job where the maker’s choices are visible.

If that is true, the first consequence is about where to work. A hacker who wants to develop as a maker needs work in which authorship survives. That usually means owning a thing, not a ticket. It means having a subsystem, a product, a tool, or a process that can be pointed to and seen as a whole. It means being close to the user, or at least close to the consequences, so that feedback is not only a green build but a person saying, “I now do this differently.” It means working in a team small enough that the shape of the system reflects someone’s judgment. In a very large organization, a programmer can be excellent and still be a component, the way a glass maker in a factory can be skilled without being a glass artist. The work may be necessary. It will not make a style.

It also means leaving room for study. Painters make studies: a hand, a drape, a patch of light. Programmers should make prototypes that exist only to answer a question: Would this be easier if the state lived here? What does this feel like if the animation is shorter? What happens if I delete this setting? These are not wasted side projects. They are the way a maker learns the material. A hacker who only writes code inside approved tickets learns the company’s taste, not their own.

The second consequence is that hackers should build a body of work. Painters are known for a way of seeing, not for a list of places they have been employed. Programmers are often known for companies, languages, or job titles, because software is invisible and institutions provide a proxy for quality. But the proxy is weak. A better reputation is attached to things: a library that made a hard problem easy, an interface that set a standard, a compiler that revealed a language’s possibilities, a product that solved a real annoyance. A body of work does not have to be famous. It can be a set of maintained tools, a public notebook of failures, a small product with paying users, a codebase that other people describe as clear. The point is to accumulate evidence of judgment. A résumé says what you were allowed to do. A body of work says what you made.

The economic consequence follows from that. If programming is a commodity, the unit of sale is time or lines or tickets, and the hacker competes downward with every other pair of hands that can produce plausible code. If programming is craft, the unit of sale is a thing that works and has a point. Clients do not wake up wanting more code. A shop does not need “more backend”; it needs the inventory screen to stop making the owner guess. A research lab does not need “more infrastructure”; it needs the notebook pipeline to stop eating an afternoon. A hacker who can deliver that can charge for the delivery, not for the hour.

In freelance work, that means choosing clients who care about the artifact and refusing to be a body for someone else’s vague plan. In a product job, it means taking responsibility for an outcome, not just a feature. In consulting, it means selling diagnosis and design first, implementation second. The market will still pay for reliability, so the craft cannot be all surface. The painter-hacker must be the person who ships, tests, documents, and maintains. The style is in the choices; the trust is in the follow-through.

There is a further economic problem: software is invisible, and invisible work is priced by fear. When a system is working, nobody sees it. When it fails, everyone sees the failure. Companies therefore often buy programming as insurance against failure, which encourages them to treat programmers as interchangeable risk-reducers. The maker who wants a living must make the work visible without turning it into marketing. A demo that shows the real thing, a document that explains a hard tradeoff, a public postmortem that says what broke and why, a product that can be touched in three minutes—these are not vanity. They are the frame around the painting. They let the buyer see that there was a maker.

Art school does not teach you to code. It teaches you to look, to handle materials, to accept that every choice is a statement, and to spend time on a thing until you can tell what is wrong with it. Computer science teaches you the opposite virtues: precision, abstraction, proof, scale. A programmer who has only the first makes toys. A programmer who has only the second makes machines that may be correct and dead. The useful life is in the tension between them. You need the science to know what the medium can do. You need the engineering to keep the thing standing. You need the painting to decide what it is for.

So when people ask why I went from computer science to art school, I do not say I left one world for another. I went to learn how to make. Programming had already shown me that making was possible inside a discipline full of rules. Art school asked the harder question: what are you making it for, and why does this shape, and not some other shape, answer that?

prompt: A friend swears by 'training your inner pigeon', using behaviorism on yourself by rewarding yourself when you do what you want to do more of. Does that actually work? Think it through skeptically, using what you know about conditioning.
response:
It works in the narrow sense that reinforcement is a real mechanism. If a behavior is followed by a consequence you actually want, the behavior becomes more likely. A pigeon presses a key when the pebble is reliable. If you write five hundred words and then allow yourself a walk, the pairing can make writing and walking more likely. That part is not delusion.

The trouble is that the arrangement you want to create—behavior, consequence, repetition—is easy to corrupt when you are both pigeon and experimenter. A pigeon cannot decide that it actually pressed the key. You can. On a bad day you can reinterpret “I worked on the report” to mean you opened the file, read the last paragraph, and felt inspired. The reward still comes, but the behavior you intended has not happened. Conditioning requires a stable relationship between response and consequence. Self-reward is unstable because the scorer is also the player.

The first failure mode is a fuzzy target. “Do more of what I want” is not trainable. “Write for twenty-five minutes before lunch” is trainable. If you reward the vague thing, you get vague behavior. If your goal is to get fit and you reward yourself for “exercising,” a slow walk to the mailbox may qualify. If you reward “run three miles,” the criterion is harder to fake. The unit you reward becomes the unit you train. Reward showing up and you train showing up. Reward completion and you may train avoidance of completion, because submission makes the criterion visible and the reward harder to earn.

The second failure mode is the reward itself. A reinforcer is not whatever you have labeled a reward. It is whatever increases the behavior in that context. A nice dinner after a workout may not work if you would have eaten the dinner anyway. A podcast is a better reward for walking if the podcast is only accessible while walking. The consequence has to be contingent, immediate enough to register, and desirable at the moment. If you are exhausted after training, the desired consequence may be sleep, not a treat. If you are hungry, the desired consequence is food, and the exercise is just a delay. Pairing a behavior with something you already get for free does almost nothing.

This is where “reward yourself” often collapses. Suppose you promise to buy a book after a week of early bedtimes. The promise sounds like a system, but on the fourth night you are tired and the book is not urgent. You go to bed late, then either skip the book because you feel you have ruined the week, or buy it anyway because you want the book. In the first case the consequence becomes a punishment for a single slip. In the second case the consequence is no longer contingent. The system has become a mood: good days earn treats, bad days earn self-judgment, and the behavior follows neither reliably.

External consequences do not have this problem because they do not care about your feelings. A paycheck arrives or it does not. A reader replies or does not. A deposit is made or not. If you want behaviorism to work on yourself, you usually need to make the consequence less internal. Pay a friend who calls you out if you miss a workout. Put money in an account that is locked until a milestone is reached. Use an app that will not let you open your phone until the task is logged. Ask someone to see the artifact. These are still behavioral interventions, but they move the Skinner box outside your head. That makes the rules harder to fudge.

Delay is another skeptical point. Conditioning is good at bridging small gaps between action and payoff. It is bad at making a present effort feel like a distant benefit. If the reward is “a better life in ten years,” it will lose to the immediate pull of rest, food, or entertainment. Long goals need proximal consequences, but those consequences can become the whole point. You start running for the post-run smoothie, writing for the dopamine hit of a completed word-count bar, saving for the permission to spend. If the artificial reward is stronger than the original reason for doing the thing, you have trained a dependency on the treat.

There is also the risk of crowding out. If you already find some activity worthwhile, adding a reward can shift the reason. A person who reads for curiosity may read less later if reading becomes a way to earn points. The effect is not universal, but it is real enough to take seriously. Behaviorism can make a behavior more likely while making it less meaningful. You may become a person who does the right actions for the right external reasons, and then stops when the economy of treats becomes inconvenient.

Still, the method is not useless. Its best role is to make a fuzzy ambition concrete and to attach a consequence soon enough that the natural consequences have a chance to arrive. “Become a writer” is too large for a reward schedule. “Produce one page a day and keep a dated file” is small enough. The reward can be modest: the satisfaction of having a file, a coffee after the page, a mark on a calendar. The value is not the coffee. The value is that the behavior has a visible edge, a cue, and a feedback signal. After enough repetitions, the behavior may no longer need the treat. It may have become a habit, or the natural consequences—finished drafts, reader responses, pride, competence—may have become strong enough.

That transition is the part people skip. If you keep the reward forever, you have not trained yourself; you have made yourself a wage laborer for your own future self. If you remove the reward abruptly, extinction can set in. The better move is to let the consequence move from artificial to natural. Reward daily pages for a few weeks, then reward only finished chapters, then stop rewarding and rely on the fact that chapters exist. The behavior is more likely to survive if it has produced something that matters independent of the treat.

The hardest case against the “inner pigeon” idea is that it can be a comforting story for bad design. You can feel like you are doing self-improvement when you are really just negotiating with yourself. “I’ll allow myself a break after this task” is not a system if the task is undefined, the break is available without the task, and you can choose the break anyway. A system needs a criterion that would be recognizable to a skeptical stranger, a consequence that is not freely available, and a record that is hard to alter. If those are missing, the phrase “I rewarded myself” can describe almost anything: a small act of self-soothing, a rationalization, or a genuine increment in behavior.

So the friend’s method works when the behavior is pigeon-sized, the reward is real, the contingency is hard to cheat, and the reward is eventually retired. It fails when it is used as a substitute for choosing a specific action, changing the environment, or accepting that some behaviors are trained by consequences you do not control. The inner pigeon is a useful image for building habits, not a complete account of motivation. A pigeon does not need to decide whether it deserves the pebble. You do, and that is where the experiment usually goes wrong.

prompt: You worked at Yahoo in the late 90s after they acquired your startup. Write an essay about what actually went wrong there, and what lessons today's software companies should take from it.
response:
The first sign was the org chart. It arrived before the roadmap.

We had a small product: one screen, one job, a few thousand users who came back every day. When Yahoo acquired us, the story was simple. We would keep doing what we were doing, but now we would have infrastructure, brand, distribution, and money. No more fundraising. No more server outages at 2 a.m. No more arguing with a board about whether the company was a business. We would be part of something bigger.

For a while, that felt true. Then the integration began.

I am not reconstructing a boardroom. I am reconstructing a pattern, because the exact offices and emails matter less than the mechanism. Yahoo in the late 1990s was not a software company that happened to run a website. It was a media company with a software problem. Its revenue came from advertising, its identity came from being a front door to the internet, and its internal logic came from traffic, page views, channels, and brand placements. That was not a bad model. It was a model. The mistake was assuming that every acquired product would fit inside it without changing either the product or the company.

The first thing an acquirer does is impose itself. Not always consciously. The new company gets a logo, a login, a billing system, a support process, a security review, a legal review, a finance review, a quarterly planning cycle, and a set of metrics that the parent company understands. Each one is reasonable in isolation. Together, they become a different product. The startup had been optimized for speed and user value. The parent was optimized for risk reduction and revenue recognition. The acquired team spent its energy translating itself into the parent’s language until it forgot its own.

At Yahoo, this was especially visible because the company was acquiring so much. There was WebTV, Inktomi, PointCast, GeoCities, AllTheWeb, MapQuest, and others. Some of those assets were genuinely interesting. WebTV was a bold idea: put the web in the living room. GeoCities had real communities. Inktomi had useful caching technology. AllTheWeb had search ambition. MapQuest had a product people actually used. The problem was not that the assets were bad. The problem was that Yahoo did not know what it was becoming by buying them.

A portfolio can make sense if there is a thesis. Microsoft buying a database company, a browser company, a cloud company, and a developer tools company all made sense because the center of gravity was clear: enterprise computing. Google buying a video company, a phone company, and an advertising company made sense because the center of gravity was attention and distribution. Yahoo’s center of gravity was the portal. But the portal was not a product thesis. It was a layout. It was a home page with boxes. It could absorb almost anything, which is exactly why it could not explain why anything mattered.

That strategic fog showed up in product decisions. An acquired team would come in with a clear user problem. The parent company would ask how the product could drive traffic to Yahoo properties, how it could carry Yahoo branding, how it could support Yahoo ad formats, how it could be featured on the home page, how it could be sold to enterprise customers, how it could be integrated with other Yahoo services. Each question was plausible. The cumulative effect was that the product was no longer solving its original problem. It was becoming a Yahoo product, and Yahoo was a diffuse thing.

The ad model made this worse. Advertising rewards surface area. More page views, more impressions, more branded placements, more sponsored links. It does not reward depth. If your product helps someone complete a difficult task quickly, that is great for users, but terrible for ad revenue if they leave after two clicks. A portal wants you to drift. A tool wants you to finish. Yahoo’s incentives were built for drifting.

WebTV is the clearest example. It was not just a web portal with a remote control. It was a device business, a cable business, a content business, and a consumer electronics business. It needed hardware partnerships, carrier relationships, living-room software, and a content strategy. Yahoo had none of those as core competencies. It had a web brand and ad sales. So WebTV became a strange object: too strategic to ignore, too different to manage, too expensive to abandon. It was eventually sold to Microsoft, a company that actually lived in the world of devices, operating systems, and media platforms. That outcome was not surprising. It was the logical endpoint of a mismatch that existed at acquisition.

GeoCities showed a different failure. It had users and culture, which are hard to build. But Yahoo treated it mostly as a content and advertising surface. It did not become a platform for the next generation of personal publishing in the way that the web was beginning to demand. The company that owned a network of personal home pages did not invest in the tools, moderation, and product surfaces that would keep those pages alive. By the time social networks and easier publishing platforms arrived, GeoCities had become a museum. It had nostalgia, which is not a growth engine.

Search was the most painful case because Yahoo had pieces that could have mattered. It had Inktomi technology. It had AllTheWeb. It had a consumer brand. It had distribution. What it did not have was a unified, ruthless commitment to becoming a search engine. Google’s advantage was not only that its ranking was better, though it was. It was that Google’s entire organization was aligned around one problem: index the web, rank it, scale it, and improve it every day. Yahoo had search teams, search partnerships, sponsored search experiments, and portal widgets. It also had Overture and pay-to-play dynamics that put commercial pressure on result quality. The product became a compromise between what a search engine should do and what a portal should sell.

The bubble made all of this more expensive. In a market where every internet company was being valued as if it were the future, acquisitions stop being investments and start becoming status. You pay for fear. You pay for the right to say you own a category. You pay for a team because you do not want a competitor to have it. The price matters because it changes behavior. A cheap acquisition can be killed, spun off, or absorbed without tragedy. An expensive acquisition becomes a strategic commitment. The company defends it for years because admitting it was a mistake would mean writing off not just money but judgment.

Talent retention was treated as a personnel problem instead of a product problem. When key engineers left, the response was often to replace them, add managers, or tighten reporting lines. But the reason they left was usually simpler: the product no longer had a clear owner. The founders had sold. The mission had been diluted. The roadmap was now a negotiation between the acquired team, the parent company’s product organization, the sales team, and the executives who wanted the asset to justify its purchase. A retention package can keep someone for a quarter. It cannot replace a reason to care.

The hardest objection to this account is obvious: Yahoo did not fail because it bought too many companies. It failed because Google made better search, Microsoft had Windows, and the internet moved faster than Yahoo could adapt. Even a perfectly integrated Yahoo might have lost some of those battles. That is true. Market shifts do not care about your org chart. But the acquisition pattern still matters because it consumed the company’s attention and capital at the exact moment when focus was required. Yahoo was not merely out-executed by a cleaner competitor. It was distracted by its own balance sheet. It paid for options and then could not choose among them. It had the raw materials for a serious internet company and used them to build a more complicated portal.

That is the lesson for today’s software companies.

The first lesson is that integration is a product problem, not an HR problem. If you are buying a team, you need to know what the product will be after the deal. Not what the product is today. What it will be in six months, in twelve months, and what you will stop doing. If the answer is “we’ll figure it out,” you are not acquiring a capability. You are acquiring a liability with a press release.

The second lesson is to buy for a specific capability you cannot build quickly, not to remove a threat. Defensive acquisitions are seductive. A competitor has a good feature. A startup is getting too close. A founder is about to raise a round. The easiest response is to buy them. But if the product does not fit your core strategy, you will not inherit its momentum. You will inherit its maintenance. The team will leave, the code will rot, and the category will move on without you.

The third lesson is to keep the product owner accountable. The people who built the thing should remain responsible for the thing for long enough to prove whether the integration is working. If you replace the founder immediately, demote the CTO into a director role, or scatter the team across your existing organization, you have told them that you wanted their code, not their judgment. In many cases, the code is the least valuable part. The valuable part is the sense of what the product should become next.

The fourth lesson is to preserve distinct metrics for a period. A startup has its own numbers: activation, retention, task completion, time to value, developer adoption, community growth. The parent company has its own numbers: revenue, margin, pipeline, brand lift, cross-sell. If you force the acquired team to optimize for the parent’s metrics too early, you will get the parent’s product. That may be fine if that is what you want. But then you should have said so and priced the deal accordingly.

The fifth lesson is price discipline. Overpaying is not just a finance issue. It is a product issue. A high purchase price makes the asset politically protected. It becomes harder to kill, harder to pivot, harder to sell. The team becomes a hostage to success. In hot markets, especially now with AI, the temptation is to pay whatever is necessary to get the team or the technology. The companies that do this most often end up with a cost center that has a startup logo.

The sixth lesson is to decide the exit early. If the asset is not core, define what success looks like and when you will stop. WebTV should have been evaluated as a device and media business from the beginning. If Yahoo did not want to be that kind of company, the rational move was to partner, license, or sell sooner. The worst strategy is to keep something alive because it is too big to kill and too weak to lead.

The seventh lesson is that scale is not a product strategy. Big companies often believe that if they put a good product in front of their existing users, it will work. Sometimes it does. But user access is not the same as product-market fit. A cloud company can give its customers a new tool, but if the tool does not solve a painful problem, adoption will be ceremonial. A consumer platform can feature a startup’s app, but if the app requires a different behavior than the platform’s native loop, it will stay in a corner. Today’s version of the Yahoo mistake is buying a startup and then asking why it does not behave like the parent company’s existing product.

The eighth lesson is to know what you are not buying. Yahoo bought communities, maps, search, TV, news, and local services. It did not buy the operational discipline to run any of them well. A company that builds advertising technology is not automatically ready to run a social network. A company that sells enterprise software is not automatically ready to run a consumer app. A company that has distribution is not automatically ready to support a product that requires constant iteration. The acquisition agreement cannot create those capabilities after the fact.

The deepest lesson is about identity. A company can acquire assets, but it cannot acquire a mission without changing itself. If the parent company’s identity is selling ads, it will manage the acquired product like an ad channel. If its identity is enterprise sales cycles, it will manage the acquired product like an enterprise SKU. If its identity is platform control, it will manage the acquired product like a threat to be contained. The product will eventually become legible to the acquirer, and in becoming legible, it will lose whatever made it worth buying.

In the late 1990s, Yahoo had the pieces of a serious internet company. It had consumer trust, engineering assets, communities, search technology, and a brand that meant “the web” to many people. It lost them by treating every new piece as a line item on the portal. The failure was not that the company grew. The failure was that growth did not come with a clearer theory of what the company was for.

Today’s software companies will face the same test. They will have more capital, more talent, and more anxiety about missing the next platform shift. The temptation will be to buy their way into the future. Some of those deals will work. But the ones that fail will not fail because the acquired team was bad. They will fail because the acquirer could not resist making the startup into a smaller, sadder version of itself.
