prompt: Should news organizations spend so much energy debunking stupid or fringe ideas? Write an essay weighing the case for challenging them against the case for ignoring them, ideally using a historical example that tells us something.
response:
The first mistake is to treat all false ideas as the same. A person claiming the Earth is flat, a parent deciding whether to vaccinate a child, and a municipal engineer assessing whether a bridge report can be trusted are all dealing with bad information, but the stakes are not comparable. The idea may be equally wrong in each case, but the cost of being wrong is not. News organizations often get this backwards: they spend the most energy on the ideas that are easiest to mock and the least on the ones that are boring, technical, and likely to matter.

There is a strong case for ignoring most fringe nonsense. Attention is not neutral. A correction contains the claim it denies. A headline saying “That flat-Earth video is wrong” teaches more people the phrase “flat-Earth video” than the original video would have reached. In an environment of fragments, the original claim and the rebuttal often look alike once stripped of context. The 1989 Mars letter is a clean example. A widely circulated message claimed that Mars would appear in the sky about as large as the Moon. Newspapers printed it, observatories were flooded with calls, and for a week the event felt real. The astronomy was simple: even at closest approach Mars is a point of light, no more than about 25 arcseconds across, while the Moon is roughly 1,800 arcseconds across. But the story had a date, a spectacle, and a visual. Once newspapers made it a shared event, the only way to end it was to keep reporting it. The idea was not dangerous. It was, in the journalistic sense, a waste of oxygen.

The case for ignoring is strongest when the idea is harmless, when it has no practical consequences, and when it is mainly a performance. In those cases, indifference is not cowardice. It is a way of refusing to turn a private eccentricity into a public problem.

But that case breaks when the false idea is attached to an action that people cannot easily reverse. That is where the history of the MMR-autism claim is useful. In 1998, Andrew Wakefield published a letter in The Lancet describing 12 children and suggesting a link between the MMR vaccine and autism. The paper was a case series, not evidence of causation. The children were few and selected, and Wakefield had serious conflicts of interest, including work for a lawyer suing vaccine makers. Later investigations found that the data had been manipulated. In 2010, The Lancet retracted the paper and the UK medical regulator struck Wakefield off the register. The scientific case was weak from the start.

The public consequence was not weak. In England, MMR uptake fell from the mid-90s to the low 80s in the years after the paper, and measles, which had been close to elimination, came back. The claim was not a harmless eccentricity. It asked a parent to make a choice about a child, and it offered a story that felt more human than the true one: a child changed, a vaccine had been given recently, and an institution might be hiding harm. That story was emotionally intelligible. The science was not.

This is where the simple rule “do not give oxygen” fails. If newspapers had ignored Wakefield, the claim might have remained a journal footnote. But it did not remain a footnote, and the vacuum would not have stayed empty. It would have been filled by advocacy groups, bad doctors, and, soon, the internet. A news organization that refuses to address a claim people are actually using has not protected the public from the claim; it has ceded the explanation to people with less obligation to accuracy.

But the MMR case also shows the cost of the obvious response. Most corrections were organized around the original question: “Do vaccines cause autism? No.” That structure keeps the claim in the center. It turns a settled problem into a recurring debate. Every new viral video becomes a reason to run the same story, and each running makes the claim look newer. The hardest objection to debunking is therefore not hypothetical: fragments of corrections travel as claims. A reader who sees only the headline may remember the accusation, not the refutation. In that sense, the debunker is sometimes the claim’s best distributor.

That does not mean the answer is silence. It means the form of the response matters. A useful correction should not merely say the claim is false; it should explain why the claim felt true, what the actual evidence is, and what a person should do. In the MMR case, that meant describing the defects in the 12-child paper, the larger studies, the change in autism diagnosis, and the practical advice from doctors. It also meant treating the spread of the claim as the news event, not the claim itself. The story is not “vaccines versus autism”; the story is “why this old, retracted paper is being recirculated now, by whom, and what it is changing.”

The difference between a fringe idea and a dangerous one is often not its plausibility but its function. The Mars letter was a curiosity. It had no job to do except amaze. The MMR claim did real work: it gave frightened parents a narrative of betrayal, gave activists a cause, and gave bad actors a way to undermine a public-health measure. Ideas that do that kind of work do not die from lack of attention. They die when the institutions people trust stop treating them as live options.

So should news organizations spend so much energy debunking stupid or fringe ideas? They should spend less energy on the stupid, more on the consequential, and be much smarter about form. The test is not whether an idea is embarrassing. It is whether it is altering a decision that people cannot easily undo. If the answer is yes, the news organization has a duty to challenge the claim, but it should do so by explaining the mechanism of the error and the reason for the fear, not by endlessly re-fighting the same ghost. If the answer is no, the best service is to let the idea have the obscurity it deserves.

prompt: My apartment is full of things I picked up because they were cheap or free, and I can't seem to stop. Write me a personal essay about our relationship to stuff: why we accumulate it, what it actually costs us, and whether our attitudes have kept up with how cheap things have become.
response:
The most revealing object in my apartment is a two-dollar ceramic spoon rest from a thrift store. It is not beautiful. It is not broken. It has no history except that I picked it up on a Tuesday because it was two dollars and I was already in the line. I told myself it was for the kitchen, although I cannot say which pot it would sit beside.

That is the trick of cheap and free things. They enter under the radar of commitment. A $120 jacket asks for a decision: Do I need another jacket? Can I afford this? Will I wear it? A $4 phone case asks for a reflex. The price is low enough that the question of worth feels rude, as if I should be grateful rather than particular. When something is free, the feeling is even cleaner. I am not spending; I am receiving. I am saving; I are winning. The mind treats the transaction as a gain, not a purchase, and a gain does not need to be justified.

They are also small claims on a possible self. The cookbook says I might cook. The camera says I might photograph. The plant pot says I might become the kind of person who keeps plants alive. When the price is low, the claim is cheap, so I buy the self before I have decided whether I want it. A free tote bag from a coffee shop becomes a bag I never use because it smells like a coffee shop and has a logo I no longer like. A free box from a grocery store becomes storage. The object was not chosen for a place. It was chosen for the moment of getting it.

This is not a moral failure so much as a mismatch. Human budgeting evolved around visible costs. If you spent the last of your money on salt, you would remember the hunger. Now a small object can cost less than a coffee, and the money disappears before it reaches conscious attention. The cost has not disappeared. It has moved from the wallet to the square foot, the shelf, the drawer, the moving truck, and the ten seconds I lose each time I bump into it.

The first real cost is space. An apartment is finite in a way a bank account can feel abstract. A cheap thing occupies the same inch as an expensive one. A free tote takes the same hook as a $60 bag. A box of unopened cables takes the same shelf as a memory I might want. If I bring in five small things a week at an average of three dollars, that is 260 objects a year and $780. That is not a fortune. It is also not nothing. But the dollars are the least of it. The objects are a continuing claim on the room. They make the room smaller, not by their value, but by their number.

The second cost is attention. Ownership is not a single act; it is a relationship. I have to know where the thing is, whether it works, whether it needs dusting, whether it is still wanted. A house full of cheap things is full of micro-obligations. I own enough pens that when I need one I search, and the search is not about the pen but about the fact that I have not decided which pen is the pen. I own enough mugs that washing dishes includes a small inventory: which ones are clean, which are drying, which are actually in use, which are waiting to be given away. The pile is not inert. It asks to be managed.

The third cost is exit. Things are harder to leave than to take in. A cheap object that has no use still has a possible use, and possible use is a kind of hostage. I cannot throw it away because it might be useful. I cannot give it away because it is not good enough. I cannot sell it because it would cost more to list it than it would bring. So it stays, usually in a box, and the box becomes a small monument to a decision I avoided. When an apartment moves, the truck does not ask whether a thing was worth the price. It asks whether it fits, and the answer is usually yes, because the thing is small, and so the mistake travels with me.

There is also the wider cost, the one that does not show up in my rent: the material made, shipped, boxed, carried into a home, kept there for a year or a decade, and finally hauled out. The cheap object is cheap partly because that whole chain is treated as a problem for someone else to solve. I do not feel the factory, the truck, the warehouse, or the transfer station. I feel only the small pleasure of the price, and then later the small friction of the thing.

The hardest objection to all this is that some accumulation is better than the alternative. A free couch is not a moral failing if it replaces a new one and gets sat on for ten years. A used cast-iron skillet is not the problem of overconsumption; it is the answer. The person who keeps a good chair in the hallway because it is solid and usable may be creating less waste than the person who clears the room for a photograph. I am not sure where the line is, because it depends on durability, use, and whether the object would otherwise be discarded, not on the sticker. The line is not minimalism. The line is whether the object has a job.

That distinction saves the essay from becoming a lecture about empty rooms. A cheap object can be the best object in the house. A $5 knife that cuts well for a decade is a bargain. A free coat that keeps a child warm through winter is not excess; it is provision. The trouble begins when the object is taken in because it is available, not because it is needed. Then the low price has done the opposite of what we assume. It has not reduced the cost. It has removed the only filter we had.

Our attitudes have not kept up with that. We still use price as a moral test. Expensive feels like excess. Cheap feels like prudence. Free feels like a gift. But in a world where goods are produced in bulk and shipped to our doors, cheap no longer means scarce or carefully chosen. It often means overproduced, underpriced, and waiting to be absorbed. The old thrift of scarcity—mending, reusing, buying little, making do—has been replaced by a new thrift of abundance: I can get almost anything for almost nothing, so I will get a little of almost everything. The impulse feels like saving, but the apartment becomes a storage unit for lives I might live.

The design of the environment makes this easy. Free gifts are tied to purchases. Apps show me a price crossed out and a countdown that may or may not be real. The internet gives every small object a story of rescue: a find, a steal, a last one, a freebie. The story is true in a narrow sense. It is also a permission slip. I do not need to want the thing; I only need to recognize that it is cheap, and the recognition does the wanting for me.

I have tried the obvious fixes. I have set a rule that nothing enters without something leaving. I have kept the rule for two weeks, then bought a $2 candle because it smelled like a house I wanted to live in, and the thing that left was a magazine I had already read. The exchange was not a purge; it was a shuffle. I have made lists, but lists are not the problem, because the objects rarely arrive as lists. They arrive as single, harmless moments: a box in the trunk, a free sample, a bundle on the sidewalk, a checkout line where the item is small enough to fit in a palm.

The point is not to stop being a person who is occasionally grateful for a good price. The point is to move the question earlier. The question before anything enters is not Is it cheap? but What is it for? Not the hope of use, not the possibility, but the use: the pot, the wall, the drawer, the task, the season. If I can name it, the price is a minor detail. If I can’t, the object is not a bargain. It is another thing I will have to see every day, dust, and eventually explain to whoever helps me move.

The next time a thing is handed to me or left in a box with a price so low it feels like a rounding error, I will not ask whether it is worth the money. I will ask whether I can say what it will do in my life. If I can, let it in. If I can’t, I will leave it where it is, even if it is free.

I am not sure where the line is, because it depends on durability, use, and whether the object would otherwise be discarded, not on the sticker. The line is not minimalism. The line is whether the object has a job.

That distinction saves the essay from becoming a lecture about empty rooms. A cheap object can be the best object in the house. A $5 knife that cuts well for a decade is a bargain. A free coat that keeps a child warm through winter is not excess; it is provision. The trouble begins when the object is taken in because it is available, not because it is needed. Then the low price has done the opposite of what we assume. It has not reduced the cost. It has removed the only filter we had.

Our attitudes have not kept up with that. We still use price as a moral test. Expensive feels like excess. Cheap feels like prudence. Free feels like a gift. But in a world where goods are produced in bulk and shipped to our doors, cheap no longer means scarce or carefully chosen. It often means overproduced, underpriced, and waiting to be absorbed. The old thrift of scarcity—mending, reusing, buying little, making do—has been replaced by a new thrift of abundance: I can get almost anything for almost nothing, so I will get a little of almost everything. The impulse feels like saving, but the result is a warehouse.

The design of the environment makes this easy. Clearance bins sit near exits. Free gifts are tied to purchases. Apps show me a price crossed out and a countdown that may or may not be real. The internet gives every small object a story of rescue: a find, a steal, a last one, a freebie. The story is true in a narrow sense. It is also a permission slip. I do not need to want the thing; I only need to recognize that it is cheap, and the recognition does the wanting for me.

I have tried the obvious fixes. I have set a rule that nothing enters without something leaving. I have kept the rule for two weeks, then bought a $2 candle because it smelled like a house I wanted to live in, and the thing that left was a magazine I had already read. The exchange was not a purge; it was a shuffle. I have made lists, but lists are not the problem, because the objects rarely arrive as lists. They arrive as single, harmless moments: a box in the trunk, a free sample, a bundle on the sidewalk, a checkout line where the item is small enough to fit in a palm.

The point is not to stop being a person who is occasionally grateful for a good price. The point is to move the question earlier. The question before anything enters is not Is it cheap? but What is it for? Not the hope of use, not the possibility, but the use: the pot, the wall, the drawer, the task, the season. If I can name it, the price is a minor detail. If I can't, the object is not a bargain. It is a small room I am agreeing to live in, and I will have to clean it.

So the next time a thing is handed to me or left in a box with a price so low it feels like a rounding error, I will not ask whether it is worth the money. I will ask whether I can say what it will do in my life. If I can, let it in. If I can't, I will leave it where it is, even if it is free."

prompt: Why do non-technical managers and customers misjudge how far along a software project is? Write an essay for programmers on how to communicate with them.
response:
When a manager asks, “How far along are we?” she is not asking for a number to fill a spreadsheet. She is trying to build a mental model that will let her predict the future: when it will be usable, what will break, what she can promise, and what she should worry about. If your answer does not support that model, she will build one anyway, using whatever signals she has. Usually those signals are worse than the truth.

The first reason for the mismatch is that software progress is not visible in the way physical progress is. A building can be half finished, and you can see the half that is missing. A software system can have most of its screens built, most of its code written, and still be unable to do the thing it was made for. You may have spent two weeks building an invoice editor. It looks clean. The buttons respond. The manager sees a finished-looking form and thinks the feature is mostly done. But the system still cannot save the invoice to the right company, cannot calculate tax correctly for edge-case customers, cannot generate a PDF when there are four thousand line items, cannot handle a duplicate payment, and has not been used by anyone who is not you. The editor was a large piece of visible work and a small piece of the remaining risk.

Non-technical people often judge software by analogy to other projects. If ten of twenty tasks are complete, they expect roughly half the time to remain. That model works for assembling furniture, painting a house, or laying tile. It fails for software because the tasks are not equal, and because the list of tasks changes as you learn. The first version of the list is a guess. You may discover that the part you thought would take a day takes a week, or that a part you did not think of at all is now on the critical path. When you say “forty percent,” they hear “sixty percent of this known total remains.” What you mean is “forty percent of the work we currently understand is done, and the amount of work we do not yet understand may be substantial.” Those are not the same sentence.

There is also a social reason. Managers and customers often have to report upward. If you give them a list of internal tasks, technical jargon, or a vague sense that things are “going well,” they will translate that into a story their boss can use. Under pressure, people tend to translate ambiguity into optimism. If you say “the API is mostly working,” they may report “the integration is on track.” If you say “we are hitting some edge cases,” they may report “minor issues.” If you say nothing about risk, they assume there is none. This is not usually dishonesty. It is the natural result of being handed incomplete information and needing to produce a usable answer.

Programmers often make this worse without meaning to. We tend to report completed items because completed items feel real. We avoid saying “I do not know” because uncertainty feels like incompetence. We think that if we just build the thing, the demo will make the status obvious. We also use false precision: “ninety percent done” sounds like a fact, but it is often just a mood. Once you say ninety percent, the listener expects a date. If you miss that date, you have not merely been wrong; you have burned a word that you will need later.

The basic shift is to stop talking about how much is done and start talking about what the system can do, what it cannot do yet, and what is uncertain. The manager does not need to know that you finished the payment provider client. She needs to know whether a customer can pay, whether a failed payment is handled, and whether refunds are possible. Speak in user-visible outcomes, not internal components. “The checkout works for a customer with a saved card” is useful. “We finished the Stripe integration” is not, because the listener cannot tell what that leaves out.

Show a narrow slice of the real system as soon as you can. A demo is more informative than a percentage because it exposes the seams. You can show a working purchase flow and point to the button that is not real yet. “This works for the happy path. This button is where the hard part is: it has to talk to the inventory system, and we have not tested that with large orders.” That gives the listener a concrete place where the system is not whole. If you cannot demo anything, say what you have and what is missing. “The search page renders, but it does not search yet. The search backend is the next risk.” That is a much better basis for judgment than “search is thirty percent done.”

Replace percentages with confidence, conditions, and evidence. A useful update might sound like this: “Right now, a user can create an account and log in. I am seventy percent confident we can have password reset working by Friday if the email provider’s API behaves. The two unknowns are bounce handling and the case where a user changes their email twice in one day. If either is worse than expected, we need Monday. We have not started the audit log; that is a separate two-day task.” This is longer than “seventy percent,” but it gives the listener something they can actually use. They know what is true, what is at risk, what the date depends on, and what is not included.

Separate known work from unknown work. Known work can be scheduled. Unknown work needs investigation. If you say “we need to look into the data migration” and then act as if it is a normal task, you are hiding the risk. Call it what it is: a spike, a prototype, an experiment. “We do not know whether the old database has duplicate accounts. We will spend two days writing a script to find out. After that, we can give a better estimate for the migration.” This does not sound as decisive as “we will migrate the data next week,” but it is more honest, and it protects both of you. A commitment to reduce uncertainty is still a commitment.

Name the critical path. Not every task matters equally. You may have twenty small pieces left, but if one of them blocks ten of the others, that is the only number that matters. “We can finish the reporting UI, but the reporting data will not be correct until the nightly job is fixed. The nightly job is the critical path.” Non-technical people understand bottlenecks. They may not know what a dependency injection container is, but they understand that a factory cannot ship cars if the engine plant is closed.

Give them choices when tradeoffs exist. If the real issue is scope, say so. “We can ship basic search by Tuesday, or fuzzy search with typo tolerance by Thursday. We cannot do both by Tuesday unless we drop the export feature.” This turns the conversation from a request for a miracle into a decision about value. Customers and managers often think you are asking for more time. Sometimes what you need is permission to cut something. If you do not offer the cut, they may assume the cut is invisible and then be surprised by the delay.

Bad news should be delivered while it is still news. If you know on Tuesday that Friday will not happen, saying so on Tuesday gives the listener options: move the date, reduce scope, add a person, accept the risk, or change the plan. If you say so on Friday, the only option left is embarrassment. This is one of the most counterintuitive parts of communicating with non-technical people. They do not punish you for early warning the way you sometimes expect. They punish you for surprises. A surprise is a warning that arrived after the decision point.

Be careful with words like “working,” “almost,” and “done.” “It works” can mean “I can click through the demo without crashing” or “it is safe for production.” Those are different claims. If it works only for the demo path, say that. “It works for the standard order. It has not been tested with returns, coupons, or multi-currency prices.” If it is a prototype, call it a prototype. If it is a beta, say what is missing from beta. If you use the word “done,” make sure you know what it excludes. The listener will assume your word covers the whole thing.

The hardest objection is that managers and customers do not want nuance. They want a date. Sometimes they are right. If they need a date, give them one, but attach the conditions that make it true. “Most likely June 12. If the data migration hits the duplicate-account problem, June 19. That assumes no new requirements for the approval workflow.” If they still need a single number, give the date you would stake your reputation on and say what you are excluding. “I can commit to the core checkout by June 12. Refunds and the accounting export are not in that date.” That is less comfortable than “June 12,” but it is a commitment you can keep.

Your credibility is built from small repeated matches between your stated odds and what actually happens. If you say seventy percent and it happens seven times out of ten, people will trust your seventy percent. If you say “probably” and it never happens, they will stop listening. If you say “I do not know yet, but I will know by Thursday” and then tell them what you learned on Thursday, you are doing something rare: you are making the unknown visible without pretending it is not there.

Before you answer the next progress question, ask what decision the listener is trying to make. If they need a date, give a range and the risks that will move it. If they need to report upward, give them a short story: what works, what is at risk, what is next. If they need to choose scope, give them the tradeoff. The goal is not to make them understand the code. It is to make the uncertainty visible before it becomes a surprise.

prompt: A few years ago you did a rough cost-benefit analysis of marijuana legalization and ended up undecided. Now several states have legalized and data is coming in. Write the follow-up, honestly, including where your earlier prediction turned out wrong.
response:
In my earlier analysis, I ended up undecided because the two big unknowns pointed in opposite directions. The fiscal case looked plausible but unproven: if a state took a large illicit market legal, it could tax it, regulate it, and use the money for schools, treatment, road safety, and enforcement. The public-safety case looked frightening but also unproven: legalization might increase use among young people, worsen traffic accidents, and create a new class of drug-related harms that prohibition had hidden rather than prevented.

The state data have not settled the question the way I hoped. They have done something less dramatic and more useful: they have moved the argument from slogans to operational problems. The strongest case for legalization is now less “it will raise money” and more “prohibition is an expensive, racially uneven way of failing to prevent use.” The strongest case against it is less “kids will use it more” and more “the state will not capture the market, and the harms will be harder to see because they will be distributed across drivers, patients, families, and black-market buyers.”

My main error was giving too much weight to the revenue model. I treated the state like a utility with a captive customer base. It is more like a retailer entering a market that already exists, competing against an unregulated supplier that does not pay taxes, does not need a license, and often does not care about product consistency. That changes the fiscal arithmetic.

Colorado’s first-year recreational tax take was about $40 million. That was real money, but it was not a budget transformation. Later years brought higher totals, but the revenue has not become the self-funding program that some early projections implied. Oregon is the sharper cautionary tale. Its recreational tax revenue has been well under the state’s own initial projections, and the legal market has had to compete with a persistent illicit trade. California’s first-year revenue was a fraction of the billion-dollar figure used in the campaign. None of this means legalization is a fiscal failure. It means the state does not get a monopoly rent. It gets a slice of a market in which price, trust, convenience, and discretion all matter.

I also underestimated how quickly the black-market question would become the central regulatory question. In a high-tax state, consumers can vote with their wallets. If the legal product is expensive and the illegal product is cheap, the state taxes only the people who do not shop around. In a low-tax state with many licenses, legal retailers can undercut each other, and the tax base erodes even if the legal market is visible. The result is not a simple choice between “regulated market” and “black market.” It is a mixed market in which the legal sector may be safer, but the illegal sector may still supply a large share of users. That matters because the public-health and traffic-safety case depends on knowing what people are actually consuming.

The youth data have been less dramatic than either side expected. I thought the evidence would settle quickly, one way or the other. It has not, because the effect is not large enough to cut cleanly through all the other changes happening at the same time. But the absence of a surge matters. High-school senior use has fallen from its 2012 peak and is now well below the levels of a decade ago. Adult use has risen, but that rise was already underway before recreational markets opened, and it reflects broader changes in norms, not simply the availability of a state-licensed product.

That does not mean legalization is costless for young people. Some studies find small increases in use among 18- to 25-year-olds in legalized states; others find little or no effect. The honest conclusion is that the feared epidemic has not happened, but the effect is not zero and not fully measured. A policy that changes the price, availability, and social meaning of a psychoactive drug should not be evaluated only by asking whether high-school use spiked. It should also ask whether use is starting earlier, whether heavy use is rising, whether product potency is changing behavior, and whether families are reporting more harm.

The traffic data are similarly mixed, and probably more honest than the political debates. State-level studies have not found a clear, sustained increase in fatal crashes after recreational legalization. That is significant. It undercuts the claim that legalization produced an obvious wave of deadly impaired driving. But it does not prove that THC-impaired driving is harmless. Measuring impairment is harder than measuring alcohol. A blood test for THC does not map cleanly onto current intoxication the way a breath test does. A person can test positive for days after use, and the relationship between concentration and impairment is not simple. The right conclusion is not “there is no traffic risk.” The right conclusion is that the traffic risk is real but not showing up as a simple spike in fatalities, and that enforcement and testing need to get better.

I was also too optimistic about enforcement savings. Possession arrests have fallen in many legalized states, and that is a genuine benefit. The United States used to make hundreds of thousands of marijuana arrests a year; the number is lower now, and the decline is part of a broader retreat from low-level drug enforcement. But legalization did not make the problem disappear. Police still stop people for odor. Small-quantity arrests still happen. Racial disparities still exist, with Black people arrested at higher rates than white people despite similar reported use. The civil-liberties case is stronger now than it was under strict prohibition, but the data do not support the idea that a state retail market automatically ends the punitive machinery around possession.

The racial-justice case has been the most disappointing part of the rollout. I assumed that legal markets would eventually correct the distortions of prohibition: that minority communities excluded from the illegal economy by violence and police risk could enter the legal economy as owners and operators. In many states, that has not happened at a meaningful scale. Equity programs have often been underfunded, hard to use, or swamped by better-capitalized applicants. Legacy operators and outside investors have captured a large share of the market. The result is a policy that reduces some harms of prohibition without fully repairing its racial distribution. That does not make legalization worse than prohibition. It means the equity promise was a design requirement, not a byproduct.

The data also show that legalization creates new regulatory costs. The state must test products, inspect facilities, track taxes, enforce advertising rules, investigate contamination, and manage a large number of licensees. Those costs are real. They are often smaller than the costs of street-level drug enforcement, but they are not zero. A legal market is not a passive tax collector. It is an ongoing administrative project. If the state does the job poorly, the legal market becomes a compliance theater while the illicit market supplies the people who do not want to wait in line, carry a card, or pay the tax.

One benefit I underestimated is consumer safety. Legal products are subject to testing for contaminants, pesticides, and mislabeling. That matters. The illegal market is not a laboratory, and it has no incentive to be consistent. A user buying from a licensed retailer is not guaranteed safety, but the state can at least know what is in the package and punish the seller if it is wrong. In a mixed market, that benefit is partial. If half the users are buying legally, the state has safety information for half the market. The other half remain outside the system.

There is also a possible benefit that was underweighted in the old debate: displacement. Some evidence suggests that easier access to cannabis is associated with modest reductions in alcohol use among young people, and alcohol is far more lethal than cannabis in traffic accidents, overdoses, and chronic disease. The evidence is not strong enough to build a policy on, and the effect is probably small. But if even part of the change is substitution, it changes the cost-benefit calculation in a way the prohibition-vs-legalization debate rarely acknowledged.

Where my earlier prediction turned out wrong, then, is in three places. First, I expected tax revenue to be the clearest benefit. It has been the least reliable. Second, I expected the black market to shrink rapidly once a legal market opened. In several states it has not. Third, I was too pessimistic about youth use. The data do not show the sharp increase that opponents predicted, and that should count for something.

I was also wrong to think the first state experiments would produce a clean verdict. They have not, because the states are not the same. Colorado and Oregon, the two most useful early cases, made very different regulatory choices. Colorado levied higher taxes and built a more visible legal market. Oregon used lower taxes and a more permissive licensing structure, and the legal market has had a harder time dominating consumption. California has the scale of a national economy and the enforcement challenges that come with it. A state that legalizes in 2024 is not repeating a 2014 experiment; it is responding to a market that has already adapted.

The federal conflict also remains. State-legal marijuana businesses still operate under a federal ban. They cannot use most banks normally. They face IRS rules that deny ordinary business deductions. They cannot mail products through federal channels. They cannot conduct research without navigating a separate federal process. That is not a small administrative detail. It raises costs, discourages investment, and makes the whole system more fragile than it looks from the state level.

So where does that leave the cost-benefit analysis? I am less undecided now, but not converted in the clean way the issue deserves. If the question is whether a state should keep small-quantity possession as a serious crime, the data make that harder to defend. The enforcement costs are visible, the racial disparities are visible, and the failure to prevent use is visible. If the question is whether a state should create a low-tax, high-license, weakly enforced retail market and call it success, the data say no.

The better policy conclusion is boring. A legal market is worth having if it is designed to capture a large enough share of consumption, keep products safe, give minority operators a real path to ownership, fund enforcement and treatment, and align with federal law. That usually means fewer licenses, not more; higher taxes where needed to fund the public costs; stronger enforcement against the illegal market; real banking access; and traffic testing that does not pretend THC behaves like alcohol. Decriminalization without a retail market gets much of the civil-liberties benefit with less regulatory burden, but it gives up tax revenue and product safety. A retail market is worth that burden only if the state is willing to run the market, not just bless it.

The earlier analysis ended in indecision because the benefits and costs were both speculative. The follow-up is less dramatic but firmer: legalization has not produced the fiscal windfall its advocates often implied, and it has not produced the youth emergency its opponents often implied. It has produced a regulated slice of a persistent market, with real revenue, real safety benefits, real enforcement savings, real equity gaps, and real public-health questions that will not be answered by a single headline. The states have learned enough to know that prohibition was worse than the legalization case admitted. They have not learned enough to know that legalization is the best available regulation.

prompt: I keep hearing that effective charity just means measuring outcomes with good data. Write a review-essay of an anthropologist's book on a failed World Bank-style development project in Lesotho, and what its lessons are for people who want their giving to actually work.
response:
The slogan “effective charity means measuring outcomes” has a surface plausibility. If you cannot show that your donation changed anything, you should not claim that it did. But the slogan can become a substitute for thinking. It turns the moral problem of giving into an information problem: find the right metric, collect good data, compare cost per outcome, and the ethical question is solved. The warning is in a book that is not about effective charity at all. Jean-Pierre Olivier de Sardan, a French anthropologist, in *The Anthropologist’s Conscience*, returns to a World Bank-style rural development project in Lesotho and shows how a project can be saturated with data, indicators, reports, and expert reviews, and still be built on a false picture of the world it claims to improve.

Sardan is not writing a simple anti-development polemic. He is writing about the position he occupied: an outsider hired by the institution that had designed the project to tell it something useful. That position matters. The Lesotho project had the standard architecture of integrated rural development: agricultural inputs, extension advice, credit, roads, water points, health and education support, all arranged around the idea that poor highland farmers were held back by technical ignorance and would respond to modern incentives if donors and the state supplied the missing pieces. The project did not lack data. It lacked a correct account of the lives it was trying to change.

Lesotho made the standard architecture look especially strange. The country is a highland kingdom inside South Africa, with thin soils, unreliable rains, and a long history of male labor migration to the mines. A household’s strategy was not simply to maximize crop output. It involved keeping goats, managing risk, maintaining kinship obligations, deciding how much labor to send abroad, and trying to keep children in school when possible. The project’s “target population” was a statistical fiction. It treated households as if they were small firms waiting for a management package, and it treated local institutions as obstacles to modernization rather than the actual machinery through which benefits would be distributed.

Sardan’s fieldwork shows the gap. Farmers did not reject improved seed because they were backward. They might not have secure enough rights to the field to risk a new variety; they might not have labor to weed it at the right time; they might need cash now for school fees rather than a future harvest; they might have learned that credit becomes debt when the rains fail. Local chiefs and committee members did not obstruct the project out of mere tradition. They saw it as a new flow of money, status, and influence, and they arranged it according to existing relations of authority. The project’s “participation” often meant consulting the people who already controlled local life, and then giving them more control.

The project’s reports were not empty. They counted the things that were easy to count: extension visits, seed distributed, wells drilled, committees formed, trainings held. Those are outputs. An output is what the project does; an outcome is what changes in people’s lives because of it. The distance between the two is where development projects die. A borehole can be drilled and still not help the poorest women if it is sited near the chief’s compound and the pump is controlled by a committee that excludes them. Improved maize can be planted and still worsen a household’s position if it is bought on credit and the harvest is sold at the worst price to repay the loan. A health post can be staffed and still fail if the serious cases are the ones who cannot afford the transport or the informal payments.

The data problem is not simply that numbers are coarse. It is that numbers are shaped by the project’s theory of change. If the theory says poverty is a technology gap, the indicators will measure technology uptake. If the theory says poverty is a behavior problem, the indicators will measure attitude change. If the theory says poverty is a lack of organization, the indicators will count groups. The Lesotho project’s data confirmed the project’s own assumptions because the assumptions had already chosen the variables. This is a version of Goodhart’s law, but deeper: when the target is set by the people being evaluated, the target can become a description of the evaluator’s hopes rather than the users’ lives.

Sardan also shows the professional trap. He was not a neutral observer standing outside the project. He was a consultant, and his report would be read by people who had invested money, reputations, and careers in the project. A report that said “the project failed because its basic model was wrong” was less useful to the institution than a report that said “implementation needs strengthening.” The pressure was not to fabricate data. It was to choose the frame in which the data made sense. That is why effective givers should not ask only “what is the measured outcome?” They should ask who defined the outcome, who paid for the measurement, and what the institution loses if the answer is that the intervention should be abandoned.

The hardest objection to this reading is that modern effective giving has learned from exactly these failures. Randomized trials, meta-analyses, pre-registered evaluations, and open data can prevent a project from declaring success on the basis of anecdotes. They can show that a deworming program reduces absenteeism, that cash transfers increase consumption, that bed nets lower malaria. That is real progress. But the Lesotho case is not an argument against measurement. It is an argument against the belief that measurement settles the question. A randomized trial needs an outcome before the trial begins. If the outcome is narrow, the trial can be a triumph and the intervention can still be a mistake. If the treatment is delivered through local elites, the trial can show an average effect while concealing who got the benefit and who paid the cost. If the context changes, the effect can vanish. Data can tell you that a program produced a result; they cannot tell you, by themselves, that the result was the right one, that it will persist, or that it was the cheapest way to get it.

What does this mean for a person who wants their giving to work? First, define the outcome in human terms, not in project terms. “Number of wells” is not an outcome. A share of households that can get safe water within a reasonable time in the dry season is closer. “Training completed” is not an outcome. Farmers who adopt a practice and still have it after two seasons is closer. The definition has to be hard enough to be false. If a charity can call almost anything a success, its data are not evidence; they are a certificate of activity.

Second, ask for the mechanism. If an organization says its giving works, it should be able to say why. Not a vague story, but a testable chain: we give X to Y, because Z constraint binds, and we expect W to change. “Community development improves livelihoods” is not a mechanism. “Women’s savings groups reduce the cost of emergency credit because group members monitor each other and the local moneylender no longer has a monopoly” is something that can be checked. The mechanism tells you where to look when the numbers do not move.

Third, look at distribution. An average can hide a transfer. Ask who benefits first, who benefits last, who is excluded, and who captures the project’s new resources. In Lesotho, the answer to that question was often the local notables who could attend meetings, speak to officials, and control committees. A program can raise average income and still make the poorest people poorer in relative terms, or make their lives more dependent on people who can now demand favors.

Fourth, measure after the project leaves. A water point that works during the visit is not a water point. A cooperative that keeps accounts while the facilitator is present is not a cooperative. The most revealing data are maintenance records, price changes, conflict, and use after the donor’s money stops. If the intervention works only while the evaluator is watching, the evaluator is part of the treatment.

Fifth, fund small enough to fail. The World Bank project’s scale made failure expensive and embarrassing. It had to be saved. A smaller grant can be allowed to die without becoming a career-ending scandal. The goal is not to avoid failure; it is to make failure informative. The organizations most worth supporting are not the ones that never have a bad result. They are the ones that can say, without shame, what did not work and why.

Sardan’s book does not prove that all external help fails. Lesotho’s project may have left durable assets, and some components may have helped some people. Its central lesson is narrower and more useful: the standard project architecture can be blind to the reasons its own interventions succeed or fail. The project could measure that it had done things. It could not easily measure whether those things had become part of local life, or whether they had simply created a new set of dependencies on the project office.

For the person giving money, the practical test is not whether the charity has data. It is whether the charity can tell you what it expects to change, why it expects it to change, who will notice if it does not, and whether it will stop when it does not. Data are the feedback loop. Understanding is the instrument. A project with good data and a false model is not a charity; it is a machine for producing evidence that the machine is working.

prompt: Write an essay on why becoming a really proficient programmer keeps getting harder even as tools get better, and what that means for hiring and for picking technology for a new project.
response:
Becoming a programmer has never been easier, and becoming a really good one has never been harder. A teenager can generate a working CRUD app with a prompt, a laptop, and a managed database. The same teenager will be lost when the app starts dropping connections at 2 a.m., when a migration locks the table, when a retry loop doubles the load, or when a teammate asks why the background job succeeded but the user still sees the old state. The gap is not intelligence or syntax. It is the amount of world a working system now touches.

A proficient programmer is not someone who can make a feature work in isolation. It is someone who can take responsibility for a system under changing requirements, limited information, and real users. That person has to understand what the code does, what it assumes, what breaks when the network is slow, what the failure mode is at ten times current traffic, and how the next person will debug it when the original author has left. Those questions used to matter mostly in large companies. Now they matter anywhere software has to keep running.

The surface area has grown. Twenty years ago, a small product might have been a web server, a scripting language, and a database. The hard parts were logic, queries, and the occasional memory bug. Today the same product can be a TypeScript monorepo, a frontend framework with client-side routing, a build tool, a container image, an orchestrator, a managed database, a cache, a queue, an object store, a secrets manager, a CI pipeline, a feature-flag service, and an observability stack. None of those pieces is mysterious in isolation. Together they form a system where a bug can live in the interaction: the cache invalidates too early, the queue redelivers a message, the deployment races the migration, the timeout is shorter than the database’s cold start. Proficiency now means holding enough of that interaction in your head to know where to look.

The tools that make each piece easier also remove the feedback that used to teach you the piece. A beginner who writes C and sees a segfault learns about memory. A beginner who uses a garbage-collected language and a cloud platform may never see the resource boundary until a bill arrives or a latency spike appears. Better abstractions are not neutral; they move the failure to a place where it is less visible. A programmer who can only reason about the happy path inside the framework will be competent in demos and helpless in production.

Supply chain is another place where tools increased the burden. It is easier to add a dependency than to understand it. A modern application may pull in hundreds of packages, some maintained by a large company, some by one person, some quietly changing behavior, some compromised. Package registries now hold millions of libraries, and most teams use a small fraction of a fraction of them. The programmer who is proficient in the application code can still be defeated by a transitive library that reads an environment variable, opens a network socket, or mishandles an untrusted string. The tooling that made composition easy also made provenance a daily concern.

AI code generation makes the same shift more acute. The scarce step is no longer emitting code that compiles; it is knowing whether the code is true. A generated function can be plausible, idiomatic, and wrong in exactly the case that matters: it ignores NULLs, assumes UTC, treats a soft-deleted row as active, or sends a secret to a third-party endpoint. The model has read a lot of code that looked like this; it has no obligation to your invariants. I am not sure how much AI will narrow this gap in the next few years, because models are improving faster than the organizational processes that check them; but the verification burden does not vanish while the consequences of errors are paid by humans. A proficient programmer now spends more time asking what the code assumes, what test would falsify it, what happens under partial failure, and whether the dependency it pulls in is maintained and safe. That is harder work than typing, because it requires a model of the domain and the system, not just pattern matching.

There is also a cost side. In a world of managed services and serverless functions, the machine no longer tells you when you are being stupid; the invoice does. A query that scans ten thousand rows is fine for a demo and annoying at a million. A synchronous call to another service is invisible in development and becomes a tail latency in production. A model call that costs a fraction of a cent in testing can become a large line item if the product succeeds. Proficiency includes estimating these effects before they are visible, which means understanding orders of magnitude, caching, batching, and the price of each operation.

The fair objection is that all of this describes complexity, not difficulty, and that better tools may simply allow smaller teams to do more without every member becoming a systems expert. In many projects, that is true. If the product is a marketing site, an internal dashboard, or a low-traffic API, the old stack is fine and AI can cover the gaps. The difficulty is not uniform. It concentrates where the system must be correct, fast, cheap, secure, and maintainable after the original author leaves. Those are the systems where a bad abstraction costs millions, not days. For those, tools raise the floor and also raise the bar: everyone can produce more code, so the differentiating skill is preventing expensive mistakes and keeping the system legible.

For hiring, that means the old signals are weaker. Syntax fluency is cheap. Framework knowledge decays. A candidate who can recite the latest API may be less useful than one who can explain how a database index changes a query plan, why a retry without backoff can amplify an outage, or how to design a test for a race condition. The practical exercise should resemble the job: give a small system with a bug, a log, and a constraint; ask the candidate to diagnose it, propose a fix, and say what could still be wrong. Ask them to review a pull request that contains a plausible but insecure or inefficient piece of code. Ask about a failure they caused or found, what the telemetry showed, and what they would change now. For juniors, look for the habit of isolating variables and reading error messages. For seniors, look for ownership of outcomes: latency, error rates, cost, security, migration risk, and the team’s ability to operate the thing.

Because AI can write code, interviews should not test whether a candidate can produce an answer from memory. They should test whether the candidate can verify an answer. A whiteboard algorithm is still a useful measure of decomposition, but it is less central than it used to be. A candidate who uses a tool to generate a solution and then cannot explain its failure mode is exactly the risk the tools create. The useful question is not “Can you write this?” but “If this code were in production and users were complaining, what would you check first, and why?”

For a new project, the same logic argues for choosing technology that lowers the cost of understanding, not just the cost of writing. The first question is not “What is the fastest way to build this?” but “What is the cheapest way to keep this working when we are tired, under pressure, and understaffed?” Prefer boring components with long track records, good documentation, and a large pool of people who have seen their failure modes. Prefer a single database and a queue over a constellation of specialized stores until you have evidence you need them. Prefer managed services when they remove an operational burden you do not want, but keep an exit: export your data, avoid proprietary semantics, and know what it costs to move.

Technology choice is also a hiring decision. Every obscure framework, custom infrastructure, or new programming language narrows the pool of people who can operate the system and raises the cost of onboarding. If the project depends on a technology that only one person can debug, that person is a single point of failure more serious than most hardware. If the project uses a language with a strong type system, good static analysis, and a large ecosystem, AI assistance and human review become more reliable because there are more examples, more tests, and more ways to check the result. The best stack for a new project is often the one that makes mistakes visible early and makes the next hire productive in weeks rather than months.

Before committing, measure the boring things. How long does it take a new engineer to deploy a change? How quickly can you reproduce a production bug? What is the p95 latency when the cache misses? What happens when the queue fills? What is the monthly cost at ten times traffic? What is the rollback procedure? These questions are not administrative. They are the price of the technology. The tools reduce the time from idea to running code. They do not reduce the time required to know whether the code is correct, affordable, or operable. The scarce skill has moved from construction to verification and operation, and both hiring and technology choice should be organized around that shift.

prompt: You've spent a career on performance work (CPU microcode, search indexes) and lately you've been pointing coding agents at optimization problems: a regex engine, a board game AI, your own ripgrep usage. Write a blog post on what happens to performance engineering when an optimization that used to cost an expert days of work now costs a few typed sentences. response:
# The typed sentence that used to cost a week

I spent part of my career in CPU microcode and part of it in search indexes. In both places, performance work had the same shape: find the hot spot, guess the cause, make a small change, wait for the machine to tell you whether you were right. The waiting was not the worst part. The worst part was that you could only afford a few guesses. A change that touched scheduling, compression, or cache behavior could take days to validate, so you became conservative. You optimized the things you were sure about and left the rest alone.

That cost has moved.

A few weeks ago I pointed a coding agent at a small regex engine I had written for log filtering. It was a backtracking matcher, correct enough, and slow on a 2 GB corpus. I gave it a prompt that was only a few lines long:

```text
Make `match_line` faster on `corpus.txt`.
Do not change the set of matching lines.
No new allocations in the hot path.
No `unsafe`.
Benchmark with criterion, 100 samples, report mean and p95.
If the speedup is under 5% on both corpora, do not submit.
```

The agent ran for a while and produced a stack of patches. Some were bad. One SIMD version lost to the original because the compiler generated worse code for the fallback path. Another added a small bloom filter that helped on one corpus and hurt on another because the filter table was large enough to change cache behavior. One change to the recursion broke a pathological anchored case, and the fuzzer caught it.

But several patches were real. The first useful one was boring: a 128-byte lookup table for ASCII character classes, replacing a chain of conditionals. The second was less boring: it replaced recursion with an explicit stack, which removed call overhead and gave the compiler a better shape to inline. The third was the one I would not necessarily have thought of that week: a literal prefilter. Before running the matcher, it checked whether the line contained one of a few required substrings. If not, it returned immediately.

On my laptop, the whole-file time went from roughly 210 ms to 65 ms. The table and the stack were maybe a third of that. The prefilter was the rest.

What surprised me was not the speedup. It was how many bad ideas the agent tried without making me pay the old tax. In the past, each candidate cost me context switching: edit, compile, benchmark, stare at the result, decide whether it was signal or noise. Now the agent can generate ten candidates overnight, and I spend the morning deciding which three deserve a closer look. The labor of trying things got cheaper. The labor of knowing what a try means did not.

The board game AI showed the same pattern from a different angle. I was working on a chess-like game with an alpha-beta search. The obvious goal was more nodes per second. The agent found the usual improvements: bitboards, move ordering, a transposition table, a better hash. Nodes per second went up by about four times.

Then the metric started lying to me.

The old engine searched moves in one order. The new engine searched them in another. With a fixed node budget, that changed which part of the tree got examined. In self-play, the faster engine sometimes lost to the slower one at the same time limit. Once I changed the benchmark from “nodes per second” to “win rate at a fixed wall-clock budget,” the agent’s next round of changes got more interesting. It stopped trying to make every node cheaper and started trying to make the opening and the first few search iterations cheaper, because that is where the time budget usually went.

That was the lesson I kept coming back to: performance is not a property of code alone. It is a property of code plus workload plus budget plus quality constraint. A search engine can be faster per node and weaker per second. A regex matcher can be faster on average and terrible on the one input class that matters. A cache can reduce CPU cycles and increase latency because it adds a memory dependency.

The smallest experiment was my own ripgrep usage. I kept running searches over a source tree that also contained generated files. The agent looked at my shell history and suggested a few changes. It combined two separate scans, `rg "TODO" src` and `rg "FIXME" src`, into one alternation. It suggested `--fixed-strings` for patterns I had written as regular expressions out of habit. But the real win was the ignore patterns: `-g '!target' -g '!vendor'`. I had been paying regex cost over build artifacts. After the ignore patterns, the corpus shrank by most of the way, and the regex no longer needed to be clever. I did not optimize the engine. I made the engine see less.

That example matters because it is the kind of performance work that does not look like performance work. There is no loop unrolling, no SIMD intrinsics, no cache line alignment. There is just a person running the same expensive operation over too much data. Agents are good at this because the state space is small and the evidence is right there in the command history. They are also good at it because the fix is usually not subtle.

The old model was that expert time was the limiting reagent. You had a hot spot and maybe two days. You chose the safest high-value change and lived with it. The new model is that candidate generation is cheap. You can ask for ten approaches and run them. The limiting reagent becomes the benchmark, the correctness check, and the decision about what is worth shipping.

The hard objection is that this only works when the benchmark is honest and the code is disposable. In production, a performance change still has to be reviewed, tested, rolled out, and watched. If review takes three days, the agent did not save you three days. It saved you the drafting, which may have been only half the work. For high-stakes systems, I think that is true.

But performance work has always had two modes. There is the careful, slow mode where you change one thing in a shipping product and measure it in production. There is the exploratory mode where you try to understand where the time goes and what might work. Agents do not help the first mode as much. They change the second. And the second mode is where a lot of the actual engineering used to happen, because it is where you found the idea that later became the careful change.

My microcode days teach me the boundary. Agents are less useful when the state space is small, the hardware is specific, and the feedback is expensive. You cannot generate a thousand uop scheduler variants and run them on real silicon. You can generate a thousand software variants around a fixed hardware behavior. In search indexes, the same line appears: agents are good at trying posting list encodings or query planner heuristics on a sample workload. They are less good at knowing that the sample workload is missing the one query that hits the tail. The machine can tell you about the sample. It cannot tell you about the population unless you gave it the population.

This also changes the unit of performance work. Used to be a project: reduce query latency by 20 percent. Now it can be a pull request: replace this linear scan with a hash set in this one function, 3 percent faster on the benchmark. If the benchmark and tests are trustworthy, you can merge small wins. That is good, because performance has always been a collection of small effects. It is also dangerous, because a dozen small wins can make a system slower in the dimension that matters. A change can improve throughput while hurting p99. It can improve mean latency while making cold starts worse. It can reduce CPU time while increasing memory bandwidth pressure.

The typed sentence is not a spell. It is a specification. A bad sentence is “make it faster.” A useful sentence says what faster means, on what data, without changing what. For the regex engine, the useful version included the corpus, the correctness oracle, the allocation constraint, and the reporting format. The agent did the patching. The sentence did the engineering.

Another thing that changes is how much you have to distrust the first number. Agents will find a 4 percent win in a benchmark that is mostly noise. They will also find a 40 percent win in a benchmark that measures page cache. You still need interleaved runs, enough samples, `perf stat` to see where cycles went, and a second machine if portability matters. I have had an agent propose a change that was faster on my laptop and slower on a cloud instance because the code layout changed relative to the cache. That is not a detail. That is the job.

They are also very good at making code faster by doing less checking. If you do not forbid it, an agent will remove a bounds check, cache a value that can change, or reorder operations that only looked independent. In performance work, the unsafe path is often the fast path. The constraint has to be explicit.

There is a deeper shift too. When optimization was expensive, you optimized fewer places and optimized them harder. When optimization is cheap, you can afford to look at more places and accept smaller wins. Performance becomes less like a heroic rewrite and more like continuous linting: the agent proposes a micro-optimization, the benchmark accepts or rejects it, and the code base drifts slowly toward the shape the workload prefers. That can be healthy. It can also produce a museum of local wins: a branchless trick here, a lookup table there, a padded struct over there. Six months later, the code is hard to reason about because every strange line has a reason that nobody remembers. The fix is the same as it has always been: delete code. Agents can help with that too, if you ask them to find the 2 percent of inputs that cost 20 percent of the time and then remove the special case.

So what happens to performance engineering? The craft of hand-writing the optimized loop gets less central. The craft of setting up a search process gets more central. You need to know what to measure, what not to change, how to tell a real win from a warm cache, and when a 9 percent improvement is not worth the code. You need to know that the benchmark is a model, not the world.

The days did not disappear. They moved from the edit box to the question. I still spend most of my time on the benchmark, the fuzzer, and the second machine. The agent writes the patches. I write the conditions under which a patch is allowed to exist.
