prompt: Write an essay about what it means for a programmer to really have a program loaded in their head, what helps or hurts that state, and what it implies about how companies organize software work.
response:
A programmer has a program loaded in their head when they can stop reading the code and start predicting it. If someone says “the retry queue is growing,” the loaded programmer does not first ask where the queue is defined. They already know it sits between the order service and the payment worker, that the worker has ten slots, and that the queue length usually rises when payment calls time out. They can form a hypothesis before opening a file. They can also mark the edge of their model: “I don’t know what happens if the same payment callback arrives twice.” That edge is part of the state. It is not a perfect copy of the code. It is a working simulation, compressed into a handful of moving parts, with known holes.

The loaded program is not a picture of every line. No one holds a million-line system as a single image. A two-hundred-line state machine can be held in considerable detail. A two-million-line codebase cannot, but a useful model of it may consist of a dozen named state stores and the transitions between them. In an inventory service, one chunk might be “stock is checked optimistically and decremented only after the order row is inserted.” Another might be “the email is sent after commit, and the email consumer can run twice.” A programmer who has those chunks can reason about a change to the order flow even if the change is made in a file they have not read that day. A programmer who has only the file names can reason locally, but every step outside the local function is a guess.

This matters because software change is prediction. To add a field to an API, you need to know where the field comes from, where it goes, what breaks when it is null, and who else reads the table. To fix a flaky test, you need to know what shared state the test touches and whether the flake is timing, data, or environment. The more of the program is loaded, the farther a small edit can safely travel. The less that is loaded, the more the programmer must compensate with caution, tests, and review. The same change can be a two-minute edit for one person and a dangerous excavation for another, not because of skill alone, but because of what each of them can simulate.

The state is built by contact. Running the program helps more than almost anything. A log line that carries a request id through three services is a peg for the model. A database query plan shows where an abstraction lies. A failing integration test forces the programmer to admit that the assumed boundary was wrong. Repetition helps, but not the boring kind. What sticks is the repetition of consequences: seeing the same bad assumption produce the same bug, or seeing a clever shortcut become a maintenance cost. A programmer who has debugged cache invalidation once is not memorizing code; they are carrying a scenario.

Consistent names help too, because names are the smallest chunks. If “reservation” always means a temporary hold that expires, and “allocation” always means a committed decrement, the reader can infer behavior from vocabulary. If the same word is used for three related but different states, the model has to be rebuilt in every module. Explanation builds the model as well, especially when it is offered to someone who can interrupt. Pair programming works partly because one person’s private assumptions become visible in the other’s questions. A junior engineer asks, “Why do we need this flag?” and the senior discovers that the flag was a workaround for a database migration that finished in 2021. Teaching a design review forces the author to choose which invariants matter. Documentation can do the same, but only when it is written as a model rather than a record. A good page says what the system promises, what it does not promise, and where the promise becomes expensive. A bad page lists components and makes the reader rebuild the model from scratch.

The state is destroyed quickly by context switching. A programmer can hold a small number of active scenarios at once; that is a limit of attention, not willpower. If they spend twenty minutes in a meeting about a different service, the first service does not pause politely. It fades to a set of names. When they return, they must reload the entry points, the current branch, the open bug, and the half-formed idea. The cost is not just the minutes lost. It is the increase in local guessing. After enough switches, people start making changes that are safe in the file but wrong in the system, because the system is no longer present.

Some structures hurt the loaded state more than others. Hidden side effects are expensive: middleware that rewrites requests, database triggers that update other tables, feature flags that change behavior by user cohort, decorators that retry calls. Each one adds state that is not visible at the call site. Distributed boundaries are more expensive still, because the programmer must model not only code but clocks, networks, retries, and partial failures. A synchronous call across a service boundary is not the same as a function call, even when the interface looks identical. The loaded model must include the failure mode, or it is a toy.

The same is true of organizational boundaries. If a user-facing behavior is split among frontend, backend, data, and platform teams, no one may have the full path loaded. Each team can be excellent inside its slice, while the product becomes a handoff problem. The classic microservice failure is not that services are small; it is that the real business process spans many small services and no team owns the process. A checkout flow that touches eight services can be harder to change than a checkout module in one large codebase, because the mental model required is larger than the code in any one service. The boundary between teams should usually be a boundary that a human can understand: a domain concept, an actor, a workflow, or a data lifecycle. If the boundary is “everything that uses Postgres” or “everything in the mobile app,” the model is organized by technology, not by meaning.

Companies therefore have a design problem that is often mistaken for a people problem. They want work units that are large enough to produce a coherent model but small enough to be finished. A ticket that says “add a field” may be a tiny model if the field lives in one object, or a huge one if it crosses persistence, search, exports, and client contracts. prompt: People often argue that fear of new technology has historically done more harm than the technology itself (nuclear power being the classic case), and so we shouldn't be too cautious about AI. Is that argument right? Write an essay on how to think about it.
response:
The argument has a real core. Novelty is not a reason for fear. Many technological anxieties have been overblown, and caution can become a way of avoiding hard choices: local opposition dressed up as public safety, regulatory inertia dressed up as prudence, or powerful institutions using “risk” to slow rivals. If that is the whole point, it is worth taking seriously. But as a reason for thinking about AI, the argument is too coarse. It mistakes a warning about rhetoric for a fact about risk.

The nuclear case is the one people reach for, and it is less clean than it looks. There is a defensible claim that fear of nuclear power did harm. After Three Mile Island in the United States, new nuclear construction largely stalled, public support fell, and a number of existing plants closed earlier than they would otherwise have. Some of the generation that replaced nuclear was fossil generation. If more nuclear plants had been built and kept running, some coal and gas would not have been burned, and carbon emissions would have been lower. That is a real harm, and it matters in a climate-constrained world.

But nuclear technology itself also caused harm. Chernobyl killed thirty-one people acutely, displaced hundreds of thousands, and left a contaminated region; estimates of later excess cancer deaths range from a few thousand to tens of thousands, depending on assumptions. Fukushima caused massive evacuations and plant damage, with no deaths officially attributed to radiation. More broadly, nuclear fission produced weapons. Hiroshima and Nagasaki killed roughly two hundred thousand people, and Cold War arsenals peaked at around seventy thousand warheads. Nuclear power also created persistent waste-management problems and expensive safety regimes. So the claim “fear did more harm than nuclear” depends on which nuclear harms you count, which counterfactual emissions you assign to anti-nuclear sentiment, and whether you include weapons at all. It is not a settled fact, and it is certainly not a general law.

The deeper problem is that nuclear power’s worst civilian accidents are of a kind we know how to manage. A reactor has a containment building, a coolant system, a physical location, and a regulatory history. You can inspect it, license it, modify it, and shut it down. The worst case is terrible, but it is bounded by geography and time. AI’s worst plausible failures are not like a leak in a containment vessel. They involve systems that can act at network speed, across jurisdictions, using language, code, and scientific reasoning. The harm may not be a visible cloud of contamination. It may be a coordinated manipulation of political institutions, an autonomous cyberattack on critical infrastructure, a research assistant that accelerates the creation of a dangerous pathogen, or a financial system exploit that unfolds faster than humans can understand it. These harms are harder to see, harder to reverse, and harder to assign responsibility for.

The historical argument also has a selection problem. We remember the panics that faded. We are less likely to remember the ones that were right. Leaded gasoline, tobacco, DDT, unsafe factories, passenger cars before crash standards and airbags: in each case, the unease was not merely irrational fear. It was an early signal that a technology had serious harms that could be reduced only by design changes, regulation, or social policy. Technology is not a moral category. The same machine can create wealth and injure workers. The question is never “is it new?” but “what specific harm is it likely to cause, how fast, to whom, and can we stop it?”

That distinction matters because AI fears are not one thing. Some are ordinary software complaints: bias, hallucination, copyright infringement, phishing, bad advice. They are real, but they are usually manageable with better testing, disclosure, liability, and user controls. Some are like industrial accidents: an autonomous system makes a bad decision in a power grid, a hospital, or a warehouse. They need safety cases, monitoring, fallbacks, and clear accountability. Some are strategic: AI that lowers the threshold for war, enables mass surveillance, or automates offensive cyber operations. They need arms-control-like thinking, not just product design. And then there is the tail that worries people most: a system with broad capabilities, weak alignment, and the ability to improve itself or manipulate its overseers. That scenario is not proven. But it is not the same category as the computer panic of the 1990s, where the feared harm was mostly social dislocation and the technology was already constrained by human labor and physical infrastructure.

The cost of caution is real, and anyone who ignores it is thinking badly. AI could speed scientific discovery, improve diagnostics, help manage energy grids, and increase productivity. If we freeze development, we may forgo benefits that save lives. If we impose heavy rules only on regulated firms, we may hand advantage to states, black markets, or less accountable actors. If we demand certainty before deployment, we will never deploy anything useful, because empirical systems are uncertain. So “caution” cannot mean “stop.” It has to mean “measure the risk reduction per dollar and per unit of delay.”

The hardest objection to a cautious view is that we may repeat the anti-nuclear mistake: allowing a low-probability worst case to dominate policy while blocking widespread benefits. The climate case is the sharpest version. If nuclear power would have reduced carbon emissions, then the people who said “we should be cautious” may have caused more harm through climate change than the reactor accident they feared. And AI safety, like nuclear safety, can become a language for powerful institutions to slow rivals, concentrate control, or avoid democratic accountability. This objection is strong enough to demand humility. It means we should not build our case on vibes or on the idea that intelligence is inherently dangerous. We should specify the capability, the failure mode, and the control. If we cannot do that, the caution is probably bad.

But the objection does not imply the opposite. It implies a different standard. For risks that are local and reversible, require disclosure and testing. For risks that are severe but manageable, require safety cases and liability. For risks that are global and potentially irreversible, require more evidence before deployment and international coordination. The nuclear analogy actually supports this if we use it honestly: we do not ban all pressure vessels because boilers exploded; we build codes, inspections, and certifications. We do not ban all flight because planes crash; we certify airworthiness. The mistake would be either to ignore the risk because the technology is new or to treat every AI system as if it were a reactor.

The specific AI tail differs from nuclear in one respect that should worry us: nuclear weapons are fixed. A warhead does not redesign itself. A reactor does not negotiate with its inspectors. AI systems can be updated, can use language to persuade, can write code that changes their environment, and may be deployed in many contexts before a problem is understood. That does not mean an intelligence explosion is coming. It means the object of regulation is not a static artifact but a process. We need methods for evaluating general behavior, not just checking that a model passed a benchmark.

So how should we think? First, separate the fear from the mechanism. “AI will take over” is not an argument. “A system with autonomous planning and access to financial markets could exploit a vulnerability faster than humans can detect it” is. Second, ask about reversibility. If the harm can be undone, we can learn by doing. If it cannot, we need pre-deployment evidence. Third, ask who bears the cost of delay. If delaying a medical diagnostic tool kills patients, the bar for caution is high. If delaying an autonomous offensive cyber capability preserves optionality, the bar is low. The harm may not be a cloud of radioactive particles; it may be a coordinated manipulation of institutions, an autonomous cyberattack on critical infrastructure, or a research assistant that accelerates the creation of a dangerous pathogen. These are harder to see, harder to reverse, and harder to assign responsibility for.

The same machine can create wealth and kill workers. The question is never "is it new?" but "what specific harm is it likely to cause, how fast, to whom, and can we stop it?"

They are real but usually fixable with better testing, disclosure, liability, and user controls. Some are like industrial accidents: an autonomous system makes a bad decision in a power grid or hospital. They need safety cases, monitoring, fallbacks. Some are like strategic weapons: AI that lowers the threshold for war, enables mass surveillance, or automates offensive cyber. They need arms-control-like thinking. Some are the scary tail: a system with broad capabilities, weak alignment, and the ability to improve itself or manipulate its overseers. That last category is not proven, but it is not the same as the computer panic of 1994.

If we impose heavy rules only on regulated firms, we may hand advantage to states or black markets. If we demand certainty before deployment, we will never deploy anything useful, because empirical systems are uncertain. So "caution" cannot mean "stop." It must mean "measure the risk-reduction per dollar and per unit of delay."

P7: Hardest objection: If we treat AI as an existential risk, we may repeat the anti-nuclear mistake of allowing a low-probability worst case to dominate policy. The climate case is the sharpest version. If nuclear power would have reduced carbon emissions, then the people who said "we should be cautious" may have caused more deaths through climate change than the reactor accident they feared. And AI safety, like nuclear safety, can become a language for powerful institutions to slow rivals, concentrate control, or avoid democratic accountability. This objection is strong enough to demand humility. It means we should not build our case on vibes or on the idea that intelligence is inherently dangerous. We should specify the capability, the failure mode, and the control. If we cannot do that, the caution is probably bad.

P8: But the objection does not imply the opposite. It implies a different standard. For risks that are local and reversible, require disclosure and testing. For risks that are severe but manageable, require safety cases and liability. For risks that are global and potentially irreversible, require more evidence before deployment and international coordination. The nuclear analogy actually supports this if we use it honestly: we do not ban all pressure vessels because boilers exploded; we build codes, inspections, and certifications. prompt: I just finished reading a book about bee cognition and I can't stop wondering: are bees actually smart? Write a funny but serious review-style essay that works through what we know about bee behaviour and where the line between instinct and real thinking might lie.
response:
**Review: The Bee as Small, Serious Mind**

The first sign that a book about bee cognition has done its job is that you stop seeing bees as punctuation. They are no longer tiny yellow commas landing on the sentence of your afternoon; they become small, furious colleagues with opinions about flowers. That is a useful feeling, because it forces you to abandon the comfortable idea that intelligence begins somewhere around the size of a rat’s brain. Bees do not fit that boundary. They are too clever for their bodies, which is either a miracle or an accounting error.

A honeybee’s brain is about the size of a pinhead and contains roughly 100,000 neurons. For scale, that is less than the number of neurons in a fruit fly’s visual system alone, and vastly less than a mouse. If you hold a bee up to the usual mammalian standard, it should be a flying reflex with wings. It is not. Bees navigate, remember, learn categories, communicate about distant places, and in some experiments appear to have a sense of number. The puzzle is not whether they are “really” smart; it is what counts as real.

Start with navigation, because that is where the case becomes hard to wave away. A foraging bee does not simply fly out and hope. It uses the sun as a compass, and on cloudy days it can read polarized light in the sky to estimate where the sun is. It uses landmarks. It uses smell. It can learn a route to a flower patch and remember it for days. If you move the landmarks, it does not merely crash into the world; it re-evaluates. That matters. A fixed instinct might say, “go left at the big rock.” A navigating animal says, “the big rock is supposed to be there; it is not; therefore my model of the world needs revision.” The bee’s model is not a map in the human sense—nothing so tidy—but it is a working representation. It has content, and the content can be wrong.

Then there is the waggle dance, which is the part of bee cognition that tends to make people reach for the word “language” a little too quickly. When a honeybee finds a good source of nectar, it returns to the dark comb and performs a dance: a straight run with a waggle phase, followed by loops back to the starting point. On the vertical comb, the angle of the waggle run relative to gravity encodes the angle of the food source relative to the sun. The duration of the waggle phase encodes distance. So a bee that found clover three hundred metres away, forty degrees left of the sun, does not simply announce “clover.” It draws a vector. Other bees watch or follow the dance, then fly out in roughly the right direction.

That is astonishing, but it is not human language. Bees do not have open-ended syntax. They cannot argue about the clover, invent a clover, or describe a hypothetical clover that might have been better if the sun had been elsewhere. The dance is more like an embodied advertisement: a directional recommendation with enthusiasm as amplitude. A good source produces a vigorous dance; a poor one produces a weak one, or none at all. That last point is important. The dance is instinctive in form, but not empty. A bee cannot dance about a flower it has not found. The template is inherited, but the data come from experience.

That distinction is where the line between instinct and thinking gets interesting, because “instinct” is often used as a magic word that means “not thinking.” But instinct is not the opposite of cognition. It is a prior. A bee is born with a brain already organized to solve certain problems: finding food, finding the way home, telling others where the food is. What it is not born with is the location of the clover. The colony has built a very good default operating system, but each forager still has to install local updates.

The learning is where the bees get troublesome. They can associate colours, odours, shapes, and places with reward. Train a bee to visit a blue card for sugar, and it will tend to prefer blue cards later. But it can do more than memorize a single card. It can generalize. Show it a new shade, a slightly different shape, a novel context, and it may still make the right bet. That is not a lookup table. That is categorization. In experiments, bees can be trained to prefer panels with small numbers of items over panels with large numbers—up to four, in the clearest cases—and then choose between numbers they have not seen before. Some studies even suggest they can learn the idea of “none,” which is a concept so abstract it feels like a bee-sized philosophical trick.

They are not doing arithmetic. Nobody should claim that a bee is sitting in a flower column and solving equations. What they appear to have is a quantity sense: a distinction between “a few” and “more than a few,” good enough to improve foraging decisions. That is still cognition. An animal that can extract a rule from repeated experiences, apply it to new stimuli, and adjust when the rule stops paying is not merely reacting. It is learning a pattern.

Then there are the puzzle experiments, which are where the internet likes to declare bees “geniuses” and scientists quietly sigh. In a lab, a bee can be taught to push a small disk aside to reach sugar. At first, that sounds like a rat in a box: animal bumps thing, sugar appears, animal bumps thing more. But the interesting version is not the first bump. The interesting version is the next puzzle, slightly different, where the bee has to figure out that the disk, not the wall, is the part that gives. If it goes for the disk with less random thrashing, something has been extracted from the previous experience. It has formed a representation of the task’s structure, however thin.

The same caution applies to all of this. Bees are small, their lives are short, and their cognition is built for flowers, not for human tests. A bee’s cleverness is not general intelligence in the way a chimpanzee’s or a crow’s is. It is compressed, sensory, and practical. Bees do not sit under a tree wondering what it means to be a bee. They do not have the metabolic luxury of an inner monologue. Their mind, if that is the right word, is a flight path.

And that is the hardest objection: maybe none of it is “real” thinking, just very elaborate instinct plus conditioning. A bee dances because bees dance. It chooses the blue card because it was rewarded. It pushes the disk because the disk happened to move before the sugar arrived. Why call that thinking?

Because the alternative cannot explain the flexibility. Pure instinct would not adjust when the landmark moves. Pure conditioning would not generalize from three dots to two dots against six. A fixed routine would not produce a dance whose angle changes depending on where the flower actually is. The content is not fixed. The bee’s behaviour changes with the world in ways that track the world’s facts. That is what thinking is for.

There is also the social dimension, which makes the whole thing stranger. A bee that has watched a dance can fly to a food source it has never visited. It is using another bee’s experience as evidence. The colony can regulate its temperature, allocate foragers, defend itself, and decide when to swarm in ways no single bee could manage alone. But one should not turn the hive into a giant brain too quickly. The colony is not a mind in the way a human is a mind. It is a system. The bees inside it are still individual animals, each with its own errors, preferences, and limited memory. The hive is smart the way a city is smart: through division of labour, feedback, and a lot of local decision-making that looks coordinated from above.

So where is the line between instinct and real thinking? There is no clean line, because the question assumes there is one. In bees, the line is a slope. At one end you have the inherited machinery: the dance pattern, the sun compass, the flower-loving visual system. At the other end you have the individual bee’s learned additions: this patch is good, that colour is risky, the disk is the handle, the sky is cloudy but the polarization says the sun is over the barn. The instinct provides the tools; the experience provides the information. Remove either and the bee performs badly.

That does not make bees wise. It does not make them self-aware, or moral, or capable of sitting in judgment on your life choices. They are not little philosophers. They are not little humans with wings. They are a different solution to the same problem: how to move through a changing world and extract energy from it without a big brain. Their cognition is not a smaller version of ours. It is a different shape, optimized for speed, economy, and flowers.

The honest answer, then, is that bees are smart in the sense that matters for an animal. They can learn, remember, generalize, communicate, and solve novel problems within the limits of their lives. They are not smart in the sense of being able to explain themselves. We will never know what it is like to be a bee, and they probably have no business to report. But the behaviour is too flexible, too informative, and too well matched to the environment to be dismissed as mere instinct.

So the next time a bee lands on your arm, do not make the usual mistake of treating it as a small accidental decoration. It is checking a situation. It has a compass, a memory, a preference, and a brain the size of a grain of rice. It is not pondering your soul. It is deciding what to do next. That is not nothing. In a creature that weighs less than a paperclip, that is a great deal.

prompt: A magazine article says polyamory has a problem because black people are underrepresented in it. Write a response from someone in the poly community, thinking about why any group might be demographically skewed and what the framing does.
response:
I read the article’s claim as a report card: polyamory, failing, reason: not enough Black people. The oddness is not that the writer cares about race. The oddness is that the sentence makes a racial population the test of a relationship practice’s success.

I am in the poly community, so I have a stake in this. I also don’t have a clean number, and I want to be plain about that. I don’t know how many Black people are polyamorous, because the label is self-applied and because people who maintain more than one relationship do not always organize their lives around the word. If “polyamory” means the people who show up to meetups, use the term in profiles, or appear in community directories, then the sample is already filtered by visibility, class, geography, and comfort with a particular kind of outness. If it means actual relationship patterns, the visible scene is a poor map. “Underrepresented” has to mean underrepresented relative to something: a city, a nation, an online platform, a neighborhood. A room in a wealthy suburb will look like a wealthy suburb. That is not automatically a moral failure, but it is not neutral either.

Any group is demographically shaped by the roads that lead to it. A climbing gym, a vegan co-op, a software meetup, a church, a mutual aid network: each one ends up looking like the people who can reach it. Access matters. Money matters. Safe housing matters. Language matters. Trust in institutions matters. If a practice spreads through online forums, college towns, progressive media, and private homes where people can talk without fear of family or employer consequences, it will not look like the whole population. It will look like the population with the most access to those channels. That does not mean the practice is bad. It means the visible form of the practice has traveled along certain lines.

But that explanation does not let a community off the hook. A demographic shape can be the residue of barriers. If Black people are underrepresented in a space because the space is in a place they do not feel safe in, costs money they cannot spare, assumes a communication style they were not rewarded for learning, or meets them with stereotypes the moment they arrive, then the underrepresentation is a trace of exclusion. The problem is not the number. The problem is what produced the number.

That is where the magazine’s framing gets shaky. “Polyamory has a problem because Black people are underrepresented in it” sounds like a concern, but it locates the problem in the absence rather than in the conditions. It turns Black people into the missing ingredient. Put them in, and the community becomes healthier, more legitimate, more modern. Without them, the community is incomplete. That is a strange thing to say about a group that has often been treated as morally suspect simply for existing in certain intimate arrangements. It implies that polyamory needs Black presence to prove that it is decent.

I think I understand the impulse behind the article. If you care about racial justice, an overwhelmingly white room can look like a moral failing, especially when the room is full of people who talk about consent, boundaries, and challenging norms. The mismatch is embarrassing. But the embarrassment is not the main issue. The main issue is whether Black people can enter, stay, and be believed without paying a special tax.

Representation is not the same thing as safety. A community can add a few Black members to its panels and feel better while leaving the underlying dynamics alone. It can celebrate diversity in the abstract while still treating Black anger as “too intense,” Black sex as “natural” or “spicy,” Black grief as a burden on the group, and Black relationship choices as a problem to be managed. Polyamory’s favorite tools are communication, honesty, and boundaries. Those tools do not automatically balance power. If a Black woman is in a triad with two white partners, the racial script does not vanish because everyone agreed to be transparent. Her feelings may be interpreted through old stereotypes. Her partners may be read as “evolved” while she is read as “exotic.” The structure can be consensual on paper and still feel unequal in practice.

The same is true for Black men, though the stereotypes are different. A Black man in a relationship with white women may be seen through a lens of predation or promiscuity, while the white partners are seen as open-minded. The community may say, “We don’t do racism here,” while nobody notices the racism happening in the micro-interactions. That is why a demographic audit is not enough. The question is not only who is in the room. It is who is trusted in the room, whose story is taken seriously in conflict, whose presence is treated as normal rather than illustrative.

There is also a cultural question the article seems to skip. Black intimate life has not been a simple mirror of mainstream marriage. It has been shaped by slavery, separation, migration, religious communities, extended family, economic survival, and constant surveillance. Some Black people may be deeply skeptical of a label that emerged from white progressive and therapeutic cultures. Some may find it useful. Some may have relationship patterns that overlap with polyamory without using the word. Some may be in churches where nonmonogamy is not a lifestyle option. Some may be queer and already outside the marriage script. Some may be parents for whom being open about multiple partners is a risk they cannot take. A demographic category cannot carry all of that. To say “Black people are underrepresented in polyamory” can flatten a lot of different lives into one absence.

I do not want to defend a white room by calling its whiteness natural. If poly spaces are hostile to Black people, that is a serious flaw. Polyamory claims to be about more honest relationships and more consensual structures. If it cannot handle its own racial dynamics, that claim rings hollow. The community should ask concrete questions: Are meetups accessible by transit? Are they cheap enough for people without disposable income? Do moderators actually intervene when someone is racially mocked? Do people of color have to explain themselves repeatedly? Are Black poly people treated as experts on race whether they want to be or not? Are relationships involving Black partners met with the same seriousness as other relationships? Are the community’s assumptions about privacy, family, and disclosure built around a particular class and racial experience?

Those questions matter more than the percentage.

The framing also does something subtle: it makes the community the victim of its own demographics. “Polyamory has a problem” suggests that the community is suffering because it is not representative enough. But if Black people are staying away, the suffering is not primarily the community’s missing diversity credential. The suffering is the lost possibility of connection, the avoided space, the repeated decision not to go where you will have to justify yourself. A magazine can turn that into a neat narrative about a movement’s failure to include, but the people on the outside may not be thinking about the movement’s image at all. They may be thinking about their own lives.

I also don’t think the answer is a quota. A quota can turn Black members into exhibits. “Look, we have representation now” is not the same as “we have changed the conditions that kept people away.” Inclusion should not mean that Black people are recruited to fix the room’s self-image. It should mean that the room stops being a place where whiteness is the default and everyone else is an addition.

There is a difference between a community being too white and a community being obsessed with its racial composition. The first is a fact about power and access. The second is a symptom of vanity. A group that is mostly white should not be proud of that, but it should be careful about how it complains about it. If the complaint is, “We are failing to reach Black people,” that can sound like a marketing problem. If the complaint is, “Black people report that they are not safe here,” that is a moral problem. The first invites strategy. The second demands accountability.

The hardest part of the article’s claim is that it is not entirely wrong to notice the skew. If a community says it is universal and then only one group shows up, something is off. But the notice has to be aimed correctly. The skew is evidence, not verdict. It points toward questions about access, safety, culture, and power. It does not by itself prove that polyamory is defective as a relationship form. It proves that the institutions carrying the form have a particular shape, and that shape may be exclusionary.

If I were responding to the magazine directly, I would say this: stop treating Black people as the measure of polyamory’s respectability. Polyamory does not need Black bodies to validate it. Black people do not need polyamory to be valid. The useful question is whether Black people who want to be in these spaces can be in them without being turned into a lesson in diversity. The less useful question is whether the scene has achieved the right demographic balance to look progressive in a magazine.

A relationship practice can be widespread and still be invisible in the institutions that claim to represent it. That gap is worth examining. But the examination should start with the people being kept out, not with the community’s discomfort at its own mirror.

prompt: I just finished a big political biography and realized my school-taught picture of how power works is basically a cartoon. Write an essay on how real political operators actually accumulate power, and what that implies for the rest of us.
response:
The school version is easy to state: candidates win elections, legislators pass laws, presidents sign them, and the person with the office has the power. A biography usually ruins that picture. It shows power as something assembled before the office, maintained through the office, and sometimes surviving after it. By “operator” I mean anyone who works inside the machinery: elected officials, party managers, lobbyists, senior bureaucrats, and the local notables who connect them to communities. The operator is not the person who holds the gavel; the operator is the person who knows which lever the gavel is attached to.

Real power accumulation starts with process. In any institution, the person who controls what is considered, when, and in what form controls much of the outcome. In Congress, that means committees, the calendar, amendment rules, and the whip count. Lyndon Johnson understood this better than most. Before becoming president, he had spent years as Senate majority leader, a job that let him shape the flow of business and use committee assignments as rewards. When he pushed the Civil Rights Act in 1964, he did not win it with a single speech. He worked senator by senator, knowing who needed a hearing, who feared a primary, who could be flattered, and who had to be threatened. The Senate vote, 73 to 27, was the result of a process he managed, not a sudden conversion of minds.

The second source is a network of obligations. Power is not only what you can do; it is what others feel they owe you. The classic local version is the political machine. In Chicago, the strength of the Daley organization under Richard J. Daley and later his son Richard M. Daley did not depend on a detailed philosophy. It depended on ward bosses, city jobs, permits, favors, and the sense that the organization would show up when a family had a problem. That network made the mayor powerful because it connected city government to thousands of small local relationships. The lesson is not that politics is a racket; it is that influence is built through repeated exchange. A person who has helped you once is useful; a person who has helped your neighborhood for a decade is a structure.

The third source is information. Operators accumulate power by knowing the constraints that are not on the public agenda: which budget line cannot be touched, which agency will block a bill, which donor is angry, which story the press is about to run. They also learn to release information in a way that shapes reaction. A controlled leak lets an official test an idea without committing to it. A carefully timed memo can turn a setback into a warning. The person who is believed to understand what is possible gains a kind of deference: even those who disagree on goals may accept his judgment on means.

Tenure compounds all of this. Institutions reward people who stay. In Congress, seniority and committee chairmanships used to be almost automatic rewards for longevity; Strom Thurmond became chairman of the Armed Services Committee in 1981 largely because he had served so long. In agencies, the career official who has written a rule before knows where the legal traps are and which industry group will object. The outsider sees a policy debate; the operator sees a route through signatures, staff comments, and precedents. This is one reason political power is often boring and cumulative: it is the product of being present when small decisions are made.

At this point the cynical reading feels natural: if power is process, favors, information, and tenure, it is just manipulation. That is the hardest objection to the view, and it is not wrong. Much of what operators do is manipulation. But the cartoon and the cynical manual both miss the same thing: constraints. An operator cannot simply will outcomes. He or she needs votes, money, legal authority, public legitimacy, and the cooperation of people who can defect. Paul Ryan was House speaker from 2011 to 2015, one of the most powerful offices in American politics, and he lost it in a revolt by the Freedom Caucus over a budget fight. The gavel did not save him because the gavel was not the source of his power. His power had come from a coalition, and when the coalition decided he was no longer delivering what it wanted, the office was not enough.

I am less sure how to separate skill from luck, because biographies also show wealth, family position, and historical moment doing as much as cunning. A charismatic outsider with money can disrupt a system that rewards incumbency, but usually cannot govern without eventually learning the levers. Money matters, but not as a magic wand. It buys time, access, research, and the ability to endure. It also creates obligations. An operator who takes money from a sector becomes, whether willing or not, an interpreter of that sector’s interests.

There is also a moral difference between a network and a corrupt network, though the line is often thinner than reformers like. A bureaucracy that follows rules and builds working relationships with the people it regulates is administration; one that trades enforcement for private loyalty is corruption. The test is whether the exchange is tied to a public task and can survive being seen. Operators who depend on secrecy are vulnerable; operators who can say why they are doing something are harder to displace.

For the rest of us, the implication is not that we should become operators in a sneaky sense. It is that the amateur’s map is wrong. If power is not a throne, you cannot reach it by waiting for the moment of the speech or the election. You have to enter the institutions where decisions are actually made. In most people’s lives that begins locally: the zoning board, the school board, the municipal budget, the union local, the hospital board, the professional association, the party precinct. These places are small enough that a persistent person can learn the rules, meet the people, and build a record. The person who shows up, asks questions, and helps resolve one dispute becomes a node in the network. That is how influence starts.

The practical skills are unglamorous. Learn who has to sign what. Keep a record of promises and votes. Use public comment, campaign finance disclosures, meeting minutes, and freedom-of-information requests not as symbolic protests but as tools for making the operator’s ledger visible. Build coalitions that survive the issue: a group formed to stop one project dies when the project is decided; a neighborhood association, workers’ group, or patient advocacy organization can be called on for the next fight. Be useful before you need something. If your only appearance is when you want a concession, you are a cost to an operator, not an asset.

But the same logic explains why democratic counterweights matter. If power is relational, it can be checked only by other relationships that are not controlled by the operator. Independent journalists, courts, auditors, opposition parties, and civic organizations matter because they create alternative ledgers and alternative audiences. A mayor who answers only to ward bosses can be challenged by a newspaper that knows the bosses’ deals. A regulator captured by an industry can be checked by a court that reads the administrative record. Transparency is not a virtue in the abstract; it is a way of forcing private networks to become public institutions. Operators often have staff and money that ordinary people do not, so the democratic task is not merely “get involved.” It is to build organizations that pool time and resources, and to keep rules that prevent wealth from buying the process outright.

The school cartoon makes power look like a person standing on a stage. The biography shows a web of meetings, memos, favors, threats, rules, and reputations. That is a less comfortable picture, because it means power is made in the unglamorous places where most people do not watch. But it is also a more workable one. The person who can explain why a permit was delayed, who called whom, and what the alternative vote would have been has more power than the person who merely objects. The rest of us are not powerless; we are usually just outside the process where power is being assembled.

prompt: In what situations does teaching technical topics with comics actually help, and is 'some people are visual learners' a good enough answer? Write a reflective blog post from the perspective of someone who makes programming zines.
response:
## What Comics Are Good For

I make little programming zines, the kind you staple in a bathroom and hand to someone who says, “I always thought APIs were magic.” A few weeks ago I made one about git merge conflicts. It is eight pages. Two of those pages are a comic: two versions of a file walk into a room, argue, and a third, uglier file is born. The other six pages are code, diffs, and commands.

When people finish it, they often say the comic helped. Then they add, “I guess I’m a visual learner.” I don’t buy that answer. It sounds like a preference, but the useful question is what the picture did that the prose couldn’t.

Comics help when the technical idea has a shape. Not just a fact or a rule, but a relationship: who talks to whom, what changes state, where the waiting happens, what breaks when the order changes. A network request is a sequence with delays and failures. A closure is a value that carries a small environment with it. A race condition is two events that are safe separately but unsafe interleaved. Those are easy to make into panels because the meaning is in the arrangement. If I draw a client, a server, and a packet moving between them, the reader gets a spatial model before the words arrive. The picture is not decoration. It is a compressed diagram with a narrative order.

This is where the visual-learner answer goes wrong. It treats the help as a property of the person, not the representation. “Some people are visual learners” does not tell me why a comic about DNS helps one reader and confuses another. It also quietly suggests that if you are not visual, a comic will not help you, which is nonsense. A comic is words and pictures. The words carry the precision. The pictures carry the structure. If the structure is the hard part, the comic can help almost anyone. If the hard part is exact syntax, edge cases, or formal proof, the comic can get in the way.

I have learned to separate three jobs that people lump together: making a topic approachable, making a model memorable, and making a skill executable. Comics are often good at the first two. They are not automatically good at the third. A comic can make HTTP feel less intimidating. It can give you a story about request, response, status code, retry. But it cannot replace the experience of reading a curl error, watching headers in DevTools, or debugging a redirect loop. If the zine ends with a cute mascot and no commands, the reader has a mood, not a method.

The best programming comics I have made are the ones where the image is doing work that code alone would make invisible. Take state machines. In code, a state machine is an enum, a switch, and some guards. It is hard to see the lifecycle. In a comic, the object can be a person at different stations: created, pending, active, cancelled. The panels show that some transitions are allowed and others are absurd. You can draw the illegal transition as a door that is bricked up. That is a concrete image for a constraint. It is not the implementation, but it is the thing the implementation is trying to enforce.

Concurrency is another case. A text description of a deadlock can be accurate and still hard to hold in your head: two threads each hold a lock and wait for the other. A comic can show two characters standing in a doorway, each holding the other’s key. The joke is almost unavoidable, but the joke is not the point. The point is that the waiting is mutual and structural, not accidental. Once the reader sees the shape, the code becomes a description of the shape rather than a spell to memorize.

But comics fail when the technical topic is mostly local detail. Regular expression syntax is a bad comic subject unless you are teaching the very first intuition that a pattern is a search with constraints. You can draw a little creature scanning a string and catching the words it wants, but the creature does not teach backreferences, non-capturing groups, or why your pattern fails on the twelfth test case. For that, you need the actual pattern, the actual string, and the actual error. The comic becomes a sugar coating that makes the reader overconfident. I have seen this with zines about regex: people love the pages where the dot is a wildcard and the asterisk is a greedy mouth, then get stuck when the real pattern has anchors and character classes. The mental model was too cute.

That is the hardest objection I keep coming back to: comics can teach a false model and make it feel obvious. In programming, false models are expensive. If a comic suggests that the browser “sends the request and then waits politely,” the reader may not think about DNS, TLS, connection reuse, or intermediate proxies. If it suggests that a database transaction is just a save button, the reader may not understand isolation levels. The comic’s strength—making something feel simple—can become its danger.

The fix is not to avoid comics. The fix is to make the boundary of the model visible. In the zine, I try to include a page called “What the cartoon leaves out.” It lists the simplifications: the network is not a tube, the server is not a person, the merge conflict is not a fight that can be settled by picking a side. The comic gets to be useful because it is not allowed to be the whole truth.

This is also why “visual learner” is not enough as an answer. Learning-styles talk has a comforting symmetry: visual, auditory, kinesthetic. But I don’t think the popular version of that idea explains much. A person who says they learn visually may actually benefit from diagrams because diagrams reduce working-memory load, or because they can compare alternatives side by side, or because the image gives them a place to attach a verbal explanation. A person who says they learn by doing may benefit from a comic if it motivates them to open the terminal. The medium is not the style. The medium is a set of constraints. Comics force sequencing. They force economy. They force you to choose one image per idea. That can be excellent pedagogy or terrible pedagogy depending on the idea.

I think comics are most useful at the boundary between ignorance and confusion. A beginner facing a new technical domain often has two problems at once: the content is hard, and the reader is anxious about being bad at it. A comic can lower the second problem without fully solving the first. The panels say you are allowed to be lost. The jokes say the experts are not solemn. The small page count says this will not eat your evening. That matters. I have handed zines to people who would not open a long article. Not because they are visual, but because the zine looks like a toy. They read it standing up. They laugh at a bad pun. Then they notice they have an image of the thing in their head. The image is not the knowledge, but it is a hook.

Where comics are less useful is when the learner already has a working model and needs to refine it. If you understand how garbage collection works at a high level and need to understand generational assumptions, a comic of little objects aging in rooms may be charming but too coarse. You need numbers, thresholds, allocation rates, and the specific behavior of the collector you are using. The comic can orient you, but it cannot replace the precision. At that stage, a diagram may be better than a comic: static, zoomable, less narrativized. A comic adds time and character. Sometimes the topic needs less story and more structure.

There is also a practical zine constraint: the page is small. A comic panel can hold a label, a code snippet, and a face. It cannot hold a long stack trace. So when I make a programming zine, I am always deciding what the comic is for. Is it the first page, meant to make the reader trust the zine? Is it a summary at the end, meant to turn a list of facts into a picture? Is it the central explanation, because the topic is inherently sequential? Those are different uses. A comic as frontispiece can be decorative and still useful, because it sets the tone. A comic as summary can be useful if it compresses. A comic as core explanation is useful only if the core is structural.

I have become suspicious of comics that only translate text into pictures. If you can remove the images and the words still make sense, the images may be redundant. If you can remove the words and the images still make sense, the images may be too vague. The best cases are in between: the words say what is true, the images show what it is like. For example, in a zine about DNS, the text can say that a domain name is resolved through a chain of servers. The comic can show a child asking, “Who is in charge of this name?” to one adult, then another, until reaching the house. The text prevents the comic from implying that DNS is a phone tree. The comic prevents the text from being a dry list.

Is “some people are visual learners” a good enough answer? No. It is a good enough conversation stopper, which is why it persists. It is also hard to test. If the comic works, the person must have been visual. If it fails, they must not have been. But it does not tell a maker what to make. If I ask, “Who is this for?” and the answer is “visual learners,” I have not learned whether the topic has a spatial structure, a sequence, a contrast, or a failure mode. I have only learned that the audience prefers a label. The better question is: what is the reader supposed to be able to see after this that they could not see before?

If the answer is a shape, a comic may help. If the answer is a procedure, a checklist or code may help. If the answer is a feeling of permission to try, a comic can help even if the technical content is thin. My current rule of thumb is this: use comics when the hard part is holding several things in relation. Use them when the reader needs a first model, not a final one. Use them when the topic has moving parts, boundaries, or embarrassment. Do not use them when the hard part is exact notation, dense edge cases, or performance numbers.

And never hide the simplification. A programming comic can be honest if it says, on the page, what it is not showing: the timeout, the retry, the exception, the version difference. Then the reader can use the picture to find the room, without mistaking the door drawing for the lock.

I have learned to separate three jobs that people lump together: making a topic approachable, making a model memorable, and making a skill executable. Comics are often good at the first two. They are not automatically good at the third. A comic can make HTTP feel less intimidating. It can give you a story about request, response, status code, retry. But it cannot replace the experience of reading a curl error, watching headers in DevTools, or debugging a redirect loop. If the zine ends with a cute mascot and no commands, the reader has a mood, not a method.

The best programming comics I have made are the ones where the image is doing work that code alone would make invisible. Take state machines. In code, a state machine is an enum, a switch, and some guards. It is hard to see the lifecycle. In a comic, the object can be a person at different stations: created, pending, active, cancelled. The panels show that some transitions are allowed and others are absurd. You can draw the illegal transition as a door that is bricked up. That is a concrete image for a constraint. It is not the implementation, but it is the thing the implementation is trying to enforce.

Concurrency is another case. A text description of a deadlock can be accurate and still hard to hold in your head: two threads each hold a lock and wait for the other. A comic can show two characters standing in a doorway, each holding the other’s key. The joke is almost unavoidable, but the joke is not the point. The point is that the waiting is mutual and structural, not accidental. Once the reader sees the shape, the code becomes a description of the shape rather than a spell to memorize.

But comics fail when the technical topic is mostly local detail. Regular expression syntax is a bad comic subject unless you are teaching the very first intuition that a pattern is a search with constraints. You can draw a little creature scanning a string and catching the words it wants, but the creature does not teach backreferences, non-capturing groups, or why your pattern fails on the twelfth test case. For that, you need the actual pattern, the actual string, and the actual error. The comic becomes a sugar coating that makes the reader overconfident. I have seen this with zines about regex: people love the pages where the dot is a wild card and the asterisk is a greedy mouth, then get stuck when the real pattern has anchors and character classes. The mental model was too cute.

That is the hardest objection I keep coming back to: comics can teach a false model and make it feel obvious. In programming, false models are expensive. If a comic suggests that the browser “sends the request and then waits politely,” the reader may not think about DNS, TLS, connection reuse, or intermediate proxies. If it suggests that a database transaction is just a save button, the reader may not understand isolation levels. The comic’s strength—making something feel simple—can become its danger. The fix is not to avoid comics. The fix is to make the boundary of the model visible. In the zine, I try to include a page called “What the cartoon lies about.” It lists the simplifications: the network is not a tube, the server is not a person, the merge conflict is not a fight that can be settled by picking a side. The comic gets to be useful because it is not allowed to be the whole truth.

This is also why “visual learner” is not enough as an answer. Learning styles talk has a comforting symmetry: visual, auditory, kinesthetic. But I do not think it explains much. A person who says they learn visually may actually benefit from diagrams because diagrams reduce working-memory load, or because they can compare alternatives side by side, or because the image gives them a place to attach a verbal explanation. A person who says they learn by doing may benefit from a comic if it motivates them to open the terminal. The medium is not the style; the medium is a set of constraints. Comics force sequencing. They force economy. They force you to choose one image per idea. That can be excellent pedagogy or terrible pedagogy depending on the idea.

I think comics are most useful at the boundary between ignorance and confusion. A beginner facing a new technical domain often has two problems at once: the content is hard, and the reader is anxious about being bad at it. A comic can lower the second problem without fully solving the first. The panels say you are allowed to be lost; the jokes say the experts are not solemn; the small page count says this will not eat your evening. That matters. I have handed zines to people who would not open a long article. Not because they are visual, but because the zine looks like a toy. They read it standing up. They laugh at a bad pun. Then they notice they have an image of the thing in their head. The image is not the knowledge, but it is a hook.

Where comics are less useful is when the learner already has a working model and needs to refine it. If you understand how garbage collection works at a high level and need to understand generational assumptions, a comic of little objects aging in rooms may be charming but too coarse. You need numbers, thresholds, allocation rates, and the specific behavior of the collector you are using. The comic can orient you, but it cannot replace the precision. At that stage, a diagram may be better than a comic: static, zoomable, less narrativized. A comic adds time and character; sometimes the topic needs less story and more structure.

There is also a practical zine constraint: the page is small. A comic panel can hold a label, a code snippet, and a face. It cannot hold a long stack trace. So when I make a programming zine, I am always deciding what the comic is for. Is it the first page, meant to make the reader trust the zine? Is it a summary at the end, meant to turn a list of facts into a picture? Is it the central explanation, because the topic is inherently sequential? Those are different uses. A comic as frontispiece can be decorative and still useful, because it sets the tone. A comic as summary can be useful if it compresses. A comic as core explanation is useful only if the core is structural.

I have become suspicious of comics that only translate text into pictures. If you can remove the images and the words still make sense, the images may be redundant. If you can remove the words and the images still make sense, the images may be too vague. The best cases are in between: the words say what is true, the images show what it is like. For example, in a zine about DNS, the text can say that a domain name is resolved through a chain of servers. The comic can show a child asking “who is in charge of this name?” to one adult, then another, until reaching the house. The text prevents the comic from implying that DNS is a phone tree. The comic prevents the text from being a dry list.

Is “some people are visual learners” a good enough answer? No. It is a good enough conversation stopper, which is why it persists. But it does not tell a maker what to make. If I ask “who is this for?” and the answer is “visual learners,” I have not learned whether the topic has a spatial structure, a sequence, a contrast, or a failure mode. I have only learned that the audience prefers a label. The better question is: what is the reader supposed to be able to see after this that they could not see before? If the answer is a shape, a comic may help. If the answer is a procedure, a checklist or code may help. If the answer is a feeling of permission to try, a comic can help even if the technical content is thin.

My current rule of thumb is this: use comics when the hard part is holding several things in relation. Use them when the reader needs a first model, not a final one. Use them when the topic has moving parts, boundaries, or embarrassment. Do not use them when the hard part is exact notation, dense edge cases, or performance numbers. And never hide the simplification. A programming comic can be honest if it says, plainly, that it is a map of the map. The reader can then use it to find the room, as long as they do not mistake the door drawing for the lock.
