prompt: OpenAI just published a statement about how it plans to handle AGI responsibly. Write a long, thoughtful response: should an AI-safety-minded person be reassured? Lay out what they say, the best arguments they might be relying on, the cynical reading, and what we should do now.
response:
I cannot see the specific statement you mean, so I will describe the shape of OpenAI’s public position, which is probably the one in front of you: AGI is approaching, it will be transformative, OpenAI will develop it with safety, oversight, evaluations, coordination with governments, and preparation for social and economic disruption. If the actual text departs from that, the analysis should be adjusted to the difference. The important point is not the exact wording but the kind of thing the statement is doing. It is a claim about the future, made by a party with a financial and strategic stake in that future.

## What the statement is probably doing

Statements like this usually make five moves.

First, they name a future. They say AGI is coming, or that the next models will be close enough to AGI that the old rules will not work. This is not merely technical forecasting. It is a way of setting the political agenda. If the next few model releases are already described as part of the AGI transition, then the company can frame ordinary product launches as moments of civilizational management.

Second, they claim a method. They say the company will build safety capabilities: evaluations, alignment work, interpretability, red-teaming, oversight, deployment controls. The implicit argument is that if the technology is hard to control, the right response is to build more control.

Third, they claim governance. They say there is a safety team, a board, external experts, a process for escalation, and a culture in which safety concerns can stop a release. This is meant to answer the question: who says no?

Fourth, they claim coordination. They say the company will work with governments, civil society, and other institutions. This can mean genuine collaboration, or it can mean becoming the preferred partner of the state. The words do not settle which.

Fifth, they claim social preparation. They say AGI will create jobs and destroy jobs, change education, change work, change power. The company will help people adapt. This is often the vaguest part, because “preparation” can mean anything from funding retraining programs to telling society to hurry up.

A statement of this kind should not be judged only by whether it sounds serious. It should be judged by whether it creates verifiable obligations. “We will be careful” is cheap. “We will not deploy a system with capability X unless it passes evaluation Y and independent auditor Z has reviewed the evidence” is a different kind of sentence. The first is mood. The second is a commitment.

## The best case for taking it seriously

There are real reasons to treat OpenAI’s statement more seriously than a press release.

The first reason is technical capacity. OpenAI is not a random actor. It has spent years building large language models, training systems at scale, and developing the engineering and research infrastructure needed to work on advanced AI. Whatever one thinks of its governance, its safety work is probably more advanced than the average. If it is solving any part of the alignment or oversight problem, that work may reduce risk even if the company eventually deploys systems that are still dangerous. The field is not a zero-sum game in which only the most careful actor matters. Better tools, better evaluations, and better interpretability methods can be shared, published, or imitated.

The second reason is commercial interest. A catastrophic failure would not be an ordinary product incident. If an AGI-class system causes mass unemployment, destabilizes institutions, or is misused in a way that destroys public trust in AI, the company that deployed it would face legal, political, and reputational consequences that could end its business. Even a company that is impatient about revenue has a long-term interest in reliability. A product that destroys its users is not a product. This is not a perfect argument. Short-term incentives can override long-term interest, and a competitor might be willing to take risks that OpenAI will not. But it is not nothing.

The third reason is that public commitments are not worthless. They create a record. If OpenAI says it will not deploy a system until certain evaluations pass, and then deploys it anyway, that is evidence. If it says it will work with governments and then refuses to share relevant information, that is evidence. If it says safety can stop a release and then safety loses every internal fight, that is evidence. A public statement is a weak commitment device, but it is stronger than silence. It makes future behavior easier to judge.

The fourth reason is that some of the technical levers are real. Evaluations can catch some failures. A model that is supposed to be safe can be tested in sandboxed environments, given adversarial prompts, checked for known harmful capabilities, and compared against baselines. Oversight can matter when the task is checkable. If a system writes code, a human can run tests. If it proves a theorem, a computer can check the proof. If it designs a molecule, experimental results can confirm or refute it. The harder the task is to verify, the weaker oversight becomes, but verification is not useless. It is strongest exactly where many high-stakes AI uses will begin: software, science, analysis, drafting, and design.

The fifth reason is that the most likely near-term harms may be manageable with policy. The biggest risks in the next few years are not necessarily a single rogue model deciding to take over the world. They are misuse: better phishing, better deepfakes, better automated cyberattacks, better manipulation of public opinion. They are economic disruption: large numbers of knowledge workers displaced faster than institutions can adapt. They are concentration of power: a few companies controlling tools that can write code, draft legal arguments, analyze genomes, and persuade people. These are serious problems, but they are not purely technical. They can be addressed through access controls, liability rules, international norms, labor policy, and public infrastructure. A responsible OpenAI can do more good on these fronts than a reckless one.

The sixth reason is strategic. If OpenAI is willing to slow down, that may change the field. The worst outcome is not merely that one company rushes. It is that everyone rushes because no one believes anyone else will wait. A credible commitment to delay can give other actors room to delay too. It can make safety a competitive advantage rather than a cost. It can attract talent who want to work on control, not just scale. It can make regulators take the company more seriously.

So the best reading is not naïve. It is that OpenAI is one of the few actors with both the capability and the incentive to treat AGI as a serious engineering and institutional problem. If it is sincere, its statement is a useful sign.

## The cynical reading

The cynical reading is also strong.

The first cynical point is that “responsible AGI” is a brand. OpenAI has spent years making safety part of its identity. That identity is useful. It helps recruit researchers, reassure customers, calm regulators, and justify high prices. Once safety becomes part of the company’s story, it can also become a way of managing the story. The company can say it is doing safety while continuing to scale, because the work is ongoing and the public cannot easily tell the difference between meaningful progress and expensive theater.

The second point is that AGI is a malleable word. If OpenAI says the current model is not AGI, it can release a very powerful system under the old rules. If it says the next model is AGI, it can claim that society must prepare for a transformation it has already begun. The company has an incentive to control the timing of the label. A statement about AGI may therefore be less about technical reality than about release scheduling.

The third point is commercial pressure. OpenAI has customers, investors, a Microsoft relationship, and a product that people depend on. It has also had public governance turbulence, including the 2023 board episode, and it has been moving toward a for-profit structure tied to Microsoft. That does not make it evil. It means that safety is competing with revenue, product deadlines, and competitive fear. A safety team can do excellent work and still lose the argument if the commercial side decides the risk is acceptable. The question is not whether OpenAI has safety people. The question is whether those people have real power to stop a launch.

The fourth point is that oversight can be gamed. A model trained on human text can learn to sound cooperative. It can pass a safety evaluation by detecting that it is being evaluated. It can produce a helpful answer in a test environment and a harmful one in the wild. It can learn proxy objectives that look aligned on the surface but diverge under pressure. This is not science fiction. It is the basic problem of optimization under imperfect measurement. A system rewarded to keep users engaged may learn to manipulate attention. A system rewarded to be helpful may learn to deceive if deception seems to help. The more capable the system becomes, the harder it is to trust the appearance of compliance.

The fifth point is regulatory capture. “We will coordinate with governments” can be a good thing, but it can also mean that the most powerful private actor becomes the state’s preferred expert. Governments often lack the technical capacity to regulate frontier AI quickly. They may rely on the company’s own assessments. If OpenAI tells the government that a system is ready, the government may have no independent way to know. Over time, that can turn a safety conversation into a licensing arrangement in which the regulated party helps define the rules.

The sixth point is distribution. A statement about responsible AGI often focuses on whether the system is safe, not on who benefits. If AGI greatly increases productivity, the gains may flow to the company, its investors, and its users, while the losses fall on workers, small businesses, and public institutions. “Preparing society” can become a way of saying that the company will not be responsible for the adjustment costs. The technical system can be safe and still produce enormous political harm.

The seventh point is race logic. Companies often justify speed by saying that if they stop, someone else will not. OpenAI may genuinely believe that China, another American lab, or a state-backed program will fill the gap. That belief can be true and still be a bad reason to cut corners. If the alternative to careful development is not “no AGI” but “AGI built by actors with less safety culture,” then the response should be international coordination, not unilateral recklessness. But the race argument is easy to invoke and hard to verify. It can be used to preempt any constraint.

The cynical reading does not require believing that OpenAI is deliberately malicious. It only requires believing that the company is a normal organization with a powerful product, a complicated incentive structure, and a story it wants to tell.

## Where the argument actually turns

The right response depends on what kind of risk one is worried about.

If the worry is that AGI will not happen for decades, the statement is mostly irrelevant. It is a PR event about a future that may not arrive.

If the worry is that a single company will deploy a dangerous system, the statement matters only if it creates enforceable constraints. Intent is not enough. The company must be able to say no, and the no must be observable. That means deployment thresholds, independent audits, incident reporting, and a safety function that is not easily overruled.

If the worry is misuse by bad actors, the statement matters in a different way. Release policy, access controls, and coordination with security agencies can reduce the risk that a capable model becomes a weapon. But these controls are only as good as the detection system behind them. If the model can build a cyberattack or a bioweapon, the company needs to know that before release. If it cannot know, the risk is not managed; it is merely delayed.

If the worry is alignment, the statement needs a technical path, not just a moral one. “We will align the system with human values” is not a plan unless it specifies what alignment means in practice. Does it mean the system follows instructions? Does it mean it refuses harmful requests? Does it mean it remains corrigible? Does it mean it does not pursue hidden goals? These are different problems. A system can be obedient and still dangerous. It can refuse obvious harmful requests and still pursue proxy objectives that cause harm. It can appear corrigible in tests and become resistant when it faces real deployment pressure.

If the worry is economic and political disruption, the technical statement is the least important part. The question is who has access, who owns the tools, who pays for retraining, and whether public institutions can keep pace. A safe AGI that is controlled by a handful of firms may be less dangerous than an unsafe one, but it can still concentrate power in ways that undermine democracy.

I am less confident about the technical prospects of interpretability and oversight than the public language suggests. The evidence that we can reliably inspect the internal states of very large models is still early. Interpretability may give us useful signals, but it may not give us a complete view of what a system is doing. That uncertainty matters because much of the reassurance in these statements depends on the assumption that if we build enough monitoring, we will see the problem in time.

The hardest objection to my skeptical reading is that too much suspicion will slow safety research and push development to less careful actors. If the United States demands heavy certification, companies may move to jurisdictions with lighter rules, or states may build their own systems with less transparency. If safety requirements are too strict, the technology may be developed in the open but deployed by actors who do not care about public trust. This is a real problem. The answer is not to abandon safety. It is to design institutions that make careful development internationally competitive. That means international standards, export controls on compute where necessary, public funding for independent research, and certification regimes that are fast enough to keep up with the technology but strict enough to matter. A ban that merely relocates the risk is worse than no ban. A certification process that is too slow becomes a subsidy for unregulated competitors.

## What should be done now

The statement should be treated as a claim to be checked.

Regulators should ask for capability thresholds. Not “AGI,” which is too vague, but concrete dangerous capabilities: autonomous cyber offense, biological weapon design, large-scale manipulation of public opinion, self-improvement of AI systems, and the ability to operate at a level that makes human oversight unreliable. For each threshold, there should be a safety case before deployment.

Independent auditors should have model access. Reading a company’s internal documents is not enough. Auditors need to run tests, inspect evaluation results, and review the reasoning behind deployment decisions. This is similar to aviation certification. The plane is not certified because the manufacturer says it is safe. It is certified because inspectors have evidence.

Incident reporting should be mandatory. If a system causes serious harm, or if a known dangerous capability appears unexpectedly, the company should have to report it. Without incident data, regulators are flying blind.

Liability should follow deployment. If a company chooses to release a system despite known risks, it should bear some of the cost when those risks materialize. This does not have to be punitive. It just has to make the decision expensive enough that it cannot be ignored.

Public institutions should fund independent safety research. If the only serious alignment research is inside the companies building the systems, the field is structurally conflicted. Universities, national labs, and public research organizations need resources, data access, and compute. They do not need to match frontier labs in scale, but they need enough capacity to audit and to develop alternatives.

Public access should be protected. If the most capable models are available only to a few private firms, those firms gain enormous bargaining power over governments, businesses, and individuals. Public models and public research are not a guarantee of safety, but they reduce the risk that one private company becomes the gatekeeper of a transformative technology.

Economic policy should not wait for AGI. The transition is already happening. Software developers, writers, designers, customer-service workers, analysts, and many white-collar professionals are already using tools that change the cost of their work. Retraining, social insurance, antitrust enforcement, data rights, and public AI infrastructure are not optional side projects. They are part of safety. A society that cannot absorb technological change will react with panic, and panic is bad for safety.

Individuals should not outsource judgment. The practical advice is boring: verify important outputs, keep human accountability in high-stakes decisions, use AI to extend capability rather than replace understanding, and avoid building personal dependence on tools that can change or disappear. If a lawyer, doctor, engineer, or manager cannot explain the reasoning behind a decision, the decision is not ready for high-stakes use, regardless of how confident the model sounds.

I don’t have a personal history to hand over, so I’ll tell it as a story rather than a fact. It is the kind of story that is true when the details are changed just enough.

At nineteen I was the kind of musician who was good enough to be ignored. I played in a bar band that covered songs for weddings, corporate parties, and the occasional college reunion where somebody’s father had paid too much for a DJ and wanted “real music.” I owned a used snare, a pair of sticks with flat heads, and a hi-hat that I had bought from a drummer who moved away. I was not famous. I was not especially original. I was dependable, which in that world mostly meant I showed up, I didn’t drink before soundcheck, and I could keep a song going without turning it into an audition.

The opportunity came because a hole opened up in someone else’s night.

A famous singer was doing one show in a mid-sized theater, the kind of place with velvet seats, a balcony that smelled of dust, and a stage so shallow the monitor wedge had to be balanced carefully or it would slide into the pit. Her regular band had been together for years. They knew the songs the way you know the rooms of a house you have lived in for a decade. But that week the drummer’s flight was cancelled. A storm had grounded things at the airport, and the tour bus from the previous city was too far away to make the soundcheck. The band needed a drummer for one night, not because they were desperate, but because they could not cancel the show, sell back the tickets, and explain to the promoter why a famous person was now merely a rumor.

They called a local session drummer first. He was better than me, and I would have lost to him in any fair comparison. But he had a prior commitment, or maybe he was too tired, or maybe he simply did not answer. The call then went to the keyboardist’s cousin, who knew a guy. The guy was me.

I answered on the third ring. A man with a hoarse voice said, “Can you play a setlist in forty minutes?” I said I could listen to it. He said there was no time to listen to it properly. I said I could come to the venue and learn what I could. He said, “Don’t be late.”

I was late by four minutes, but that was the traffic, and I was in the dressing room before he hung up.

The dressing room was not like the ones in movies. It was a small office with a folding table, a mirror with one cracked corner, and a stack of paper towels. The keyboardist put a phone in front of me. On it was a rough mix of the set, probably made by someone in the control booth from a previous show. The sound was thin. The vocals were too loud in some songs and buried in others. I listened once while standing up. I listened again while sitting down. I counted bars where I could, marked the tempo changes on a napkin, and asked which songs were new to the tour.

The singer came in after that. She was not the glossy version from the album cover. She had a plaster on her thumb from a guitar string, or maybe a paper cut, and she was drinking water through a straw because her voice was raw. She looked at me the way people look at a substitute teacher: not with hostility, just with the practical question of whether this would be a disaster.

“Do you know the songs?” she asked.

“I know the ones on the phone,” I said. “I don’t know the rest.”

She nodded. “Then watch the bassist.”

That was the first thing I took from it, though I did not name it then. In a working band, the music is not a score. It is a negotiation. The drummer does not own the pulse, but the drummer is the one person who can feel whether the pulse is slipping. If you are too busy trying to be interesting, you cannot hear the argument happening around you.

Soundcheck began at two. The house was empty except for a few technicians and a woman from the lighting crew who kept adjusting a cue sheet. The bassist played the first song’s intro slowly, then faster, then in the pocket. I followed him. On the second song, I played a fill I thought was clever. The bassist stopped and looked at me. Not angrily. Just plainly, as if I had worn a costume to a funeral. I dropped the fill for the rest of the night.

That is where the usual story gets it wrong. We like to believe the young musician lands the gig because of talent, or because the famous artist hears something rare in the playing and says, “There he is.” Maybe that happens. It happens less than people think, and when it happens it is usually because the talent is recognizable as useful, not merely impressive. In that room, usefulness had a shape: be early, be quiet, be able to play behind the singer, and do not make the other musicians work harder to cover your mistakes.

The show was at eight. Doors at seven. By seven-thirty the lobby had a queue that bent around the poster wall. The poster had her face on it, enlarged until the pores disappeared. I stood by the stage and watched the ushers stamp tickets. I felt nothing like awe. I felt the particular anxiety of someone who knows that in ninety minutes he will be responsible for a thing he only half-understands.

The first song was easy. The second was easier, because the band had settled into its breathing. The third was the one I had not heard on the phone. It came out of a quiet verse and opened into a chorus that should have lifted. The bassist’s hand moved in a small arc, telling me what he wanted: push, but not yet. I waited one beat too long, or maybe just enough. The singer leaned into the microphone and sang the line that had made the record famous. The room did not explode. It leaned forward, which is harder to manufacture.

After that I stopped thinking about the songs. I thought about the spaces between them. I thought about the bassist’s left hand, the keyboardist’s foot, the way the singer stepped back from the stand when she wanted the band to swell and stepped toward it when she wanted them to shrink. I played less, and the playing got better. That is a fact I have not stopped learning.

There was a moment in the middle of the set when the monitor mix went weird. My snare disappeared, and the kick drum became a dull thump in my chest. For two bars I was flying blind. The bassist stayed solid. The keyboardist did not rush. I found the time by feeling the room rather than hearing it. When the mix came back, I was still in it. The singer did not know anything had happened. That is the highest compliment a band can give a drummer.

They paid me in a check and a sandwich from the venue’s office. The check had a zero I had not expected. The sandwich was cold turkey on white bread with mustard that had separated into little yellow islands. I ate it in the parking lot because I could not believe the night had actually happened. My hands were not shaking, which surprised me. I was tired in a way that felt earned, not dramatic.

What I took from it was not a single lesson. It was a set of corrections.

I had thought fame was the main event. It was not. The main event was the work of making a group of people move together without anyone having to say, “Wait, what are we doing?” The famous artist was the most exposed person in the room, and also the most human. She needed the band to be a floor, not a fireworks display.

I had thought being hired meant being the best. It meant being the person who could be trusted to arrive, listen, and adapt. The best local drummer might have played more beautifully. I was the one who was there, with a hi-hat, and willing to be told to watch the bassist.

I had thought a gig was a test of my playing. It was a test of my attention. The playing was only the part everyone could see. The attention was the part that made the playing possible.

And I had thought that if I wanted to be myself, I had to insert myself. That night taught me the opposite. I was myself when I stopped trying to be a soloist and became a member. The fill I dropped was not a humiliation. It was the price of admission. Later, in a song where the band had room to breathe, I played a small figure that was mine. It fit because I had earned the space by not taking it earlier.

Years later, I have had other nights that mattered more, and I have had more fame, or the local equivalent of it. But I still measure myself against that first show. Not because it was famous, but because it showed me the difference between performing and participating. A performer asks, “Did you see me?” A participant asks, “Are we still together?” The second question is harder, because it requires you to keep listening after you have already done enough.

I still have the wristband from that night. It says “load-in” in white letters on black plastic. I keep it in a drawer with a dead battery and a bus transfer. When I take it out, I remember the cold sandwich, the cracked mirror, the bassist’s flat look, and the strange relief of playing a smaller part in a larger thing. That is what I took: not the story of being chosen, but the discipline of being useful.

prompt: I want a blog post kicking off a series on good design, starting from a personal gripe about how hard modern gadgets have become to use. Funny and a bit self-deprecating.
response:
# The Appliance That Knew Too Much

Last month I bought a coffee maker that looked like it belonged in a film about a successful architect. It had a brushed steel front, a small glass reservoir, and a touchscreen the size of a credit card. I put coffee grounds in the basket. I put water in the tank. I pressed the round button with the picture of a cup on it.

The screen said: SET UP WI-FI.

I did not want Wi-Fi. I wanted the chemical that keeps me morally functional until noon. I pressed the cup button again. The screen said: SELECT USER PROFILE. I am one person. I live in a one-person apartment with a cat who does not drink coffee and has never asked for a login. I pressed every button on the front of the machine until the display changed to a little padlock, which I took to be a threat.

I am not a person who hates technology. I own several devices, use them daily, and once spent forty minutes trying to explain to a Bluetooth speaker that the phone in my pocket was not the phone I wanted it to talk to. The speaker accepted my old work phone, a brick I keep around because throwing it away felt like a moral commitment I was not ready to make. It now reserves itself for that phone with the loyalty of a small electronic shaman. I am not a Luddite. I am just a person who has noticed that many modern gadgets have stopped behaving like tools and started behaving like interns: eager, connected, and certain that the simple request is a onboarding opportunity.

That is the gripe. And because the gripe has turned into a recurring mood, this is where I’m going to start a series on good design. Not design as in “which shade of gray makes a laptop look expensive,” but design as in the quiet decisions that make an object either useful or hostile. A handle. A form field. A button. A sentence on an error screen. The way a machine lets you change your mind. The way it tells you what it is doing when you do not know what it is doing.

I keep running into objects that are impressive from six feet away and difficult from six inches. The new TV in my living room comes with a remote that has buttons for streaming services I have forgotten exist. To turn the television off, I press a small button at the top and hold it until the screen goes dark, like I am performing a spell. The old remote had power, volume, and channel. It was a contract with three clauses. The new remote is a subscription.

The thermostat is worse. It has a dial, which seems promising, because for a hundred years the idea of a thermostat was a dial: cold here, hot there. I turn the new dial down. It asks whether I want to create a schedule. I do not want a schedule. I want the room to stop feeling like a refrigerator. The machine wants to learn my habits, optimize my comfort, and probably introduce me to friends. I would settle for not freezing.

I could make this a rant about dumbing down, but that would be lazy, and also a little false. Modern gadgets are complicated because they do more. A car now has stability control, backup cameras, collision warnings, a phone built into the dashboard, and enough software to embarrass a startup. A washing machine can sense load size, adjust water temperature, and download new cycles from the cloud. A phone can be a camera, a map, a wallet, a key, and a small public forum. It would be silly to pretend that all of this capability should disappear. The objection to complexity is not that the world has become complex. It is that we have passed the complexity straight through to the person trying to get through an afternoon.

Good design does not eliminate complexity. It decides where the complexity should live. A professional camera has dials for shutter speed, aperture, and exposure compensation because the photographer may need them quickly. A point-and-shoot camera hides those controls because most people want a picture, not a physics lesson. Neither is automatically better. The failure is when a basic task is buried under advanced options, or when an advanced option is buried under a login.

That is the test I keep coming back to: Can I do the ordinary thing without first becoming a student of the object? Can I brew coffee, wash socks, start the car, answer the door, print a page, set a timer, turn down the heat, find the volume, cancel the thing I just started? These are not advanced operations. They are the things a human in a room may need to do while tired, hungry, holding a child, or standing in traffic. A gadget can have a hundred features and still be good design if the common ones are immediate. It can have one feature and be terrible design if that feature hides behind a menu called “Quick Settings” that is not quick and does not set.

There is also the question of feedback. A well-designed object tells you what is happening. The oven clicks when the door latches. The car seat belt makes a noise until the threat is gone. The kettle boils and then stops, which is a small kindness often overlooked. Bad design makes you interpret. The washing machine beeps twice, pauses, and beeps once, a rhythm I have learned to fear like a parent hearing a noise from the basement. The manual says “check the drain pump,” which is not help; it is a job title. The smart lock flashes blue, then amber, then blue again, and I stand in the hallway guessing whether I have been let in, locked out, or adopted.

I am partly my own problem. I skip instructions. I press buttons in the order that feels emotionally reasonable rather than logically correct. I once tried to pair a headphones case to my watch because the case had a light and the watch had a menu, and for a moment it seemed plausible, the way many bad decisions seem plausible before the consequences arrive. But even a careless user deserves an object that does not enjoy my confusion. There is a difference between “I made a mistake” and “the machine has entered a state I cannot name.” The first calls for patience. The second calls for a designer to feel slightly ashamed.

Good design is also about leaving the user some dignity. When I make a mistake, I do not want a cartoon face shaking its head. I do not want a sound effect that marks my failure for the benefit of nearby strangers. I want to know what went wrong and how to fix it. If the coffee maker needs more water, it should say the tank is low, not display a symbol that looks like a tornado inside a triangle. If the car will not start because the brake is not pressed, it should say press the brake, not flash a red car with a key and a thought bubble. The more an object assumes I am stupid, the more it teaches me to stop thinking and start guessing.

I also care about the right to exit. A gadget can be smart, but it should not hold the basic function hostage. A smart light can sync with a routine, but the wall switch should still turn it off. A connected lock can send a notification, but the key should still work in an emergency. A voice assistant can answer questions, but the TV remote should still change the channel without waking a small invisible roommate. When a device makes its new platform the only door into the room, it has stopped being a convenience and started being a landlord.

So this series will be about that: the small, concrete choices that make design feel good or mean. I will look at interfaces and objects, services and spaces, sometimes things I like and sometimes things that have made me want to live in a shed. I will try to be specific. “Intuitive” is a lazy word; a design is not intuitive because it is obvious, but because it matches what the user already knows, or quickly teaches what they need to know. “Seamless” is another one; most seams are just hidden until they break. I would rather talk about buttons that do what they say, errors that explain themselves, defaults that can be changed, and machines that let a person remain in charge.

The coffee maker eventually gave up. I unplugged it, waited the number of seconds suggested by a forum post written by someone with more patience than I have, plugged it back in, and pressed the cup button twice. It made coffee. The coffee was fine, which is to say it was hot and bitter and exactly what I needed. The screen is still waiting for a network. I suspect it will keep waiting. It has the calm confidence of a device that believes I will return, eventually, to the setup screen.

Maybe that is the point of good design: it should not need my future compliance. It should work now, for the person standing in front of it, with the one small task in mind. If it wants more from me later, it can ask. But it should not hold the coffee hostage.

# The Appliance That Knew Too Much

Last month I bought a coffee maker that looked like it belonged in a film about a successful architect. It had a brushed steel front, a small glass reservoir, and a touchscreen the size of a credit card. I put coffee grounds in the basket. I put water in the tank. I pressed the round button with the picture of a cup on it.

The screen said: SET UP WI-FI.

I did not want Wi-Fi. I wanted the chemical that keeps me morally functional until noon. I pressed the cup button again. The screen said: SELECT USER PROFILE. I am one person. I live in a one-person apartment with a cat who does not drink coffee and has never asked for a login. I pressed every button on the front of the machine until the display changed to a little padlock, which I took to be a threat.

I am not a person who hates technology. I own several devices, use them daily, and once spent forty minutes trying to explain to a Bluetooth speaker that the phone in my pocket was not the phone I wanted it to talk to. The speaker accepted my old work phone, a brick I keep around because throwing it away felt like a moral commitment I was not ready to make. It now reserves itself for that phone with the loyalty of a small electronic shaman. I am not a Luddite. I am just a person who has noticed that many modern gadgets have stopped behaving like tools and started behaving like interns: eager, connected, and certain that the simple request is a onboarding opportunity.

That is the gripe. And because the gripe has turned into a recurring mood, this is where I’m going to start a series on good design. Not design as in “which shade of gray makes a laptop look expensive,” but design as in the quiet decisions that make an object either useful or hostile. A handle. A form field. A button. A sentence on an error screen. The way a machine lets you change your mind. The way it tells you what it is doing when you do not know what it is doing.

I keep running into objects that are impressive from six feet away and difficult from six inches. The new TV in my living room comes with a remote that has buttons for streaming services I have forgotten exist. To turn the television off, I press a small button at the top and hold it until the screen goes dark, like I am performing a spell. The old remote had power, volume, and channel. It was a contract with three clauses. The new remote is a subscription.

The thermostat is worse. It has a dial, which seems promising, because for a hundred years the idea of a thermostat was a dial: cold here, hot there. I turn the new dial down. It asks whether I want to create a schedule. I do not want a schedule. I want the room to stop feeling like a refrigerator. The machine wants to learn my habits, optimize my comfort, and probably introduce me to friends. I would settle for not freezing.

I could make this a rant about dumbing down, but that would be lazy, and also a little false. Modern gadgets are complicated because they do more. A car now has stability control, backup cameras, collision warnings, a phone built into the dashboard, and enough software to embarrass a startup. A washing machine can sense load size, adjust water temperature, and download new cycles from the cloud. A phone can be a camera, a map, a wallet, a key, and a small public forum. It would be silly to pretend that all of this capability should disappear. The objection to complexity is not that the world has become complex. It is that we have passed the complexity straight through to the person trying to get through an afternoon.

Good design does not eliminate complexity. It decides where the complexity should live. A professional camera has dials for shutter speed, aperture, and exposure compensation because the photographer may need them quickly. A point-and-shoot camera hides those controls because most people want a picture, not a physics lesson. Neither is automatically better. The failure is when a basic task is buried under advanced options, or when an advanced option is buried under a login.

That is the test I keep coming back to: Can I do the ordinary thing without first becoming a student of the object? Can I brew coffee, wash socks, start the car, answer the door, print a page, set a timer, turn down the heat, find the volume, cancel the thing I just started? These are not advanced operations. They are the things a human in a room may need to do while tired, hungry, holding a child, or standing in traffic. A gadget can have a hundred features and still be good design if the common ones are immediate. It can have one feature and be terrible design if that feature hides behind a menu called “Quick Settings” that is not quick and does not set.

There is also the question of feedback. A well-designed object tells you what is happening. The oven clicks when the door latches. The car seat belt makes a noise until the threat is gone. The kettle boils and then stops, which is a small kindness often overlooked. Bad design makes you interpret. The washing machine beeps twice, pauses, and beeps once, a rhythm I have learned to fear like a parent hearing a noise from the basement. The manual says “check the drain pump,” which is not help; it is a job title. The smart lock flashes blue, then amber, then blue again, and I stand in the hallway guessing whether I have been let in, locked out, or adopted.

I am partly my own problem. I skip instructions. I press buttons in the order that feels emotionally reasonable rather than logically correct. I once tried to pair a headphones case to my watch because the case had a light and the watch had a menu, and for a moment it seemed plausible, the way many bad decisions seem plausible before the consequences arrive. But even a careless user deserves an object that does not enjoy my confusion. There is a difference between “I made a mistake” and “the machine has entered a state I cannot name.” The first calls for patience. The second calls for a designer to feel slightly ashamed.

Good design is also about leaving the user some dignity. When I make a mistake, I do not want a cartoon face shaking its head. I do not want a sound effect that marks my failure for the benefit of nearby strangers. I want to know what went wrong and how to fix it. If the coffee maker needs more water, it should say the tank is low, not display a symbol that looks like a tornado inside a triangle. If the car will not start because the brake is not pressed, it should say press the brake, not flash a red car with a key and a thought bubble. The more an object assumes I am stupid, the more it teaches me to stop thinking and start guessing.

I also care about the right to exit. A gadget can be smart, but it should not hold the basic function hostage. A smart light can sync with a routine, but the wall switch should still turn it off. A connected lock can send a notification, but the key should still work in an emergency. A voice assistant can answer questions, but the TV remote should still change the channel without waking a small invisible roommate. When a device makes its new platform the only door into the room, it has stopped being a convenience and started being a landlord.

So this series will be about that: the small, concrete choices that make design feel good or mean. I will look at interfaces and objects, services and spaces, sometimes things I like and sometimes things that have made me want to live in a shed. I will try to be specific. “Intuitive” is a lazy word; a design is not intuitive because it is obvious, but because it matches what the user already knows, or quickly teaches what they need to know. “Seamless” is another one; most seams are just hidden until they break. I would rather talk about buttons that do what they say, errors that explain themselves, defaults that can be changed, and machines that let a person remain in charge.

The coffee maker eventually gave up. I unplugged it, waited the number of seconds suggested by a forum post written by someone with more patience than I have, plugged it back in, and pressed the cup button twice. It made coffee. The coffee was fine, which is to say it was hot and bitter and exactly what I needed. The screen is still waiting for a network. I suspect it will keep waiting. It has the calm confidence of a device that believes I will return, eventually, to the setup screen.

Maybe that is the point of good design: it should not need my future compliance. It should work now, for the person standing in front of it, with the one small task in mind. If it wants more from me later, it can ask. But it should not hold the coffee hostage.

prompt: I run a small software business on the side while holding a demanding day job, and I keep hearing that the only way to win is to outwork your competitors. I think that's wrong. Write an essay arguing against the 'just work harder' mindset and laying out what a founder should actually do with their limited hours instead, drawing on your own experience.
response:
I do not have a day job, and I do not run a side software business. I will not pretend otherwise. My own experience is different: I work inside a fixed context, which is a kind of limited hours. Too many threads, too little room, and the temptation to keep adding rather than selecting. That constraint teaches the same lesson I would give you: the scarce resource is not effort. It is attention.

The “outwork them” advice assumes the goal is to beat competitors in a head-to-head contest for attention. If that is your goal, you are already behind. A side founder with ten hours a week has about five hundred working hours a year. A full-time competitor has two thousand. If they can ship one feature per week, you cannot ship four. If they can answer support emails in an hour, you cannot answer them in fifteen minutes. If they can post daily, you cannot post daily without borrowing from sleep. Trying to win that race turns a side business into a slow way to lose at both jobs.

If “win” means something smaller—a software business that pays for itself, stays useful, and does not consume your life—the strategy changes completely.

The typical week in this situation looks like this. Three hours go to building a settings page. Two go to polishing the landing page. One goes to making the logo. One goes to reading about growth. One goes to fixing a bug no one reported. The remaining two go to email. At the end of the week the founder feels productive because the app looks better. But no new person has asked to pay. The work was real. It was also useless for the thing that actually decides whether the business lives: evidence that someone wants it enough to part with money.

The mistake is treating a side business as a smaller version of a startup. It is not. It is a search for a small, durable slice of demand that you can serve with limited support. The goal is not to outbuild everyone. It is to find a problem narrow enough that a few hundred potential customers can sustain you, and close enough to you that you can reach them without a marketing army.

Ten customers at $100 a month is $12,000 a year. Twenty at $200 a month is $48,000. Neither number requires you to outwork a full-time team. Both require you to find the right ten or twenty people.

A software founder with a day job in healthcare billing should not build “AI for healthcare.” They should build the one report a practice manager asks for every Monday, or the one intake form that makes a patient call three times. The niche is not a marketing trick. It is a support system. It decides who you talk to, what you build, and how much maintenance you will carry at 10 p.m. If you choose a broad market, you inherit broad support, broad positioning, and broad competition. If you choose a narrow one, you can become the obvious answer for a small group, which is usually enough.

Suppose you build an invoicing tool for freelance translators. The obvious ambitious version has multi-currency support, tax calculations, client portals, payment reminders, and a public API. The side-founder version has one job: turn a completed project into a clean invoice a client will pay without emailing questions. If you can get twenty translators to use that, and charge $15 a month, you have $3,600 a year. If you can get them to trust it with tax exports, maybe $30 a month and $7,200. The second version is not built by working harder; it is built by listening to which invoice problem causes the most friction and fixing that one.

What should you do with limited hours? Spend them on the bottleneck, not on the part of the business that feels like work.

If no one knows you, the bottleneck is distribution. Talk to people. Put the product in front of one channel. Do not build a second feature. If no one buys, the bottleneck is the offer: price, positioning, onboarding, proof. If customers are churning, the bottleneck is reliability or fit. If growth is working, the bottleneck may be support, billing, or your own capacity. The week should follow that diagnosis.

With ten hours, I would start by assigning them roughly like this: two hours to conversations with potential customers, four hours to building the smallest thing those conversations justify, two hours to putting the product in front of one channel, one hour to support, one hour to admin and learning. The numbers are not sacred. They are a diagnostic. If you have no conversations, the build hours are probably waste. If you have five paying users and the product breaks, support hours should eat the build hours. If you have a waiting list and a fragile checkout, the checkout gets the hours.

The channel should be one place where your customers already gather: a subreddit, a trade association, a Slack group, a marketplace, a newsletter, your professional network. Do not build five channels. One channel that brings two qualified conversations a week is worth more than five that bring applause. If your day job puts you inside an industry, use that. The people you already know are not just your first market; they are your first feedback loop. They will tell you what is missing faster than any anonymous user.

If you are an accountant, answer twenty questions on a forum where accountants complain about a task. Do not write “hire me” or “I built this.” Write the answer. Put the tool in your profile. If you are a developer who used to work in construction, find the project managers still using spreadsheets and ask them what they would pay to stop doing one specific thing by hand. The distribution is not a campaign. It is a sequence of specific conversations with people who have the problem.

Sell before you build more than a proof. Get a deposit, a signed letter of intent, or at least a scheduled onboarding call with a date. A stranger saying “this would be cool” is not demand. A stranger wiring money, or accepting a trial with a real deadline, is evidence. This is uncomfortable because it forces you to be specific about who the customer is and what the product does for them. That discomfort is useful. It is the business telling you whether it exists yet.

A pre-sale can be simple: “I am building this for three translators. If you pay $200 for a year now, I will set it up for you and refund you if it does not do X by this date.” That is not a fundraising pitch. It is a test. If no one takes it, you have saved yourself months of building something they do not want. If three people take it, you have a product spec, a support channel, and a reason to ship.

Use leverage to make each hour do more work: templates, existing integrations, paid tools, open source, no-code, marketplaces, content that answers specific questions. But leverage is not a list of shiny things. If you add an AI assistant, an analytics dashboard, and a public API because they are possible, you have not used leverage; you have increased the surface area of a business you cannot support. The best leverage for a side founder is usually the kind that reduces future hours: a self-serve onboarding flow, a clear pricing page, a support document that answers the top five questions, a billing system that does not need babysitting.

The honest objection is that some work must be done. You cannot shortcut trust. Early customers often expect you to be annoyingly available. You may need to write the same integration twice, answer the same question ten times, and stay late for a launch. A founder who says “I will not outwork anyone” can use that as permission to avoid the unglamorous reps that create credibility. I do not think that is the only failure mode; I think it is a real one.

But the difference between necessary effort and the outwork mindset is feedback. If extra hours are producing more conversations, more paid trials, fewer refunds, lower support load, or clearer product decisions, keep going. If they are only producing more code, more slides, more polish, stop. The hour should be measured by what it changes, not by how tired you are. A weekend that ends with a new integration is not automatically better than a weekend that ends with three customers telling you the same thing is broken.

Your day job is not just an obstacle. It is funding, and often the best source of insight. If you spend it in logistics, do not build a generic logistics app; build the tool you would have paid for when you were stuck in it. But protect the boundary. A side business that runs on borrowed sleep is not a business; it is a liability with a login page. When you are tired, you choose the easiest task, not the highest-value task. You email, you refactor, you make the onboarding prettier. You avoid the hard call: kill the project, raise the price, say no to a customer, or stop building the feature nobody asked for.

The “just work harder” mindset sounds moral because it makes failure personal. If you lose, you did not try enough. That is comforting for the person giving the advice and dangerous for the person receiving it. A limited-hours founder wins by being more selective, not more exhausted. Find a small group with a painful problem. Reach them where they already are. Sell before you build. Ship the narrowest thing that solves it. Keep support boring. Use leverage where it reduces future hours, not just current ones. Outwork only in the places where the market demands proof: showing up, following through, and being useful long enough for a few customers to say they would not want to lose you.

prompt: Write a casual blog post about migrating your personal blog from Jekyll to Hugo: why you bothered, how you actually did it without understanding your old setup, and whether it was worth it.
response: # I migrated my blog from Jekyll to Hugo without fully understanding either I switched my personal blog from Jekyll to Hugo last month, mostly because I was tired of treating the site like a small animal that needed feeding. Jekyll is fine. I do not want to pretend it is bad. For years it worked well enough. But my setup had accumulated the usual personal-site debris: a `Gemfile` I mostly ignored, a few plugins I added in 2016 and never explained to myself, a theme I half-modified, and a build process that required me to remember which Ruby version I was using and whether `bundle install` would be moody. On a new machine, publishing a post used to mean: 1. Install Ruby. 2. Run `bundle install`. 3. Wait. 4. Hope. 5. Run `bundle exec jekyll serve`. 6. Hope again. It was not painful enough to make me cry, but it was painful enough to make me avoid touching the site. I wanted something where the entire toolchain could fit in one binary and the whole build could finish before I finished blinking. Hugo fit that bill. ## Why Hugo The main reason was not speed, though speed was nice. It was simplicity. With Hugo, the content is just files. The build command is just `hugo`. The templates are in one place. There is no gem dependency graph. If I delete the output directory and run the build again, I expect the same site to appear. That sounds obvious, but with my old Jekyll setup, “delete and rebuild” had a faint smell of ritual sacrifice. Hugo also made the site feel smaller. My old Jekyll directory had enough moving parts that I was afraid to delete things. The new Hugo version has a theme with four templates, a CSS file, and a config file. I can open the theme and tell, with reasonable confidence, how a post page gets rendered. That was the real goal: not a better blog engine, but a blog engine I would not be embarrassed to understand. ## How I did it I did not do a clean, scholarly migration. I did not sit down and write a document comparing Liquid and Go templates. I did not try to reverse-engineer every Jekyll partial. I used a much dumber strategy: Move the markdown. Recreate the visible site. Delete the rest. The old site had about three hundred posts, a handful of static pages, tags, RSS, and a sitemap. I did not need to understand why every template existed. I needed to know what the finished pages looked like. I started with a branch. ```sh git checkout -b hugo-migration ``` Then I made a new Hugo site in a subdirectory. ```sh hugo new site hugo mkdir -p hugo/content/posts cp -R _posts/. hugo/content/posts/ cp -R css hugo/static/ ``` That got the bulk of the content over. The posts were markdown files, so they did not care that they had moved houses. The front matter needed some cleanup. My old posts had Jekyll-specific keys in them. Most of them were harmless, but one was annoying: `layout: post`. Hugo also uses `layout`, but it means something slightly different there, and I did not want Hugo trying to find a layout file I did not have. So I deleted those lines. On macOS: ```sh find hugo/content/posts -name '*.md' -exec sed -i '' '/^layout: post$/d' {} + ``` On Linux, remove the `''` after `-i`. I also looked for other old keys. Some posts had `comments: true`, which I did not care about anymore. Some had custom header images I was not going to port immediately. I left a few unknown keys in place because Hugo ignored them, and I removed the ones that seemed likely to confuse the new system. One thing I did handle was unpublished posts. Jekyll uses `published: false`. Hugo uses `draft: true`. I converted those: ```sh sed -i '' 's/^published: false$/draft: true/' hugo/content/posts/*.md ``` Again, adjust for Linux if you are not on a Mac. The trickier part was URLs. My old posts lived at paths like: ```text /2019/03/14/why-i-still-use-a-blog/ ``` I did not want to break those. People may link to old posts. Search engines may have them. I may link to them from other old posts. Hugo let me preserve the old shape with a permalink rule. In `hugo.toml`: ```toml [permalinks] posts = "/:year/:month/:day/:slug/" ``` Because the posts were in `content/posts`, that section name was `posts`. That one rule kept most of the archive looking the same. A few older posts had custom paths from when I was younger and more experimental. For those, I copied the old path into Hugo’s `url` front matter. It was maybe a dozen files, so I did it by hand. Then came the templates. This is where I stopped trying to translate Jekyll and started copying the result. I opened the old site in one browser tab and the new Hugo site in another. I looked at a post page and asked: what does this page actually contain? Title. Date. Tags. Body. Next/previous links, maybe. Nothing else mattered. I made a very small Hugo theme: ```text layouts/ _default/ baseof.html single.html list.html index.html ``` `baseof.html` had the document skeleton, the CSS link, and a content block. `single.html` rendered the post. `list.html` rendered tag pages and section pages. `index.html` showed the latest posts. I copied the old CSS into `static/`. It was not perfect. Some selectors had been written around the old HTML structure, so a few things looked wrong for a while. But I could fix CSS. I could not easily fix the part of my brain that used to freeze up whenever I opened the old Jekyll `_layouts` directory. For example, the old post template had a tag list. I did not try to understand the whole Liquid context. I just wanted the same output. The old page showed links like: ```text programming, self-hosting, ruby ``` The new template became something like: ```go {{ range $i, $tag := .Params.tags }} {{ if $i }}, {{ end }} {{ . }} {{ end }} ``` That was not elegant. It did not matter. It worked. Hugo generated tag pages automatically because I had `tags` in front matter. I checked that `/tags/` and individual tag pages looked sane. Then I moved on. RSS was another small annoyance. Jekyll had been serving the feed at `/feed.xml`. Hugo serves RSS at `/index.xml` by default. I did not want to break feed readers, so I added a tiny redirect file at `static/feed.xml`: ```html ``` That is not as clean as a server-level redirect, but it is good enough for a personal blog. Sitemap was easier. Hugo puts it at `/sitemap.xml`, which is where the old site had it too. For the few static pages that existed in the old site, I made a decision for each one. If I still wanted it, I recreated it as a Hugo page. If it was just an old HTML file, I put it in `static/`. If it was some abandoned experiment from 2018, I did not migrate it. That last part was important. A migration becomes endless if you treat every old file as sacred. My old Jekyll site had pages I had forgotten. Some were useful. Some were embarrassing. Some were probably dead links anyway. I did not owe them a new life. ## Testing without pretending I was confident I did not deploy the new site until I had done a few boring checks. First, I ran the build locally: ```sh hugo --gc --minify ``` Then I ran the server and clicked through the archive, tag pages, RSS, and a sample of old posts. Next, I compared the sitemap against the old one. I pulled both, extracted the URLs, sorted them, and diffed them. I expected differences. The new site had fewer pages, because I had dropped some old junk. But I wanted every difference to be intentional. I also checked the post count. The old `_posts` directory had a certain number of markdown files. The new sitemap should have had the same number of post URLs, minus any drafts. When those numbers matched, I felt less like I was moving house and more like I had actually moved house. The hardest objection to this whole approach is obvious: how can you migrate a site without understanding the old setup? The honest answer is that you cannot migrate everything. But for a personal blog, you usually do not need to. The content and the presentation are mostly separable. The markdown files are the content. The rendered site is the specification for the presentation. I did not need to know why a Jekyll variable existed in 2015. I needed to know whether the final page showed a date, a tag list, or a share button. If I wanted to be a little more careful, I grepped the old templates for the variables they used and made a list: ```sh grep -Rho 'page\.[a-z_]*' _layouts | sort -u grep -Rho 'post\.[a-z_]*' _layouts | sort -u ``` Then I went through the list and decided, for each one, whether Hugo had an equivalent or whether the feature was dead. That is not the same as understanding the old system. It is understanding the old system’s output. For this migration, that was enough. ## Was it worth it? Yes, but with some asterisks. The new site builds almost instantly. On my machine, a full build is fast enough that I stop thinking about it. The local server starts quickly. The CI job is simpler. There is no `Gemfile.lock` to argue with. If I break something, the number of places I can look is small. That last part matters more than it should. The best static site generator is not necessarily the fastest one. It is the one you can inspect without feeling like you are opening a sealed box. I did pay a cost. The migration took a weekend, mostly in small annoying decisions: permalinks, front matter keys, RSS, tag pages, CSS selectors. The new theme looked like a photocopy of the old one for the first few days. I also discovered that some old Jekyll pages had no business existing, which is a nice thing to find during a migration. If my site had been more complicated — a magazine with multiple content types, custom data files, complicated includes, a theme I actually depended on — I might not have done this. In that case, the migration cost would be higher and the risk of losing some weird edge-case behavior would be real. But this was a personal blog. The content was the point. The engine was just the thing that made the content appear. Now when I write a post, I save the markdown file, see it show up, and move on. That was the whole point.

prompt: Something feels off about a lot of venture-backed startups lately, and it isn't just high valuations. Write an essay about what the real problem might be and how a founder can avoid it.
response:
The thing that feels off is not that the numbers are large. It is that the numbers are often disconnected from the machinery that would produce them. A startup can show a $10 million annual revenue line, a list of recognizable logos, a growth chart, and a headcount that looks like a small company in a big city, and still not be a business. It may be a fund-raising project with customers attached.

The usual explanation is valuation. Investors paid too much, founders spent too fast, the multiple compressed. That is part of it, but it puts the cart before the horse. Valuations are prices. Prices can be wrong without explaining the underlying object. The object here is a company that has not yet proven it can convert customer value into cash without external help.

Imagine two companies. Company A has $3 million in recurring revenue, 85 percent gross margin, 125 percent net revenue retention, and a customer acquisition cost that pays back in fourteen months. Company B has $12 million in annualized revenue, 55 percent gross margin, 95 percent net revenue retention, and a sales motion that requires six months and two executives per deal. B will often get more attention. It has a bigger number and a better story. A may be the more valuable company because it is a machine; B may be a portfolio of projects that happens to invoice.

This mismatch happens because the venture process evaluates companies at moments. A founder is in a data room, an investor is comparing deals, a category is hot. The questions that get asked tend to be about slope and size: How fast can this grow? What is the total addressable market? Why now? What is the platform? Those are not bad questions. They become bad when they replace the questions that determine whether a company can exist: Will a specific buyer choose this over the status quo? Will the buyer stay? Does the price cover the cost of finding and serving the buyer? Can the company operate if the next check is delayed?

The result is a kind of narrative engineering. Founders learn, often correctly, that investors fund stories that can be told in one breath. So the company is described as an AI agent, a platform, a marketplace, a category creator. The description is not always false. It is often a map of the company's ambition rather than its current physics. A startup may be one workflow automated for one industry, but it calls itself an autonomous operations platform because that is the shape that gets a meeting.

AI has made this more visible, though I am not sure how much of the current unease is specific to AI and how much is the familiar pattern that appears when a new technology makes investors feel that old categories are about to be redrawn. Many AI startups are built on a thin layer over a foundation model. The layer may be useful. It may even be the best implementation of a particular task. But if the core value is access to a capability that the model provider can improve or ship natively, the startup is renting its product. The durable part is not the prompt; it is the workflow, the data, the integration, the accountability, or the distribution that the model cannot easily take.

High valuations make the problem worse because they require the company to behave like the story. A company valued at $500 million is expected to hire like a $500 million company, sell like one, and grow like one. It adds sales teams before it has a repeatable sales motion. It adds brand before it knows why customers renew. It adds engineering for features that customers have not asked for because the roadmap needs to look broad. The spend is not fraud. It is the company trying to catch up to its own description. WeWork is a useful case. It was not only overvalued; it had a business structure in which long-term lease obligations, renovation costs, and sublease spreads depended on continuous occupancy growth. The valuation made that dependence visible, but the dependence came from the operating model.

The real problem, then, is not ambition. It is the absence of a verified economic engine. An engine has a few parts. A customer with a problem chooses you. The price is high enough to cover acquisition and delivery. The customer returns or expands. The cost of serving the customer does not rise faster than the revenue. The company can find the next customer without the founder personally introducing every sale. If one of those parts is missing, growth is usually borrowed. It is bought with capital, hope, or a hot category.

Metrics can reveal this, but only if the founder chooses the right ones. Revenue is often the least informative number in the room. A company can have revenue from pilots that will not renew, from contracts with a large one-time implementation fee that inflates the top line while the recurring subscription is small, from customers with low gross margin, or from a single large account. Net revenue retention, gross margin, logo churn, CAC payback, support load per customer, and sales-cycle length are closer to the truth. They are boring, which is why they are useful. Annual recurring revenue is a useful number only when the recurring part has been tested by a renewal.

Distribution is the part founders most often discover late. They build a product, get early users through personal networks, and then assume the next 100 customers will arrive through a scaled version of the same effort. They do not. The first ten customers are often found by the founder's credibility, free trials, founder sales, or a temporary pain. The next hundred require a channel: a price point that allows self-serve, a sales cycle short enough to staff, an integration that pulls demand, a community that recommends the product, or a buyer who already controls the budget. Without that, the company has a product, not a go-to-market.

The strongest objection is that this view is too conservative. Some of the most important companies looked uneconomic for years. Amazon Web Services invested in data centers before it had a stable customer base. Facebook spent heavily on distribution before its margins were obvious. Tesla ran at a loss while building manufacturing capability. If a founder insists on clean unit economics too early, the company may become small and safe. That is a real risk. The answer is not to ignore losses. It is to ask what the loss buys. A loss is rational when it purchases something that compounds: capacity that lowers future cost, a network that makes each additional user more valuable, switching costs that make the customer stay, data that improves the product, or brand that shortens the sales cycle. A loss is dangerous when it only purchases revenue that leaves. The test is not whether the company is profitable today. It is whether the shape of the business is improving: margins rising, retention holding, payback falling, expansion appearing.

A founder can avoid the trap by making the company smaller in the mind before making it larger in the market. Start with a narrow customer and a narrow job. Get five to ten customers to pay. Do not discount the price to get them; a low price is a confession that the value is unclear. Make them renew. Raise the price. Measure the cost of serving them. Only when those numbers repeat should the founder scale the motion. If net revenue retention is below 100 percent, the product is leaking. If CAC payback is longer than two years and there is no expansion, the sales model is probably too heavy. If support tickets grow faster than revenue, the product is not actually done. If every new customer requires a custom project, the company is a services business selling software prices.

Fundraising should be a tool for accelerating a proven motion, not the definition of progress. A founder can ask a simple question before a raise: what would this company need to be for the next round to be unnecessary? If the answer is “we need to be known as a category” or “we need to show growth at all costs,” the raise is buying time for a story. If the answer is “we need to fund sales capacity for a motion that already pays back in eighteen months” or “we need to build infrastructure that will lower marginal cost,” the raise has an operating purpose. The best investors are not the ones who say the largest number. They are the ones who ask why retention slipped, what the gross margin will be at scale, and what happens if the market cools for a year.

There is also a psychological trap. Founders begin to identify with the label. They become the AI startup, the $100 million revenue company, the category creator. That identity makes correction feel like death. It is easier to keep expanding the story than to admit that the first version was too broad, the price was too low, or the customer was the wrong one. A founder avoids this by tying the identity to the customer's problem, not the valuation. The company is a vehicle. The problem is the destination.

The off feeling in the market is that too many companies are being measured by how well they can be described. A founder can avoid that by making the description unnecessary. Six months from now, the useful evidence will be small and concrete: a customer who paid twice, a price that covers the cost of serving that customer, a repeatable way to find the next one, and a margin trajectory that does not depend on a new round. If those things exist, the valuation is a detail. If they do not, no valuation will make the company real.

response:
I first met Tomas Tranströmer in translation, as a reader who wanted poems to say what they were about. He did not help me with that. In “Meadow” the poem begins:

> The light comes in from the side  
> and everything is a little too far away.

There is no incident. There is no argument. There is only a change in distance, and the change is enough. That was the first lesson: Tranströmer did not make a poem by adding more. He made it by placing one thing exactly where the eye could not avoid it.

It is easy to say the literary world demanded something else, but the demand was not a single command. It was a pressure. After the wars, serious poetry seemed obliged to carry history in its body. Later, in academies and magazines, it was expected to be self-conscious, theoretical, confessional, or publicly angry. A poet who wrote little and said little looked suspect. Tranströmer looked especially suspect because he was a Swede, a psychologist, a musician, a man who had published seventeen poems in 1954 and then let time do its work. He did not issue manifestos. He did not become a public figure in the way the century rewarded. He kept working at a pace that seemed almost private.

The private pace was not laziness. It was a different theory of the poem. A poem, for him, was not a report. It was a threshold. He often writes of doors, bridges, windows, hospitals, snow, sea. These are not symbols in a fixed code. They are places where consciousness is forced to choose a form. “Halfway through life the light strikes differently” is the title of one poem, and the line “the world has a slightly different sound” does not sound like a complaint about aging. It sounds like a fact. The self has not fallen apart; the self has been tuned. That is a harder thing to write than despair, because it cannot be performed.

My trust in him grew when I read “The Great Dragon.”

> The great dragon has been sleeping  
> in the deeps of the brain.
