prompt: Write a short essay from the point of view of someone who studies the internals of artificial neural networks, on the ways their job is easier than a neuroscientist's, and what follows from that for how interpretability research should be done.
response:
I work on the internals of artificial neural networks, and the claim that my job is easier than a neuroscientist’s is true in a way that is easy to miss. We both deal with systems with too many variables for intuition. A human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons; a large language model has hundreds of billions of parameters. Scale by itself is not the difference. The difference is access. A neuroscientist studying cortex is trying to infer a mechanism from a system whose full wiring is not available, whose weights cannot be measured at useful resolution, whose training history is locked inside development, and whose behavior is entangled with a body and an environment. I can read the weights. I can choose the input. I can run the same input until the estimate is boring. I can zero out a neuron, clamp an activation, replace a layer’s output, or remove a feature and watch the loss move. I can retrain the same architecture with a different seed, a different data order, or a different auxiliary loss, and compare the two machines. In the models I study, I usually know the data or can generate a close proxy, and I know the objective. The network was not trying to keep itself alive while foraging; it was trying to reduce a loss I wrote down.

That does not make the problem simple. Large networks are nonlinear, redundant, and full of interactions that no single activation pattern reveals. But the epistemic situation is different. A neuroscientist often has to decide whether a population of cells is doing something interesting before knowing what the rest of the circuit is doing. I can, in principle, log every hidden unit and ask what changes when I change one thing. The difficulty is not that the system is hiding its design from me; it is that the design is high-dimensional and was not made to be read.

That has a direct consequence for interpretability. If we can query the system, explanations should be tested by queries. A linear probe that lights up on “birds” is a beginning, not an answer. The question is what happens when the bird feature is removed, amplified, or corrupted. Does the model stop saying “bird”? Does it start making a predictable mistake, such as treating the object as a plane or a dog? Does the effect depend on another feature, such as a context feature for “small” or a grammar feature for plural nouns? An interpretation that cannot be converted into an intervention is mostly a description of the interpreter’s expectations. The same applies to attention heads, residual streams, and subnetworks. If we claim that a head implements copying, we should ablate it and see whether copying degrades. If we claim that a circuit performs addition, we should patch its intermediate activations and watch the carry propagate.

This also means interpretability research should spend more time on systems with known answers. It is unflattering to admit that we often cannot say what a network is doing on a task we could specify in one paragraph. If we train a small transformer to add two-digit numbers, we can check whether it learned place value, carrying, and digit features, or whether it learned a lookup table with a few algorithmic shortcuts. If we train it to sort lists, we can ask whether it uses positional comparisons or a fragile pattern-matching hack. These toy tasks are not the final destination, but they are the calibration equipment. A method that cannot recover the known mechanism in a small model has no business claiming to reveal the mechanism in a large one. At the same time, the method must be stressed beyond the toy: the circuit should persist across seeds, sizes, and nearby tasks, or it is probably an artifact of the easiest route the optimizer found.

The ease of retraining also pushes interpretability toward learning dynamics. A final weight matrix is a snapshot. The interesting question is often how a representation got there: when did the feature appear, what loss pressure selected it, what earlier representation it displaced, and whether a different training order produces a different but functionally similar feature. Neuroscience has development, but for us development is a log file. We can compare checkpoints, perturb the curriculum, and ask whether a feature is robust to the path that produced it. That is a kind of evidence no final-state analysis can provide.

The strongest objection to this view is that ease can become complacency. Because we can intervene, we may mistake local causal relevance for understanding. A unit can be necessary for a task in a particular model and still be an accidental byproduct of initialization. A circuit can look clean in a small model and dissolve in a larger one. The fact that we control the system does not guarantee that the system is legible; it only guarantees that we can find out when we are wrong. So the standard has to be higher, not lower. Interpretability should not be a catalog of features that seem to match human categories. It should be a set of mechanistic claims that predict the effects of interventions, survive changes in scale and training, and eventually explain why the network learned the computation it did.

Neuroscience is harder because the scientist is outside the machine. Interpretability is easier because we are inside the workshop. The consequence is not that we can understand large networks by staring at them. It is that we can hold ourselves to a standard they cannot: an interpretation is not a story that fits the observations; it is a model of the computation that tells us what will happen when we change the system.

prompt: Why are software schedules so hard to predict? Write an explanation of the phases of a software project and how each one should be scheduled differently, for a manager who has been burned by slipping deadlines.
response:
Software schedules are hard to predict because the work that consumes time is often not the work that was named at the start. A team may estimate “build the search page” in two weeks. The two weeks become six because search must rank by recency and relevance, handle typos, exclude deleted items, scale to a ten-million-row table, and behave differently for admins than for customers. None of that is padding; it is the system revealing its shape.

This is why the usual schedule method fails. A manager receives a total: 800 person-hours. The team divides that by its weekly capacity and gets a date. But the 800 was an estimate of a system that does not yet exist. In construction, an engineer can calculate the load on a beam before the beam is built. In software, the load is often discovered only when the parts are connected: the database is slower than expected, the third-party API rejects a payload, the mobile client retries and duplicates orders, the security review finds a flaw in the session model.

The hardest objection to this view is that some software is predictable. A small internal report, a straightforward CRUD tool, or an integration with a stable, well-documented API can be scheduled closely. If a manager has been burned, the pain usually comes from projects with unknowns: new data relationships, performance targets, regulatory constraints, third-party dependencies, or behavior that only appears under real use. Better estimation in the same phase does not remove that unknown. The schedule has to be organized around reducing it.

That means treating a software project as a sequence of different kinds of work, each with a different relationship to time.

## Discovery

Discovery should be scheduled as an investigation, not as a document to finish. Give it a fixed window: one week for a small feature, two to four weeks for a new system. The exit is not “requirements are done,” because completeness is a feeling. The exit is a set of decisions: we know the smallest useful version, we know the top three risks, and we know what must be true for the current date to hold. If discovery shows that offline mode requires a rewrite of the sync layer, the date changes. That is the phase working.

## Architecture and design

Architecture and design should be scheduled around irreversible choices. A database schema, a public API, an authentication model, a deployment boundary, and a data migration path are expensive to reverse. For each one, ask whether a cheap proof can reduce the risk. If the fear is that a query over 200,000 rows will take too long, run a two-day prototype with real data. If the fear is that a partner API cannot handle 50 requests per second, test it in a sandbox. Do not spend two weeks drawing diagrams for a report page. Design should end in gates: after each gate, proceed, change approach, or escalate.

## Implementation

Implementation should be scheduled in working increments, not as a lump sum of person-days. A twelve-week project with four developers is not a pile of 240 person-days to be spread evenly. It is a sequence of slices that can be inspected: by week two, a user can sign up; by week four, a user can create an item; by week six, the item syncs; by week eight, an admin can view it; by week ten, payment works; by week twelve, the release is stable. Each slice should be small enough to be wrong quickly. If a team completes three units of work per week, do not promise all twelve units by week four. Promise the first three, and let the next weeks absorb what was learned. This also makes the effect of change visible. A “small” change to a core model in week seven may invalidate the next three slices, and the manager can see that tradeoff immediately.

## Integration and testing

Integration and testing should not be scheduled as a final phase. Integration bugs are interactions: an authentication token expires while a background job is retrying; the mobile client sends a timestamp in a different format; the billing service and the inventory service disagree about what “completed” means. If integration starts only after the build is finished, those interactions are discovered when there is no time to fix them. Every increment should run against real or representative dependencies. Then reserve a separate window for the boundaries that are genuinely hard: third-party APIs, legacy systems, cross-team contracts. That window is not spare time for unknown coding. It is time to coordinate with other people and other systems.

## Stabilization

Stabilization should be scheduled as risk reduction, not feature completion. Once the core path works, the question is no longer “when will the last feature be coded?” but “when will the bug rate and severity be low enough to release?” If beta finds twenty critical bugs and the team fixes five per day, with one day of regression testing after each batch, the need is closer to eight days than four. Feature freeze is not a morale issue; it is a boundary condition. If the date is firm, scope must shrink. If scope is firm, the date must move. If both are held fixed, quality becomes the variable, and that is how a product launches with a hole in it.

## Production operation

Production operation should be scheduled because some work cannot be known before launch. A checkout flow that takes 800 milliseconds in staging may take four seconds when a thousand users hit it at noon. A data migration that succeeds on a sample may fail on a corrupted record that exists only in production. A canary release, monitoring, and a rollback plan are not ceremonial. They are the schedule for learning from real load.

For a manager, the practical consequence is to stop asking for one confident date as if the unknowns have already been solved. The plan should say what is known, what is unknown, what will reduce the unknown, and what happens if the unknown turns out differently. If the project is simple, the plan will be boring and the date will hold. If it is not simple, the plan will show where the date can bend before the deadline bends on its own.

Potential essay:

Software schedules are hard to predict because the first half of the project is about learning, and learning is not metered in person-hours. When a manager asks “how long will it take,” the team often answers by imagining the final system and counting boxes. That method works for building a bridge, where the loads are known. It fails for software because the loads are discovered while building.

Example: A project to add “real-time notifications” is estimated at eight weeks. During build, the team learns that events from three services arrive out of order, that some users have notification preferences that conflict, and that the mobile app cannot reliably reconnect. The code that was hard was not the notification API; it was the state machine that keeps users from receiving duplicate or stale messages. Nobody counted that state machine in the first estimate because it did not exist until the problem surfaced.

Hardest objection: If teams are bad, better planning tools fix it? Some projects are predictable. A small internal report, a CRUD admin page, a well-understood integration with a stable API can be scheduled fairly closely. The manager who has been burned usually has a portfolio of such projects plus a few with unknowns: new data model, third-party dependency, performance target, security constraint, or user behavior. The schedule slips on the latter, and the slip propagates to the whole date. The fix is not to estimate more carefully in the same phase; it is to treat uncertainty as a work item and schedule it explicitly.

Then phases.

1. Discovery. Schedule as a fixed investigation, not a deliverable. Give it a timebox: one week for a small feature, two to four for a new system. Exit criteria: you can state the top three risks, the smallest useful version, and the decision needed to proceed. Do not schedule “requirements complete” because completeness is a feeling. Schedule the decision: “By Friday we will know whether we can support offline mode without rewriting the sync layer.” If discovery changes scope, the date changes. That is not failure; it is the phase doing its job.

2. Architecture and design. Schedule the irreversible choices, not the whole blueprint. A database schema, a public API, an authentication model, a deployment boundary, a data migration path—these are expensive to reverse. For each, ask: can we make a cheap proof? If the risk is “can we query 200,000 records in under 300 ms,” run a prototype for two days with real data. If the risk is “can the partner API handle 50 requests/second,” test it in a sandbox. Do not spend two weeks drawing diagrams for a report page. Design should be scheduled in decision gates: after each gate, either proceed, change approach, or escalate.

3. Implementation. Schedule by increments, not by total size. A 12-week project with four developers should not be planned as 192 person-days divided evenly. It should be planned as a sequence of working slices: week 2, user can sign up; week 4, user can create an item; week 6, item syncs; week 8, admin can view; week 10, payment works; week 12, stable release. Each slice should be small enough to be wrong quickly. If a team reliably completes three story points per week, do not promise all twelve points by week four. Promise the first three, and use the next weeks to absorb what you learn. This also protects against the most common managerial mistake: adding “small” changes in week seven. A small change to a core model can invalidate the next three slices.

4. Integration and testing. Do not schedule it as a final phase. Integration bugs are interactions: auth token expires at the same moment a background job retries; the mobile client sends a timestamp in a different format; the billing service and inventory service disagree on what “completed” means. If integration starts after build, the team will discover these interactions when there is no time to fix them. Schedule integration continuously: every increment should run against the real or representative dependencies. Then reserve a separate window for the boundaries that are truly hard—third-party APIs, legacy systems, cross-team contracts. That window is not buffer for unknown coding; it is time to coordinate with other people and other systems.

5. Stabilization and release. Schedule risk reduction, not feature completion. Once the core path works, the schedule question becomes: how many days until the bug rate and severity are low enough to release? If beta finds 20 critical bugs and the team fixes five per day, with one day of regression testing after each batch, you need roughly four days, not two. Feature freeze is not a morale problem; it is a mathematical boundary. If the date is firm, scope must shrink. If scope is firm, date must move. If both are firm, quality becomes the variable, and that is how you get a launch with a hole in it.

6. Production operation. Some work cannot be scheduled before launch because it depends on real load, real data, and real users. A checkout flow that takes 800 ms in staging may take 4 seconds when 1,000 users hit it at noon. A data migration that succeeds on a sample may fail on a corrupted record that exists only in production. Schedule a post-launch window for monitoring, canary deployment, and rollback. If the manager needs a public date, the date should be “available to 10 percent” or “general availability,” not “all problems solved.”

Conclusion: The manager's job is not to extract a single confident date from engineers. It is to build a plan that says what is known, what is unknown, what will reduce the unknown, and what happens if the unknown turns out differently. A schedule for software is a map of uncertainty with checkpoints, not a straight line from start to finish. If the project is genuinely simple, the plan will be boring and the date will hold. If it is not, the plan will show where the date can bend before the deadline bends on its own.

prompt: Write a blog post about why online programming Q&A communities have so many strict rules, and how welcoming beginners fits with that.
response:
The first thing a newcomer to a programming Q&A community often learns is that asking for help is a skill with a local dialect. Post “my button isn’t working” and you may be told to include the error, the code, and what you expected to happen. Post a 400-line file with one typo and you may be asked to reduce it. Post the exact exception, the relevant function, and the input that triggers it, and you may get an answer in minutes. The contrast can feel harsh, especially when the person asking is already stuck.

But the strictness is not mainly about manners. It is about making a question answerable by a stranger who has not seen your machine, your project, or your intent. A programming bug is rarely a fact about the language. It is a relation among a lot of moving parts: a version, a path, a configuration, a data shape, a timing condition, a missing dependency. If the question does not name those parts, the answerer has to guess which one matters. With thousands of questions arriving while volunteers answer in spare time, guessing is too expensive. The rules are a way of asking the questioner to do the first pass of diagnosis.

The rules multiply because the failure modes multiply. A question can be too vague to understand. It can use the wrong tags. It can omit the error message. It can include so much code that the relevant line is invisible. It can describe a desired feature instead of a broken behavior. It can depend on a private file, a local network, or a proprietary system. It can duplicate a question that already has a good answer. Each rule addresses a different way the question can fail to be answerable.

This is why the rules look so mechanical. Titles should say what is broken. Tags should say what tools are involved. The body should show the error, the relevant code, and the expected behavior. A minimal example matters because it separates the problem from the surrounding accident. If a Python script fails only after reading a CSV, the answer may be in how the CSV is parsed, not in the loop that prints the rows. If a React component renders nothing, the answer may be a missing return, a state name typo, or a parent that never mounts the child. A pared-down example lets the answerer test hypotheses instead of reading your whole application.

The same rules also make the archive useful. A Q&A community is not only a chat room; it is a searchable record. A beginner in six months may not remember who answered their first question, but they may find the post that solved the same problem. If every question is “help, it does not work,” the archive is a wall of noise. If questions carry the error text, versions, and code, the archive becomes a library. The rules are the cataloging system. They let a person with a strange problem find the one case where someone else hit it and wrote down what happened.

The hardest objection to all this is that the rules can be used against beginners. That is real. A community can turn “show what you tried” into “prove you are competent before we talk to you.” A person who is new to the field may not know that an error message matters, that a minimal example is possible, or that the question should be in English in a particular technical register. If the response is only a downvote, a close vote, or a curt comment, the rule has been applied as exclusion. The site may be efficient and still unwelcoming.

The difference is not that a welcoming community has looser rules. It is that the rules are explained as part of the help. “Please add the full traceback” is not a test. It points to the place where the answer is likely hiding. “Can you show the smallest code that fails?” is not a dismissal. It says the problem is somewhere in that code, and the smaller it gets, the easier it is to see. “What did you try?” is not always an insult; sometimes it prevents five people from suggesting the same restart. The same sentence can be gatekeeping or guidance, depending on whether the person writing it is trying to sort noise or trying to hand the newcomer a tool.

There is also a social benefit to strict rules that newcomers underestimate. If a community accepts every question no matter how thin, it does not help the person asking; it buries them. The first answer to “my code is wrong” may be a guess, a joke, or a lecture. The question gets answered badly, or not at all, because no one can tell what is being asked. A community with clearer standards can say, in effect, “we can help, but we need these facts.” That is a more honest promise than pretending any question can be answered from a screenshot.

The rules also protect the people who answer. Programming help is cognitively expensive. A good answer may require rereading the code, reproducing the behavior, and checking versions. If the question gives no entry point, the answerer spends time constructing the problem before solving it. Volunteers can sustain that work only when a large share of questions are at least navigable. The strictness is a labor rule. It keeps the community from consuming itself.

This is where the beginner-friendly part gets concrete. A welcoming community does not wait for perfect questions. It teaches the local dialect through the first attempt. It edits the title so it can be found. It asks for the missing error. It suggests a smaller example. It answers the question that is actually there, even if the first version of it was clumsy. It treats a bad question as a draft, not as evidence that the asker is bad at programming. Many experienced developers remember their first public question as embarrassing. The community succeeds when that embarrassment turns into a habit: read the error, isolate the piece, post the parts.

Strict rules and beginner welcome are not in tension when the rules are about information. They become in tension when the rules are about status. “You must have read the docs” can be a boundary. “You must prove you read the docs before we acknowledge your problem” is a different thing. A site can require a minimal reproducible example and still respond to a failed first attempt with patience. It can close an unanswerable question and say exactly why it is unanswerable. It can downvote a duplicate and point to the post that already contains the answer. The strictness remains, but it is aimed at the question, not the person.

The rules exist because programming questions are hard to answer at a distance. The language is a small part of it. The real problem is usually in the context the asker has and the answerer lacks. The rules force that context into words. A beginner may resent the demand for the error message, the code, and the expected output. But once the demand is met, the help often arrives faster than it would have in a friendlier, vaguer place. The welcome is not the absence of standards. It is the standard, applied with the explanation that makes it learnable.

The rules are a way of asking the questioner to do the first pass of diagnosis.

This is why the rules look so mechanical. Titles should say what is broken. Tags should say what tools are involved. The body should show the error, the relevant code, and the expected behavior. A minimal example matters because it separates the problem from the surrounding accident. If a Python script fails only after reading a CSV, the answer may be in how the CSV is parsed, not in the loop that prints the rows. If a React component renders nothing, the answer may be a missing return, a state name typo, or a parent that never mounts the child. A pared-down example lets the answerer test hypotheses instead of reading your whole application.

The same rules also make the archive useful. A Q&A community is not only a chat room; it is a searchable record. A beginner in six months may not remember who answered their first question, but they may find the post that solved the same problem. If every question is "help, it does not work," the archive is a wall of noise. If questions carry the error text, versions, and code, the archive becomes a library. The rules are the cataloging system. They let a person with a strange problem find the one case where someone else hit it and wrote down what happened.

The hardest objection to all this is that the rules can be used against beginners. That is real. A community can turn "show what you tried" into "prove you are competent before we talk to you." A person who is new to the field may not know that an error message matters, that a minimal example is possible, or that the question should be in English in a particular technical register. If the response is only a downvote, a close vote, or a curt comment, the rule has been applied as exclusion. The site may be efficient and still unwelcoming.

The difference is not that a welcoming community has looser rules. It is that the rules are explained as part of the help. "Please add the full traceback" is not a test. It points to the place where the answer is likely hiding. "Can you show the smallest code that fails?" is not a dismissal. It says the problem is somewhere in that code, and the smaller it gets, the easier it is to see. "What did you try?" is not always an insult; sometimes it prevents five people from suggesting the same restart. The same sentence can be gatekeeping or guidance, depending on whether the person writing it is trying to sort noise or trying to hand the newcomer a tool.

There is also a social benefit to strict rules that newcomers underestimate. If a community accepts every question no matter how thin, it does not help the person asking; it buries them. The first answer to "my code is wrong" may be a guess, a joke, or a lecture. The question gets answered badly, or not at all, because no one can tell what is being asked. A community with clearer standards can say, in effect, "we can help, but we need these facts." That is a more honest promise than pretending any question can be answered from a screenshot.

The rules also protect the people who answer. Programming help is cognitively expensive. A good answer may require rereading the code, reproducing the behavior, and checking versions. If the question gives no entry point, the answerer spends time constructing the problem before solving it. Volunteers can sustain that work only when a large share of questions are at least navigable. The strictness is a labor rule. It keeps the community from consuming itself.

This is where the beginner-friendly part gets concrete. A welcoming community does not wait for perfect questions. It teaches the local dialect through the first attempt. It edits the title so it can be found. It asks for the missing error. It suggests a smaller example. It answers the question that is actually there, even if the first version of it was clumsy. It treats a bad question as a draft, not as evidence that the asker is bad at programming. Many experienced developers remember their first public question as embarrassing. The community succeeds when that embarrassment turns into a habit: read the error, isolate the piece, post the parts.

Strict rules and beginner welcome are not in tension when the rules are about information. They become in tension when the rules are about status. "You must have read the docs" can be a boundary. "You must prove you read the docs before we acknowledge your problem" is a different thing. A site can require a minimal reproducible example and still respond to a failed first attempt with patience. It can close an unanswerable question and say exactly why it is unanswerable. It can downvote a duplicate and point to the post that already contains the answer. The strictness remains, but it is aimed at the question, not the person.

In the end, the rules exist because programming questions are hard to answer at a distance. The language is a small part of it. The real problem is usually in the context the asker has and the answerer lacks. The rules force that context into words. A beginner may resent the demand for the error message, the code, and the expected output. But once the demand is met, the help often arrives faster than it would have in a friendlier, vaguer place. The welcome is not the absence of standards. It is the standard, applied with the explanation that makes it learnable.

prompt: Apple just refused the FBI's order to help unlock the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone, and most people I know in tech are cheering. I am too, but something about the reaction bugs me. Write a short essay on how the tech world decides whom to trust with power, companies or governments.
response:
The San Bernardino case was never really about one phone. The phone belonged to a man who had killed people; it may have contained messages, contacts, or evidence that would have mattered to victims and investigators. The FBI did not ask Apple for a favor. It asked, through a court, for a specific technical capability: a modified version of iOS that would disable the delay after failed passcode guesses. Apple’s objection was that once it built that tool, the tool would exist. It could be subpoenaed, leaked, reverse engineered, or demanded again by another prosecutor, another agency, or another country. The tech world cheered because the objection sounded like a principle rather than a delay tactic.

The principle is easier to state than to defend. Tech people tend to distrust governments because governments hold the monopoly on force and can wrap abuse in secrecy. They are more comfortable with companies because companies, at least in theory, depend on customers and can be punished by losing them. You can switch email providers, choose another cloud, buy another phone. You cannot choose another FBI. That distinction is real. When Snowden showed that the NSA had been collecting vast quantities of communications data, the outrage was not only that the government had spied, but that it had done so under legal authorities that were difficult for the public to inspect. The abuse was hidden from the courts and the press, which is the opposite of what a company’s abuse usually looks like.

But the company side is not clean. The same tech world that cheered Apple has watched Google index its way into the center of public life, Facebook turn personal profiles into ad inventory, and Amazon become the plumbing for competitors. A company can ban an app, demote a website, lock a user out of a cloud account, or collect location data for years, and the user’s remedy is usually a terms-of-service page and a complaint form. In many ways, corporate power is more intimate than state power: it shapes what you see, what you can install, and what your data becomes, every day, without a warrant. Both should be trusted only when the power is narrow, reviewable, and likely to be exposed if abused.

This is where the San Bernardino fight was subtle. If the FBI had asked Apple to turn over iCloud data it already stored, the case would have looked like ordinary law enforcement: a warrant, a court, a company complying with records it already possessed. Apple does that routinely. The request was different because it asked Apple to manufacture a new means of access. A backdoor is not a document you hand over and then keep in a file. It is a capability. Once a capability exists, control over it is a problem of physics and incentives, not of promises. The FBI said it needed the tool once. That may have been true. But legal systems are not built on the good faith of one case; they are built on the rules that survive the next one. The FBI later opened the phone with a third-party exploit, reportedly for a few hundred thousand dollars; that did not prove Apple right, but it did show that the state can sometimes buy access without forcing a particular company to undermine its product.

What bugs about the cheering is that it often stops there. Apple is not a privacy saint. It is a corporation with a walled garden, an app store that can remove software for reasons that feel arbitrary, and a business interest in making its devices indispensable. Trusting Apple against the FBI in one case does not mean Apple’s power is safe. The same people who support Apple’s right to refuse a court order may be the ones least able to escape Apple’s control once their life is stored in iCloud. The trust is not unconditional; it is a bet that corporate overreach will be visible, litigable, and competitive enough to correct itself. I am less sure that bet holds for infrastructure companies, where switching costs are high and the public rarely sees the seams.

So the tech world does not decide between companies and governments so much as it asks where the error can be found. A company abuses you, and the story may become a lawsuit, a leak, a competitor’s ad, or a product migration. A government abuses you, and the story may become a classified annex, a national-security deference, or a decade of secrecy. That is a reasonable starting point, not a moral hierarchy. The better rule is to give the state specific, judicially reviewed access to data already held, to refuse compelled creation of general tools, and to make any exception narrow enough that the next San Bernardino does not quietly become permission for everything else. The victims deserved answers from that phone. The answer should have come from better law, not from a reflexive choice between the corporation and the state.

prompt: A recent economics paper claims that each researcher is far less productive than decades ago, since scientific progress stays roughly constant while the number of researchers grows exponentially. Is science slowing down? Write an essay giving your own take, including whether we should even find this surprising.
response:
The argument has a clean shape, and that is what makes it attractive: if scientific output is flat and the number of scientists is exploding, then output per scientist must be collapsing. The arithmetic is not the interesting part. The interesting part is the first premise. “Scientific progress stays roughly constant” is doing enormous work, and what it means changes the answer completely.

My take is that science is not slowing down in the sense that matters most for the world: the total stock of usable knowledge is still expanding, often rapidly, in many fields. But science is becoming more expensive per unit of marginal progress. That is a different claim, and it should not surprise us.

Start with the ambiguity in “progress.” If progress means the number of papers, the answer is easy: it has not stayed constant. Annual scientific publications have gone from well under a million in the mid-twentieth century to several million today. If progress means the number of solved practical problems, the answer is also not “constant”: life expectancy in the United States rose from roughly 47 in 1900 to roughly 78 in 2019; cancer death rates have fallen substantially; transistor density roughly doubled every two years for decades; genome sequencing went from a multiyear, multimillion-dollar project to a routine, cheap one. If progress means “new basic laws of nature discovered per researcher,” the answer may be closer to the paper’s claim, at least in some areas. Particle physics is the obvious case: the Standard Model was essentially in place by the 1970s, the Higgs completed it in 2012, and thousands of people have been looking for new particles since without finding them. In that narrow sense, yes, the marginal researcher in high-energy physics is buying less new fundamental knowledge than a researcher in the 1920s.

But that is not “science” in general. It is one frontier, and a very famous one. Aggregating it into a verdict on all of science is like looking at the number of new gold nuggets found per miner in a depleted mine and concluding that all mining has stopped producing metal.

The paper’s conclusion is also sensitive to what one counts as a researcher and what one counts as output. Modern science is team science. A LIGO paper may have thousands of authors; a LHC result is the product of a collaboration, not a person. If you divide output by headcount, you will see a decline partly because the unit of production has changed. A single researcher in 1930 was more likely to be a generalist working in a small field; a researcher in 2020 is more likely to be a specialist contributing one component to a large coordinated effort. That can look like lower individual productivity even when the system is producing more.

There is also a measurement problem. If progress is measured by citations, then older papers have had more time to accumulate citations, fields differ in citation culture, and larger fields generate more citations simply because there are more people in them. A citation is a measure of attention, not of truth or importance. It can be normalized, but normalization is hard. I am not confident that any standard metric captures “scientific progress” well enough to support a strong conclusion about per-researcher productivity; I suspect the strongest version of the slowdown claim is really a claim about the marginal novelty or marginal citation impact of the average new paper, not about the total advance of science.

That brings me to the hardest objection to my view, because it is not trivial. The average new paper may indeed be less novel than the average new paper used to be. If the marginal contribution of an extra researcher is falling, then the engine of science is becoming less efficient, and that matters. We are not just accumulating knowledge for its own sake. We need breakthroughs in energy, medicine, materials, biology, climate, AI safety, and other areas where the current rate of progress may be too slow. If each additional scientist yields less, then the cost of future breakthroughs rises. That is a serious concern, and dismissing it as a measurement artifact would be wrong.

But the response is not to say science is stalling. It is to say that the old model of progress—small groups of brilliant individuals making discrete, high-impact discoveries in relatively isolated fields—is no longer the whole story. Some progress now requires infrastructure: telescopes, colliders, sequencers, data centers, global collaborations. The discovery of gravitational waves was not a solo flash of insight; it was a huge engineering and data-analysis project. That does not mean the people involved are less productive. It means the production function has changed.

And we should not be surprised by that. In any search process, the easy discoveries come first. The first maps of a coastline are easier to draw than the final centimeter of it. The first medicinal compounds are easier to find than the last. The first transistors are easier to improve than the last. As a field expands, the low-hanging fruit disappears. The remaining problems are harder, more contested, and often require more people. A falling return to an extra researcher is not evidence that the field is dead; it is often evidence that the field has gotten deep.

There is also an economic point that is easy to miss: the number of researchers is not exogenous. We grow the research workforce because progress is valuable. If science were not producing enough return to justify more scientists, the workforce would not have expanded. The fact that each additional researcher yields less than the first million does not mean the expansion was a mistake. It means we are paying for a larger, more complex research system because we value the output. In normal economic terms, diminishing marginal productivity is not a paradox. It is the condition under which most industries grow.

So is science slowing down? The honest answer is uneven. In some areas, yes: the rate of new fundamental discovery per researcher has fallen, and the cost per breakthrough has risen. In many other areas, no: the total rate of progress is still high, and the tools for doing science have become more powerful, not less. The per-researcher decline is real enough to take seriously as a warning about the rising cost of future progress, but it is not the same thing as a decline in science. What has changed is not that researchers are less capable, but that the frontier is larger, more crowded, more specialized, and more team-based than it was. That is not surprising. It is what happens when a small craft becomes a global industry.

prompt: Bryan Caplan argues that it's arbitrary which atrocities and scandals people get outraged about, like sexual harassment versus an abusive boss, or chemical weapons versus conventional ones. Write a response arguing there might be a rational explanation.
response:
Caplan is right about the obvious thing: outrage is not a harm counter. If it were, we would be far more outraged by road deaths, poor housing, antibiotic resistance, preventable childhood illness, and the slow violence of poverty than by a single gas attack or a single predator in a position of authority. More people die in car crashes each year than in most wars, and conventional weapons kill far more people in recent history than chemical ones. The fact that our moral alarm bells do not track total suffering should make us suspicious of any simple claim that outrage is “tracking” moral seriousness in a direct way.

But “not a harm counter” does not mean “arbitrary.” A rational explanation becomes possible if we stop asking what outrage is measuring and ask what it is doing.

Outrage is not primarily a device for allocating moral attention to the largest quantities of pain. It is a device for marking violations of boundaries that a community needs to enforce but cannot always enforce through law, price, or routine social pressure. A boundary violation becomes especially outrageous when it involves intentionality, power, concealment, and the threat that the boundary may now be treated as optional. Those features are not random. They are often exactly the features that make a violation dangerous.

Consider the comparison between sexual harassment and an abusive boss. A boss who is cruel, micromanaging, humiliating, or threatening can do enormous damage. People lose jobs, self-esteem, health, and years of working life under bad managers. If outrage were simply a response to suffering, that should be enough. But the boss’s behavior is often categorized differently: bad management, a toxic workplace, a difficult superior. It is terrible, but it is still within the general domain of work, hierarchy, and economic coercion. The boss is using power in a place where power is already present.

Sexual harassment crosses a different line. It uses power not merely to make work unpleasant, but to claim access to a domain that the subordinate has not consented to open: the body, sexual refusal, intimate dignity. The employee may be forced to endure bad decisions, long hours, and even public criticism as part of the job. The employee is not forced to submit to sexual advances. When a superior uses status to blur that distinction, the violation is not just personal cruelty; it is an attempt to expand the legitimate scope of authority. Outrage is stronger because the boundary being tested is more fundamental. If the answer is “a boss can do whatever he wants because he controls your paycheck,” then every subordinate relationship becomes a potential site of predation.

This also explains why sexual harassment often becomes a scandal rather than merely a complaint. Scandal arises when hidden use of trust is revealed. A bad boss is often known to be a bad boss. People tolerate him because they need the job, or because he is useful, or because the organization protects him. But sexual harassment frequently depends on secrecy, denial, minimization, and the threat that the victim will not be believed. The outrage is not only about the act; it is about the permissive environment that made the act possible. It is a signal that the institution is not merely inefficient or unpleasant, but that it may be protecting predators. That is a different kind of information, and a more socially dangerous one.

One could object that this still sounds like a story about salience, not morality. Sexual harassment is dramatic, personal, and easy to narrate. An abusive boss is diffuse and boring. Maybe people are just drawn to stories. That may be part of it. But salience is not the same as arbitrariness. Humans are better at detecting intentional threats, cheaters, and boundary violations than they are at aggregating statistical harms. That is not a bug from the point of view of social coordination. A community does not need every member to run a cost-benefit analysis on total expected suffering. It needs members to notice when someone is using trust for exploitation, when an institution is failing to protect the vulnerable, or when a previously forbidden practice is becoming normalized. Outrage is a crude but useful alarm for those cases.

The chemical weapons case works similarly. Conventional weapons are often deadlier. Artillery, bombs, drones, and bullets kill more people than chemical agents have in recent decades. If outrage were proportional to deaths, that should end the discussion. But chemical weapons violate a different set of boundaries. They are associated with poisoning, which is covert, lingering, and hard to defend against. They terrorize without a visible battlefield. They contaminate places that are supposed to be safe. They make war more frightening in a way that is not merely quantitative. A bomb can be located, defended against, and framed as a military strike. Poison gas or nerve agent can appear in a town, a hospital, a market, a home. It transforms war from a contest between armed actors into a threat to the basic security of daily life.

There is also a rational institutional reason for the taboo. The rules of war are not merely sentimental. They exist to keep conflict bounded. If chemical weapons are acceptable, then the logic of deterrence, proportionality, and target selection becomes harder to maintain. A state that uses poison gas is not just committing a particular atrocity; it is signaling that it is willing to abandon the framework that makes war, however horrible, less than pure annihilation. Outrage against chemical weapons is therefore not only a reaction to the victims; it is a reaction to the permission the act would create. The norm has value even when, in any one year, chemical weapons kill fewer people than conventional ones.

This is similar to the way legal systems often care about intent, not just outcomes. A doctor who accidentally kills a patient through an unusual complication and a nurse who deliberately poisons a patient may both be involved in a death, but the moral and legal response is not the same. Intent matters because it reveals character, because it is more deterable, and because it changes what the act means for future behavior. Outrage often works the same way. It spikes not only where harm is greatest, but where the harm is chosen, hidden, and emblematic of a broader violation.

This does not mean outrage is always well calibrated. It can be manipulated, exaggerated, and turned into performance. It can punish the most visible transgressor while ignoring the more damaging system around him. It can become a way for people to display virtue rather than solve problems. I am less sure that this makes outrage morally good in every case, because a norm that is valuable in one context can become a tool for cruelty in another. But that is a different question from whether the pattern is rational. A smoke alarm can be triggered by toast, and an immune system can overreact to pollen. The existence of false positives does not show that the alarm or the immune response is meaningless.

So Caplan’s observation is useful. Outrage is not a reliable measure of total harm, and anyone who thinks it is should look at road deaths and public health statistics. But the apparent arbitrariness disappears a little if we ask what outrage is enforcing. Sexual harassment outrages because it threatens the boundary between professional authority and sexual access. Chemical weapons outrage because they threaten the boundary between bounded war and indiscriminate terror. In both cases, the outrage is not simply about the immediate victims, though they matter. It is about what would become acceptable if the violation were treated as ordinary.

That is not a perfect moral calculus. It is a social one. But it is not arbitrary.

prompt: Everyone says we need to regulate AI more or less, but nobody says what a good outcome would actually look like. I want a blog post walking through one detailed, optimistic best-case roadmap for how a country could get through the arrival of transformative AI, and why you find it compelling despite how weird it sounds.
response:
**The Managed Decade**

The missing question is not whether AI should be regulated. It is what a country does in the five years when AI becomes good enough to take jobs faster than schools, firms, and welfare systems can replace them. The best-case outcome is not a ban, and it is not a free-for-all. It is a managed transition: temporary public controls that let the technology arrive without letting it arrive all at once.

I have a specific version of this in mind. Imagine a large democracy, about 330 million people, a $28 trillion economy, home to many of the frontier labs. In 2027 it passes an AI Transition Act. The law does not define AI. It defines three things: compute, economic agency, and displacement. It creates an independent authority with five-year powers, renewable only by supermajority. It builds a public compute reserve, a transition fund, and a licensing regime for autonomous economic agents. The goal is not to stop AI. It is to make the path through AI pass through institutions that can pay for the damage and repair the labor market while the technology is still being learned.

The first tool is the compute reserve. A firm that builds a new data center can take a tax credit if it reserves 10 percent of the accelerator capacity for public-interest use at cost: universities, hospitals, national labs, small businesses, and safety researchers. The state adds a 10-cent-per-kilowatt-hour charge on data-center electricity to fund smaller grants and keep the public cloud running. If U.S. data centers draw 200 terawatt-hours a year, the charge raises about $20 billion. That is not enough to build the grid, but it is enough to make public access a real option rather than a charity case. The reserve also becomes a shock absorber. When a new model makes the old public models obsolete, the reserve has cash and hardware to move the public sector’s workforce onto the new stack.

This sounds protectionist, and it is. But the protection is not against foreign AI. It is against a future in which the only people who can use the most important technology of the century are the people who built it. A country that lets five companies own the grid loses the argument before it starts.

The second tool is the transition fund. The fund is paid for by the data-center tax and by a 5 percent levy on revenue from AI products sold domestically that are certified as replacing labor in a covered occupation. Certification is not done by the seller. It is done by the authority, using payroll data, occupational task surveys, and randomized audits. If a software company sells an AI that closes a company’s books, and the authority finds that the product is displacing staff accountants, the company pays. If it merely makes accountants faster, it does not.

I am least sure this levy can be made precise. Attribution between a product, a recession, and management choice will be messy. The law would have to rely on presumptions, audits, and appeal processes, and it would still get some cases wrong. But tax administration is full of imperfect lines, and the goal is not perfect justice. The goal is to attach a social cost to the fastest forms of displacement.

The fund does not give everyone a check. It pays wage insurance. If a worker in a covered occupation loses more than 20 percent of earnings because of AI-linked layoffs, demand destruction, or firm failure, the state replaces 70 percent of the lost earnings for three years. The worker gets free retraining, relocation help, and access to public compute if the new job involves building with AI. The average benefit might be $10,000 a year. Twenty billion dollars can fully support two million workers, or top up a larger pool. That is not the whole labor market, but it is the difference between a family surviving a transition and a family becoming a statistic.

The design matters. A universal basic income is cleaner, but it is politically harder and macroeconomically noisier in the early years. Wage insurance is targeted, reversible, and easier to explain: if the machines took your job, the state holds the machines’ owner responsible for the bridge. It also creates a price signal. Companies know that deploying a model that fires people triggers a social cost. They do not pay the cost directly for every worker, but the levy and the public backlash are attached to the product. That is enough to make some firms choose slower rollout, human-in-the-loop interfaces, or upskilling tools. Not all. But some.

Take a concrete case. A software company in Austin releases a product that can close a mid-size company’s books. In the unmanaged case, its customers fire 30 percent of their accounting staff within a year. In the managed case, the product is certified as displacing staff accountants. The company pays the levy. Its customers still adopt the software, because it is better. The displaced workers get wage insurance. Some move into audit, compliance, or client advisory work that the software does not do well. Some use public compute to start small firms that sell accounting cleanup services to companies too messy for the automated close. The Austin company still wins. The accounting firms do not all die. The workers have three years instead of three months.

The third tool is licensing for autonomous economic agents. This is the weirdest part. The law does not regulate models. It regulates actions. An economic agent is software that can, without a human approving each step, spend money, sign contracts, move inventory, deploy code, or alter financial records. Below a threshold, it is just software. Above it, the operator must register, carry insurance, and submit to audit. The threshold might be $100,000 per transaction or $5 million in autonomous spending per month. A startup can build an agent that drafts purchase orders. A corporation that wants an agent to manage $10 billion in procurement must show that it can explain a decision, halt the agent, reconstruct the audit trail, and pay for mistakes. If it cannot, it can still run the agent, but a human must approve each transaction over the limit.

This is not a ban. It is closer to securities regulation. No one says we should let a new trading algorithm move billions without registration, capital requirements, and incident reporting. The reason we do that for finance is not that code is dangerous in the abstract. It is that financial systems fail in correlated ways, and a mistake can cascade before anyone understands it. AI agents will do the same thing across supply chains, software, and markets. The license does not make the agent safe. It makes the operator accountable and gives the state a place to intervene before the cascade becomes a crisis.

The hardest objection is that this will not work against code. A model is a file. Once it exists, it can be copied, hosted abroad, or run on a laptop. A country cannot license a PDF. True. The plan does not try to. It taxes the physical and financial chokepoints: electricity, accelerators, data centers, payment systems, public contracts, and employment. It can stop a company from moving money through its own rails without insurance. It can refuse a federal contract to a vendor whose agents cannot produce an audit trail. It can make the safe version of the economy more attractive than the unsafe one. If a foreign lab releases a dangerous open model, the country still has the transition fund, the compute reserve, and the authority to require human approval in critical sectors. It cannot keep the model out. It can keep the model from becoming the country’s default operating system without a social contract.

That is why the plan needs international coordination, but not as a precondition. The best case is that the United States, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Canada, and Australia agree on a small set of evaluation standards for high-risk capabilities: autonomous cyber offense, pathogen design, self-modification, and mass persuasion. They share evaluation results with each other, restrict the export of weights and training infrastructure to adversaries, and give allied firms access to the public compute reserve. This is not a world government. It is a nuclear club for intelligence. If the coordination fails, the domestic plan still works, but it becomes more defensive: more human-in-the-loop rules, more sectoral buffers, less faith in market discipline.

The safety part is smaller than people think. The country creates an independent AI Safety Institute with authority to require third-party evaluations before a model is used in covered sectors. It mandates incident reporting for outages, leaks, malicious use, and unexpected autonomous behavior. It keeps a rollback plan for critical infrastructure: power, payments, defense, healthcare, and communications. It does not try to certify that a model is safe in every possible sense. It requires the same kind of boring assurance we ask of bridges, vaccines, and aircraft: show that the known failure modes are bounded, and show that you can turn the thing off.

The labor plan has to be honest about retraining. Retraining is not a magic fix. If AI removes the middle-skill tasks that made a career legible, telling a 45-year-old dispatcher to become a data annotator is cruel. The public sector therefore buys time with work. It funds maintenance, care, local infrastructure, energy retrofits, and education. Some of this is unglamorous. Some of it will be displaced too. But the goal is not to keep people busy forever. It is to keep them attached to a wage, a schedule, and a community while the new equilibrium forms. The transition fund pays for the gap. The public compute reserve helps small firms create the new jobs. The license regime slows the worst shocks.

There is a political design, because a plan this weird will die without one. The authority’s powers expire after five years. Renewal requires a two-thirds vote in both houses. Local transition boards, made of workers, firm managers, educators, and civil-society representatives, review displacement data and recommend changes to covered occupations. A public dashboard shows jobs lost, benefits paid, compute allocated, incidents reported, and taxes collected. Courts can review the authority’s certifications. The point is not to make the process slow. It is to make the power visible and revocable. A temporary emergency power that can be thrown out is less frightening than a permanent agency that cannot.

I find this compelling because it treats the real danger as a sequencing problem. The technology will be useful. The question is whether the country arrives at usefulness with a functioning labor market, a public stake in the infrastructure, and enough trust in government to keep using it. The free market path assumes that firms will retrain workers, that productivity gains will diffuse, and that politics will not seize up. Maybe it will. But if it does not, the failure is not a small correction. It is a decade of underemployment, concentrated wealth, and a public that blames the machines for what is actually a policy choice. The managed path accepts that some growth will be delayed, some companies will be annoyed, and some capabilities will be rolled out with human approval for longer than the engineers want. In exchange, it buys the thing that cannot be bought later: time.

The plan is optimistic, and I mean that carefully. It assumes no existential catastrophe, no all-out AI arms race, no monopoly capture of the transition, and a political class willing to accept a small tax on data centers in order to avoid a larger crisis in housing, wages, and legitimacy. Those are big assumptions. The best case is not that the country controls AI. It is that the country controls the terms on which AI enters its economy. If it works, the argument in ten years will not be about whether the machines are too smart. It will be about whether the public got a fair price for the grid.

Title: The Managed Decade

The missing question is not whether AI should be regulated. It is what a country does in the five years when AI becomes good enough to take jobs faster than schools, firms, and welfare systems can replace them. The best-case outcome is not a ban, and it is not a free-for-all. It is a managed transition: temporary public controls that let the technology arrive without letting it arrive all at once.

I have a specific version of this in mind. Imagine a large democracy, about 330 million people, a $28 trillion economy, home to many of the frontier labs. In 2027 it passes an AI Transition Act. The law does not define AI. It defines three things: compute, economic agency, and displacement. It creates an independent authority with five-year powers, renewable only by supermajority. It builds a public compute reserve, a transition fund, and a licensing regime for autonomous economic agents. The point is not to stop AI. The point is to make the path through AI pass through institutions that can pay for the damage and repair the labor market while the technology is still being learned.

The first tool is the compute reserve. The country requires that 10 percent of new domestic accelerator capacity be made available at cost to public universities, hospitals, national labs, small businesses, and safety researchers. It funds this with a 10-cent-per-kilowatt-hour charge on data-center electricity and a small levy on accelerator sales. If U.S. data centers draw 200 terawatt-hours a year, the charge raises about $20 billion. That is not a fortune, but it is enough to give the public sector a real seat at the table: a cloud that can train smaller models, run evaluations, and let a mid-size manufacturer or a rural hospital use frontier tools without signing a deal with one of five labs. The reserve also becomes a shock absorber. When a new model makes the old public models obsolete, the reserve has cash and hardware to retrain the public sector’s workforce on the new stack.

This sounds protectionist, and it is. But the protection is not against foreign AI. It is against a future in which the only people who can use the most important technology of the century are the people who built it. A country that lets five companies own the grid loses the argument before it starts.

The second tool is the transition fund. The fund is paid for by the same data-center tax and by a 5 percent levy on revenue from AI products sold domestically that are certified as replacing labor in a covered occupation. Certification is not done by the seller. It is done by the authority, using payroll data, occupational task surveys, and randomized audits. If a software company sells an AI that closes a company’s books, and the authority finds that the product is displacing staff accountants, the company pays. If it merely makes accountants faster, it does not.

The fund does not give everyone a check. It pays wage insurance. If a worker in a covered occupation loses more than 20 percent of earnings because of AI-linked layoffs, demand destruction, or firm failure, the state replaces 70 percent of the lost earnings for three years. The worker gets free retraining, relocation help, and access to public compute if the new job involves building with AI. The average benefit might be $10,000 a year. Twenty billion dollars can fully support two million workers, or top up a larger pool. That is not the whole labor market, but it is the difference between a family surviving a transition and a family becoming a statistic.

The design matters. A universal basic income is cleaner, but it is politically harder and macroeconomically noisier in the early years. Wage insurance is targeted, reversible, and easier to explain: if the machines took your job, the state holds the machines’ owner responsible for the bridge. It also creates a price signal. Companies know that deploying a model that fires people triggers a social cost. They do not pay the cost directly for every worker, but the levy and the public backlash are attached to the product. That is enough to make some firms choose slower rollout, human-in-the-loop interfaces, or upskilling tools. Not all. But some.

The third tool is licensing for autonomous economic agents. This is the weirdest part. The law does not regulate models. It regulates actions. An economic agent is software that can, without a human approving each step, spend money, sign contracts, move inventory, deploy code, or alter financial records. Below a threshold, it is just software. Above it, the operator must register, carry insurance, and submit to audit. A startup can build an agent that drafts purchase orders. A corporation that wants an agent to manage $10 billion in procurement must show that it can explain a decision, halt the agent, reconstruct the audit trail, and pay for mistakes. If it cannot, it can still run the agent, but a human must approve each transaction over a set limit.

This is not a ban. It is closer to securities regulation. No one says we should let a new trading algorithm move billions without registration, capital requirements, and incident reporting. The reason we do that for finance is not that code is dangerous in the abstract. It is that financial systems fail in correlated ways, and a mistake can cascade before anyone understands it. AI agents will do the same thing across supply chains, software, and markets. The license does not make the agent safe. It makes the operator accountable and gives the state a place to intervene before the cascade becomes a crisis.

The hardest objection is that this will not work against code. A model is a file. Once it exists, it can be copied, hosted abroad, or run on a laptop. A country cannot license a PDF. True. The plan does not try to. It taxes the physical and financial chokepoints: electricity, accelerators, data centers, payment systems, public contracts, and employment. It can stop a company from moving money through its own rails without insurance. It can refuse a federal contract to a vendor whose agents cannot produce an audit trail. It can make the safe version of the economy more attractive than the unsafe one. If a foreign lab releases a dangerous open model, the country still has the transition fund, the compute reserve, and the authority to require human approval in critical sectors. It cannot keep the model out. It can keep the model from becoming the country’s default operating system without a social contract.

That is why the plan needs international coordination, but not as a precondition. The best case is that the United States, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Canada, and Australia agree on a small set of evaluation standards for high-risk capabilities: autonomous cyber offense, pathogen design, self-modification, and mass persuasion. They share evaluation results with each other, restrict the export of weights and training infrastructure to adversaries, and give allied firms access to the public compute reserve. This is not a world government. It is a nuclear club for intelligence. If the coordination fails, the domestic plan still works, but it becomes more defensive: more human-in-the-loop rules, more sectoral buffers, less faith in market discipline.

The safety part is smaller than people think. The country creates an independent AI Safety Institute with authority to require third-party evaluations before a model is used in covered sectors. It mandates incident reporting for outages, leaks, malicious use, and unexpected autonomous behavior. It keeps a rollback plan for critical infrastructure: power, payments, defense, healthcare, and communications. It does not try to certify that a model is safe in every possible sense. It requires the same kind of boring assurance we ask of bridges, vaccines, and aircraft: show that the known failure modes are bounded, and show that you can turn the thing off.

The labor plan has to be honest about retraining. Retraining is not a magic fix. If AI removes the middle-skill tasks that made a career legible, telling a 45-year-old dispatcher to become a data annotator is cruel. The public sector therefore buys time with work. It funds maintenance, care, local infrastructure, energy retrofits, and education. Some of this is unglamorous. Some of it will be displaced too. But the goal is not to keep people busy forever. It is to keep them attached to a wage, a schedule, and a community while the new equilibrium forms. The transition fund pays for the gap. The public compute reserve helps small firms create the new jobs. The license regime slows the worst shocks.

There is a political design, because a plan this weird will die without one. The authority’s powers expire after five years. Renewal requires a two-thirds vote in both houses. Local transition boards, made of workers, firm managers, educators, and civil-society representatives, review displacement data and recommend changes to covered occupations. A public dashboard shows jobs lost, benefits paid, compute allocated, incidents reported, and taxes collected. Courts can review the authority’s certifications. The point is not to make the process slow. It is to make the power visible and revocable. A temporary emergency power that can be thrown out is less frightening than a permanent agency that cannot.

I find this compelling because it treats the real danger as a sequencing problem. The technology will be useful. The question is whether the country arrives at usefulness with a functioning labor market, a public stake in the infrastructure, and enough trust in government to keep using it. The free market path assumes that firms will retrain workers, that productivity gains will diffuse, and that politics will not seize up. Maybe it will. But if it does not, the failure is not a small correction. It is a decade of underemployment, concentrated wealth, and a public that blames the machines for what is actually a policy choice. The managed path accepts that some growth will be delayed, some companies will be annoyed, and some capabilities will be rolled out with human approval for longer than the engineers want. In exchange, it buys the thing that cannot be bought later: time.

The plan is optimistic, and I mean that carefully. It assumes no existential catastrophe, no all-out AI arms race, no monopoly capture of the transition, and a political class willing to accept a small tax on data centers in order to avoid a larger crisis in housing, wages, and legitimacy. Those are big assumptions. The best case is not that the country controls AI. It is that the country controls the terms on which AI enters its economy. If it works, the argument in ten years will not be about whether the machines are too smart. It will be about whether the public got a fair price for the grid.
