Potential essay:

The confusion is real because the word has been drained of its original edge. "Meritocracy" was coined by Michael Young in 1958 as a satire, not a compliment. In his imagined future, an IQ test and school certificate assigned people to their proper stations, and the result was a society in which everyone got what he deserved and therefore had no grounds for complaint. The horror was not that smart people led; it was that the system made hierarchy look like arithmetic. When current magazines attack meritocracy, they are usually attacking that arithmetic: the belief that the existing distribution of jobs, pay and prestige is the visible residue of individual worth.

That belief is doing more work than the phrase "best people get the jobs" suggests. A job has requirements. A surgeon needs steady hands, anatomical knowledge, the ability to function under stress. A teacher needs the capacity to explain, organize a room, adapt to children. A manager needs to coordinate people and take responsibility for outcomes. These are not the same merit. A brilliant researcher may be a useless line manager; a charming salesperson may be a catastrophic finance director. "Best" is not a single number. It is a set of predictions: if we put this person here, will the work get done, and will others be helped or harmed? A society that takes those predictions seriously is not being meritocratic in the insulting sense; it is being responsible.

The critics' first point is that the predictions are often bad, and we know it. Personnel research has found for decades that structured interviews, work samples and supervised trial periods predict job performance better than unstructured chats and impressive pedigrees. A law firm that promotes the partner who bills the most hours and brings in the most revenue is not measuring legal wisdom; it is measuring a particular commercial behavior, often reinforced by whom one went to school with. A hospital that promotes the physician with the most publications may be rewarding access to a well-funded lab, a famous mentor, and the time to write, not the quality of bedside care. The test is not evil. It is a proxy. The problem is that we stop calling it a proxy. We say the person has merit, when what we have observed is success in a particular set of signals.

The second point is harder: the signals are produced by family. College admissions make this visible because the machinery is public. In the United States, children from higher-income and more-educated families are far more likely to attend college, and far more likely to attend selective colleges, than children from poorer families. At elite institutions, legacy applicants have long been admitted at higher rates than non-legacy applicants with similar grades and test scores, a fact that is not a conspiracy but a policy choice. Private schooling, tutoring, extracurriculars that require travel and fees, and the quiet cultural fluency of the interview all mean that a teenager's "merit" is often a family product. The child performs well because the family paid for the conditions of performance. When the employer later says it hired the best candidate, it has hired the downstream effect of an upstream advantage.

This is where the charge of social reproduction bites. A caste system says: you are low because you were born low. A market says: you are poor because you are not valuable. A meritocracy says: you are behind because you are not as talented or hardworking. The last is the most painful, because it turns inequality into a diagnosis. If failure is moral, the loser is implicated in his own defeat. That humiliation is not an accidental byproduct; it is part of the system's stability. People accept bad odds when they believe the race is fair.

The mobility data show that the race is not obviously fair. In American intergenerational mobility studies, a child born in the top fifth of family income has roughly a one-in-five chance of reaching the top fifth as an adult, while a child born in the bottom fifth has a smaller chance, often estimated around one in ten or less. The United States is also less mobile than several wealthier countries. None of this proves that talent is irrelevant. It proves that the pipeline from talent to position is leaky, and that the leaks are sorted by class. A gifted child in a underfunded school, with sick parents and no car, does not simply fail to show her merit; she is not given the same chances to convert it into credentials.

At this point, the strongest objection to any defense of meritocracy appears. If institutions define merit, and institutions are shaped by the powerful, then to defend merit is to defend the powerful. The boss who says "we promote on merit" may be describing a process in which his own children's friends get the visible assignments, the polished presentations, the invitations to lunches. The university that says it chooses the best students may be choosing the children who were prepared for its choices. If we always ask the institution to grade itself, we will get a report card with the grade already written on it. This objection cannot be answered by saying the system works most of the time. It requires a standard external to the institution: what is the job for?

That is why the defense of merit must be skeptical of merit. We have to separate three claims that are usually bundled together. First, this person can do the work. Second, this person earned the opportunity to learn the work. Third, this person is therefore a better person. Only the first is needed for competent administration. The second is a question of justice in preparation, not proof of worth. The third is the moral inflation that makes meritocracy poisonous. A doctor who saves lives is not morally superior to the home nurse who keeps those lives bearable; she is better qualified for a particular task. A startup founder who becomes rich may have read the market, taken risks, and been lucky in a way that has little to do with her character. Pay can reflect scarcity, leverage, and the revenue of the team, not a soul's quality.

So what is worth defending? Not the claim that the hierarchy is just. It is not. Not the claim that everyone has an equal chance. They do not. Not the claim that the winners' self-confidence is well founded. It is often a training effect: people who are told they are exceptional become better at performing exceptionality, and then mistake the feedback loop for nature. What is worth defending is the demand that serious work be assigned by evidence of relevant ability. That demand has a brutal practical content. If you choose a pilot by lottery, people die. If you choose a judge by patronage, the law becomes a branch of faction. If you choose a public health official by party loyalty during a pandemic, the metric of success becomes obedience rather than survival. The meritocratic principle is at its strongest when the consequences of error are concrete and when the selector has no private knowledge of the candidate's character. Strangers must be sorted by something, and the something should be connected to the task.

But the principle must be kept humble. A test is a hypothesis, not a verdict. If a company finds that a selection test favors candidates from certain schools, it must ask whether the test measures future performance or prior privilege. If a promotion system rewards visibility, it must ask whether visibility is a job requirement or a byproduct of office proximity. If a profession finds that one group underrepresents itself at the top, the question is not how to make the group look more meritorious, but whether the meritorious traits have been defined too narrowly. The defense of competence becomes an instrument of critique when it forces the institution to show its work.

The critics, then, have a point, but it is easier to state than they often do. They are right that "merit" has become a word for whatever the existing elite happened to do well. They are right that the story of self-made ascent hides the scaffolding of family money, cultural preparation, and arbitrary advantage. They are right that the meritocratic insult—your failure is your fault—does real damage. They are wrong, or at least incomplete, if they conclude that selection by competence is therefore illegitimate. A society cannot run on the principle that no one is really better at the job; it can only run on the principle that claims to competence must be tested, corrected, and kept separate from moral rank. The best people do not get the jobs. The people with the relevant abilities, as far as we can measure them without being fooled by pedigree, should be trusted with the work, and the rest of us should remember that the measure is fallible. That is not a pretty ideology. It is the minimum condition for a civilization that asks strangers to operate on it, teach its children, regulate its money, and decide its disputes.

prompt: Investors say determination is the best predictor of startup success. Write an essay that tries to take determination apart: what is it made of, and which parts can a person actually develop?
response:
The sentence is useful and misleading. It is useful because early-stage investing is mostly inference from small samples. When a founder says “we lost our biggest customer” and then describes the next three calls they will make, the investor sees something: a person who can keep a company alive through ordinary damage. It is misleading because “determination” is not one thing. It is a bundle of commitments, habits, interpretations, and social facts that can point in opposite directions.

A startup founder’s determination appears in many forms. One founder stays up late rebuilding the product. Another spends the week calling customers who stopped replying. Another cuts payroll and tells the team the truth. Another quits the original product and starts over around a smaller insight. All of these can be called determined, but only some of them are useful. The word often covers both perseverance and stubbornness, and the difference between those two can decide whether a company lives.

The first component is a chosen problem, not just an idea. A person can be determined to build a thing and not determined to solve a problem. The difference shows when the original product fails. If the founder says “the market is early,” that is commitment to the idea. If they say “let’s find the version of this pain that people will pay for,” that is commitment to the problem. The second is more developable because it can be specified: who has the pain, what do they do now, what would make them switch, and what would count as evidence that you are wrong.

The second component is an updating rule. Determination becomes dangerous when it is used to protect a story. Theranos is the obvious warning case. Elizabeth Holmes had determination, charisma, and a strong sense of mission, but she built a company around a claim the technology did not support. The company did not collapse because she lacked will. It collapsed because her will was attached to a false claim, and contrary evidence was treated as an obstruction rather than information. A more useful determination is the determination to keep testing. Before a launch, a founder can write down what result would make them change course. That turns determination from a mood into a decision procedure.

The third component is action under uncertainty. Many people can work hard when the path is clear. Determination is what remains when the next step is not. It shows in cold emails, demo days, procurement calls, support tickets, and the unglamorous work of making a small thing real. In 2008, the founders of Airbnb were short of money and designed political cereal boxes, raising about $30,000. The story is often told as grit. The more useful part is that they were willing to run a small, embarrassing, fast test to find out whether anyone would pay. They also kept changing the experience: better photos, better pricing, better host support. The cereal did not save them. The willingness to run unglamorous experiments did.

This part is the most trainable by repetition. The first ten requests are uncomfortable. The fifty-first is administrative. A person can build the muscle by choosing a project with real external feedback and finishing it, not by imagining hardship in the abstract. If the only evidence of your determination is that you once wanted to start something, the evidence is weak. If you have shipped a product, collected payment, handled a complaint, and made a hard tradeoff, you have data.

The fourth component is tolerance for low-grade rejection. Startups are not usually ended by one dramatic failure. They are worn down by small nos. A customer says maybe. A partner says not this quarter. A bank says no. A candidate ghost you after the second interview. Determination here is not heroic. It is the ability to treat a no as data and keep the pipeline moving. It can be developed by increasing volume and lowering the personal meaning of each response. But it depends on not tying your identity to every answer. If every rejection feels like a verdict on you, you will either stop asking or become brittle.

The fifth component is maintenance: sleep, cash, relationships. Determination is not immune to biology. A founder running on four hours of sleep and a two-week cash reserve will make bad decisions and call them conviction. They will mistake exhaustion for intensity and panic for urgency. The developable part is unglamorous: a runway, a schedule, a rule for when to raise, a reason to leave the office. Many people think they need more grit when they need more sleep or a better financial model. A determined founder who cannot think clearly is not an asset; they are a risk.

The sixth component is social commitment. Private will fluctuates. People continue when others depend on them or can see them stop. A co-founder, a small team, a board, customers who rely on the product: these create a container for determination. This is why the lone-founder myth is partly false. You can build the container even if you do not naturally feel relentless. Choose a co-founder who asks hard questions. Publish a roadmap. Take a board seat that requires metrics. Make a public commitment that would be embarrassing to break. Determination is often less a private flame than a set of obligations you have agreed to honor.

Some parts are less developable. Baseline anxiety, need for approval, chronic low energy, a temperament that turns feedback into humiliation: these vary and are hard to change by will. But startups are systems. A risk-averse founder can pair with an operator who pushes for speed. A solitary founder can hire a co-founder whose role is to challenge. A person who hates selling can build a product that attracts users and hire a founder who closes. The goal is not to become a different temperament, but to design a company where your weak points are covered and your durable points are used.

This matters because the investor’s claim is predictive, not causal. Determination may predict success because it is a marker of other things: the founder has finished hard projects, has a support network, can tolerate ambiguity, has chosen a problem they understand. It may also predict because investors need a simple story when the real variables—market timing, distribution, luck—are invisible. If you train only the visible part, you get more people who stay up late and defend bad assumptions. The causal ingredient is not the feeling of continuing. It is the pattern of continuing to take informative actions.

There is also a selection problem. The founders investors remember are the ones who persisted and won. The equally determined founders who persisted into a bad market are not on the keynote stage. That does not mean determination is useless. It means the lesson from survivors is narrower than it appears: persistence can keep a company alive long enough for a good thing to happen, but it cannot make a bad thing good.

The word also hides what success means. A startup that becomes a $2 million-a-year service business required a different persistence than one that becomes a public company. The first needs cash discipline and customer retention. The second needs a large market and a distribution edge. Determination can help in both, but it does different work. In the first, it is the refusal to let the books drift. In the second, it is the refusal to leave the table while the market is still forming.

So the practical question is not whether a person can feel more determined. It is whether they can make the next action cheaper: a clearer problem, a written test, a scheduled call, a co-founder who asks for the number, a cash buffer that removes panic. Those practices do not sound like character. They are what character is made of when it is examined.

prompt: Write an essay on how a reputation points system works in an online Q&A community, why people care about the points, and where it goes wrong.
response:
A reputation points system starts with a simple problem: in an anonymous online Q&A community, no one knows whether a stranger is competent. The system tries to solve that by making competence visible as a number. A user asks a question. Other users answer. Readers vote on what they find useful. On Stack Overflow, the most widely known example, an upvoted answer earns the answerer 10 reputation points. If the asker marks one answer as accepted, the answerer gets 2 points and the asker gets 5. A downvoted answer loses 10 points. The total is displayed next to the user’s name, on their profile, and in the order in which answers are shown.

The mechanics are deliberately coarse. A vote is not a certification. It is a fast, low-effort judgment: this helped, or it did not. The system adds up those judgments over time. A user who answers many questions and repeatedly receives upvotes accumulates reputation. A user who posts confused questions, wrong answers, or spam accumulates little or none. Some systems also give points for comments, badges, or editing, but the core loop is the same: contribute, get evaluated by peers, receive a public score.

What makes the system more than a scoreboard is that the score changes what a user can do. On Stack Overflow, for example, a newcomer has limited powers. A user with 5,000 reputation can edit other people’s posts. A user with 10,000 can delete them. Lower thresholds unlock voting, commenting, and other small privileges. Reputation therefore does not merely describe a user. It grants authority. The person with 80,000 points is not just someone the community has liked in the past; that person can reshape what the community sees.

That is why people care. The first reason is practical. When a reader lands on a technical question, they do not have time to verify every answer. They look for cues. A high-reputation author is a cue that the answer has survived previous scrutiny. It may be wrong today, but the author has often been right before. In a community dealing with code, medicine, law, or engineering, that shortcut is valuable. The points reduce uncertainty.

The second reason is status. Reputation is one of the few legible forms of prestige available in an anonymous forum. People can have good taste, deep expertise, and patience, but none of that is visible unless it is converted into a number. A profile with 50,000 points says, “This person has contributed enough that the community has kept rewarding them.” That matters because humans are status animals, especially in places where identity is thin. The number becomes a proxy for the person.

The third reason is access. Users care about points because points determine whether their future contributions will be taken seriously. A high-reputation user who posts a strange question is often given the benefit of the doubt: maybe this is a specialist problem, maybe the wording is just odd. A low-reputation user posting the same question may be treated as noise, bad faith, or spam. The system is supposed to protect the community from abuse, but it also creates a class of trusted speakers and a class of people who must prove themselves again and again.

The fourth reason is game structure. Once points exist, people notice thresholds. A badge at one number, edit rights at another, the ability to award badges or close questions at still others. Users begin to see contribution as a path. They answer not only to help, but to move from 9,900 to 10,000, or to avoid falling below a level where they lose powers. That is not corruption. It is what happens whenever a social signal becomes a resource.

The system starts to go wrong when the signal is mistaken for the thing it measures. Votes are not truth. A user upvotes an answer because it solved their problem, because it was easy to read, because it agreed with what they already suspected, or because the author explained something in a way that felt authoritative. A user downvotes because the answer was slow to load, because it used jargon, because it contradicted the user’s preferred framework, or because the user did not like the tone. None of those reactions is irrational. But none of them is a direct test of correctness.

Consider a niche technical question. A rare Linux driver misbehaves after a kernel update. One answer gives the exact patch, explains which configuration option causes the conflict, and notes that the problem appears only on a specific hardware revision. It is dense. Most readers do not have that hardware. They skim, do not understand the kernel details, and move on. Another answer says, “Reinstall the firmware and reboot.” It is short, confident, and plausible. It gets many more upvotes. The first answer may be the better one. The second answer earns more reputation. The next person with the same problem sees the high-score answer first and repeats the firmware update. The community has not discovered the truth; it has discovered which answer was easiest to endorse.

Accepted answers create a different distortion. Acceptance means the asker found the answer useful, not that the answer is best. Often it means the answer arrived first and happened to work. A questioner may accept an answer after two days because it resolved the immediate issue, even though a more complete answer appears later. The accepted check mark then becomes a visual badge of correctness. Readers treat it as a verdict. The system has confused closure with quality.

Domain mismatch makes the problem worse. Reputation is usually global, but expertise is local. A user may have 120,000 points from answering common JavaScript questions and know nothing about embedded C. In a C question, that user’s answer may still be read with extra weight because of the number next to their name. The community has a high-trust generalist and a low-reputation specialist. The specialist may be right. The generalist may be wrong. The points do not know the difference.

Downvotes add another failure mode. They are meant to push bad content down, but they often punish style, unfamiliarity, and disagreement. A correct answer written by a nonnative speaker may lose points for awkward phrasing. A correct answer that challenges the questioner’s assumption may be downvoted because it is inconvenient. A new user’s first answer may be downvoted not because it is wrong, but because the voters have no prior reason to trust it. The system tries to discount downvotes from very new accounts, but the deeper problem remains: a downvote is a social act, and social acts are noisy.

Once points matter, people optimize for points. This is the familiar Goodhart’s law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Users begin to choose questions that are likely to attract votes. Popular topics get more answers. Obscure topics get fewer. Easy problems get polished; hard problems get abandoned. A user may ask a question they already know, answer it themselves, and present the pair as a learning exercise. If the question is genuinely useful, this can be fine. But the structure invites farming. Users may split one answer into several to increase visibility, edit an answer after seeing which version gets upvoted, or retreat from a controversial but correct position because the vote count drops.

Worse forms of gaming are less subtle. Friends can upvote each other. Small groups can promote their preferred answer. A user can build reputation in a broad tag and then use that standing to defend a weak position in a narrow subfield. The system has no easy way to distinguish “this person is usually good” from “this person is being supported by allies.” It sees only the total.

The moderation layer is where reputation becomes power. Editing and deletion rights are usually granted to users who have earned enough points, on the assumption that they understand the community well enough to maintain it. Often they do. High-reputation users are frequently the ones who keep the site usable. But the same rights can be used to protect a position. If a user’s answer is edited into a form they dislike, they can restore their version. If a low-reputation user posts a challenge, a high-reputation user can delete it before it gains traction. If a question is closed, the closure can be framed as routine cleanup, even when it suppresses a legitimate but unpopular line of inquiry.

This creates a conservative bias. Reputation systems reward established norms. The user who has been here for years and has learned which phrasings get upvoted has an advantage over the newcomer who writes more clearly but does not yet know the local style. The community becomes easier to navigate, but also less permeable. Fresh ways of framing a problem are harder to introduce when the people with editing power have already invested in the existing framing. Their points are not just a record of past contributions; they are a stake in the current arrangement.

The hardest objection to this criticism is that the alternative is worse. Without reputation, an online Q&A community has no cheap way to distinguish a careful contributor from a spammer, a troll, or a confused visitor. It has no way to grant moderation rights except by manual appointment, which is slow and arbitrary. It has no way to sort answers except by time, which puts the loudest or fastest response on top. Reputation is imperfect, but it is a self-updating trust mechanism. It allows strangers to coordinate at a scale that private moderation could never handle. A community without points would likely collapse into either chaos or a closed club.

That objection is correct. The mistake is not in using reputation. The mistake is in treating the number as final. A points system works best when users understand it as a rough indicator, not a certificate. The design should make that humility visible. Votes should be easier to explain. Downvotes should carry some reason, or at least be less destructive. Reputation should be domain-specific where possible, so that a C++ expert is not ranked below a JavaScript generalist in C++ questions. Moderation powers should be separable from popularity: a user can be trusted to edit without being the most upvoted answerer. Low-reputation users should have some protected channel for dissent, so that errors by high-reputation users can be surfaced before they are locked in.

These fixes are hard. If downvotes require explanations, people may stop downvoting. If reputation is split by topic, profiles become less legible. If moderation is separated from reputation, the community loses a simple heuristic for who may be given tools. If low-reputation users get more power, abuse becomes easier. Every change trades one failure for another. The system is not a bug to be perfected into fairness. It is a compromise among trust, scale, and abuse resistance.

Still, the core failure is predictable. The points were supposed to make expertise legible. Over time, they make status legible instead. Status is more durable than expertise, more anxious to defend, and easier to abuse. When a reader sees a large number next to an answer, they often stop reading the answer. They treat the profile as a substitute for judgment. The community then optimizes for the profile. The system that was meant to surface useful knowledge ends up preserving the standing of those who have already been rewarded, and making it harder for anyone to prove that the old score was wrong.

prompt: Describe how you read when you want a book to actually change how you think: how you choose books, how you read them, and how you make time. For someone who reads a lot but retains little.
response:
For a reader who takes in a lot and keeps little, the first diagnosis is not memory. It is friction. A book changes how you think when it stops being smooth. It gives you a distinction that makes a familiar case look strange, or a standard that makes a comfortable judgment hard to defend, or a pattern you can see in a room full of people without the author’s help. If a book passes through you and leaves the same habits behind, it was probably read as entertainment, even if the subject was serious.

So choose books by the problem you are living in, not by the topic you find impressive. If you want to think differently about work, a biography of a famous founder may be exciting, but unless you are making founder-like decisions, it will mostly circulate as admiration. A book about why competent teams miss simple failures is more useful if you keep missing simple failures. If you are confused about moral anger, do not choose a book that will let you analyze other people’s anger from a safe distance. Choose one that forces you to apply the same lens to your own irritation. The question is not “What do I want to know?” It is “What am I currently doing or assuming that I would like to see more clearly?”

A book likely to change you usually has a claim strong enough to be wrong. Before you commit, look for the claim. Read the table of contents, the first chapter, the last, and the index. Ask what the author is arguing and what she would say you are missing. If the answer is a mood—elegance, outrage, wonder—put it down for now. If the answer is a position you can argue with, keep it. Also avoid books that mostly confirm a view you already hold. Confirmation feels like learning because it is recognition, but recognition does not move the furniture.

The objection here is obvious: this makes reading instrumental and misses the books that find you by accident. That is true. You can keep a small shelf of purposeless books, the ones whose first page catches you for no reason. But if the goal is to be changed, serendipity cannot be the main course. It is a dessert, or a walk in the garden.

Read one book this way at a time. You can read other things—novels, articles, letters, whatever—but the book you want to alter your thinking gets exclusivity. When many serious books are open at once, none are urgent. The mind files them under ambient. Give the book a short room, not a long hallway. For a 250-page book, a daily shape of 15 to 25 pages plus ten minutes of writing is often better than a vague promise to “get to it.” That makes the book a two- or three-week event. The schedule should be short enough that missing it costs something. If you miss three days, reduce the page count or the writing, but do not let the book drift into whenever. A book without a deadline is a book you are not really reading.

In the margins, do not underline. Underlining is a vote of appreciation: this is nice, this is important, I will never look at it again. Write the idea in your own words, then write the counterexample. “This works when the stakes are low and the group is small. It fails when the cost of being wrong is high.” Or “This explains my reaction to last week’s meeting.” If you are reading on a screen, keep a separate note that is not a dump of highlights. A list of highlights records where your eye paused. It does not show whether your mind moved.

After each chapter, or at least every thirty pages, close the book and write a short answer to three questions: What did I think before? What do I think now? What would make me stop thinking that? Then add one line: Where does this apply this week? This is not busywork. It is the difference between looking at an idea and trying to hold it. I am not sure how much writing is necessary for every reader; some people think better by walking, or talking, or staring at a wall. But for most readers who retain little, writing is the cheapest test available. It makes the absence of understanding visible.

Before the book is finished, make the idea do something. If it is about negotiation, choose one upcoming disagreement and prepare using its method. If it is about status, watch one conversation where you are trying to look competent rather than understand. If it is about probability, take a judgment you are making this month and write down the base rate you were ignoring. The point is not to prove the author right. The point is to find out whether the idea has any purchase on your actual life. If it cannot change a small decision, it probably will not change your thinking.

Once a week, stop reading and try to reconstruct the book from memory. Look at the chapter titles, or your notes, and say what the argument was. Read only the parts you cannot recover. This feels like school. It is also the part most readers skip, which is why it is the part that produces retention. Forgetting is not the enemy of learning; it is the signal that something has not been encoded. The discomfort of reaching for the idea without the page is where the idea leaves the book.

A reader who reads a lot often has a stake in being a reader. Finishing books becomes a score, and the score is soothing. It also protects you from the slower, uglier process of being revised. A book that changes you may make you look foolish in places where you used to be fluent. That is why the margin notes matter: they are evidence that you were not just performing reading. The cost of this method is that you will finish fewer books. That is not a bug. If the tradeoff feels like loss, you may be attached to the number more than to the change.

If you already read a lot, you do not need a miracle of schedule. You need to stop treating serious reading as one more input. Make time by subtracting. For the two or three weeks of the book, reduce other reading enough that this book is the main text. Protect one longer block, perhaps an hour, for the hardest chapter and the writing. Daily fragments can handle reading; the block handles thinking. If you only have fragments, the book will remain a sequence of fragments.

Three months later, you are in a meeting and someone says a thing that should have set you off. You pause, name the assumption, and answer from the other side. You do not think of the book. You do not quote it. The pause is the retention.

prompt: Why do people give each other opposite advice, 'be more selfish' and 'be less selfish', and each sound completely sure? I want an essay that explains why so many debates go in circles, with a few real examples.
response:
The two pieces of advice sound opposite because, in ordinary speech, they are. But the collision comes from a word that has been stretched over two different failures. “Selfish” can mean a person has failed to maintain the minimum conditions of their own life. It can also mean a person has treated their own wants as more important than other people’s claims. “Be more selfish” is usually a prescription for the first. “Be less selfish” is usually a prescription for the second. When the word is not defined, each speaker hears the other as defending the disease they have just diagnosed.

The difference shows up in a single afternoon. Suppose a person has worked five long days, slept badly, and said yes to three separate requests. If they now spend Saturday alone, that is not a rejection of other people; it is repair. Suppose another person has a flexible schedule, a cushion of savings, and a friend going through a hard week. If they spend Saturday alone, the act looks the same, but the moral shape is different. In the first case, the person was near empty. In the second, they are choosing comfort over someone else’s need. The word “selfish” covers both, but the advice needed is not the same.

Caregiving makes this obvious. A woman is caring for an aging parent. She has stopped sleeping, missed work, canceled plans, and is running on irritation. A friend says: be more selfish. Hire help, leave the house, take the weekend. The advice is not that the parent does not matter. It is that a depleted caregiver becomes a burden, and a person with no life outside the crisis cannot sustain the crisis. The common phrase “you can’t pour from an empty cup” is clumsy, but it points to a real limit. Yet the same woman may later say she cannot help her sister move because she is “recharging.” The sister says: be less selfish. Now the word points to a different failure. In the first case, selfishness was the missing minimum. In the second, it is the excessive maximum.

At work, the same debate appears under the name boundaries. A junior employee says yes to every request because no feels like failure. A manager says: no is a complete sentence. Protect your time. The advice is good if the employee is being used to cover other people’s poor planning. Later, the same employee calls “boundaries” when a team is short-staffed and refuses a shift they agreed to, leaving a colleague to absorb the cost. A coworker says: that is selfish. The first no was self-preservation. The second no is refusing a shared cost. Both are called boundary-setting, but only one leaves the other person whole.

The airplane instruction makes the point in miniature. Put on your own oxygen mask before helping others. It sounds selfish, but it is arithmetic. An unconscious passenger cannot pull a mask over a child’s face. Yet the same rule does not license ignoring a screaming child when you are perfectly fine. The mask rule is about capacity, not priority. Most circular debates happen because people turn a capacity rule into a priority rule, or a priority rule into a capacity rule.

Each speaker sounds sure because each has met the person who got it wrong. The person who says be more selfish has watched a good person disappear under obligation: the spouse who never rests, the friend who always pays, the employee who answers emails at midnight until they resent everyone. The person who says be less selfish has been the one left behind: the friend whose emergencies are always inconvenient, the colleague whose “limits” conveniently end where the difficult work begins, the family member whose needs are forever a burden to someone else. Resentment is a signal that a boundary has been crossed, but it does not measure the boundary. Both speakers are remembering a concrete injury, and concrete injuries feel like proofs.

A circular debate has a recognizable shape. One side says, “Selfishness is healthy.” The other produces a selfish person who hurt someone. The first side replies, “That is not healthy selfishness; that is greed or entitlement.” The second side replies, “You are just giving the bad kind a better name.” The first side says, “You are teaching people to hate themselves for having needs.” The second side says, “You are teaching people to treat their needs as the only needs.” The word has moved every time. No one is changing their mind because no one is testing the same claim.

This is why so many moral debates go in circles, not only this one. Freedom, responsibility, fairness, safety, trust: each word carries a family of cases. One side remembers the case where the value was ignored; the other remembers the case where it was abused. Both are sure because both have seen the harm. But certainty about a harm is not an account of the concept. If a word can be used to condemn a tyrant and a person trying to sleep, it cannot settle a dispute until the speaker says which kind of case is on the table.

The hardest objection to all this is that selfishness and selflessness are not only words. Time, money, and attention are finite. If I spend the last of my energy on my friend, I cannot spend it on my child. If I give the money away, I cannot keep it for my retirement. There are real cases where choosing myself means failing someone else, and choosing someone else means failing myself. In those cases, the debate is not merely verbal; it is a tradeoff with a cost.

But even there, the slogan is too crude. The question is not “selfish or selfless?” but “which obligation is stronger, what can I actually bear, and who is harmed if I refuse?” A person may be selfish in refusing to help a neighbor in an emergency, but not selfish in refusing to become a permanent rescuer for an adult friend who keeps making crises. A worker may be selfish in quitting a team during a crunch, but not selfish in leaving a job that is destroying their health before they become useless to everyone. The difference is not the amount of self-attention. It is the relationship, the promise, the vulnerability, the history, and the cost. Those details are boring compared with the slogan, but they are where the answer lives.

The opposite advice is a symptom of an unfinished analysis. The speakers have not yet said which self is being protected, which other is being neglected, what the person can actually pay, and what the relationship requires. Once those questions are asked, “be more selfish” and “be less selfish” stop being rivals and become two possible answers to different audits. The debate circles only while the word is allowed to do the work that the cases should do.

prompt: A Vox piece argues that prisons have become America's substitute for a gutted mental health system, since mentally ill people in prison outnumber those in state hospitals ten to one. As a practicing psychiatrist, write a rebuttal that checks the statistic and the story behind it.
response:
The Vox piece gets the emotional fact right: jails and prisons are full of people with mental illness, and the care they get is often poor. It gets the arithmetic and the history wrong.

The ten-to-one figure is a ratio, not a diagnosis. In recent years the state psychiatric hospitals have held roughly 50,000 patients. State prisons and local jails combined hold more than two million people. If you ask a broad screening question—do you have depression, anxiety, ADHD, PTSD, a substance use disorder, or some other DSM disorder?—a large share of the prison population will answer yes. Multiply that by two million and you can get a half-million or more. Divide by 50,000 and you get ten.

But the denominator is not the whole mental health system. It is one kind of public inpatient bed. It excludes private psychiatric hospitals, freestanding crisis units, psychiatric wings of general hospitals, residential treatment, intensive outpatient programs, assertive community treatment teams, and the many people being managed in primary care or by a psychiatrist’s office. It also ignores the fact that the old state-hospital population was not the same category as today’s “mentally ill prisoner.” In the 1950s, state hospitals held people with intellectual disabilities, dementia, chronic alcoholism, poverty, and deviant behavior—categories we now house in nursing homes, developmental centers, addiction programs, or, yes, jails. Comparing modern prison screens to mid-century state hospital censuses is comparing two different universes.

If you use the narrower category that actually matches a state hospital population—serious, persistent mental illness with functional impairment—the ratio shrinks. Estimates vary, but depending on definition the number of people with serious mental illness in jails and prisons is somewhere from about 100,000 to more than 500,000. Against 50,000 state hospital patients, that is anywhere from roughly two-to-one to ten-to-one. Only at the broad end of the numerator does the Vox number appear. And even then, it is a ratio of stocks, not a pipeline. It tells us how many mentally ill people are in two places at once. It does not tell us that one system replaced the other.

The historical story does not support “substitute.” Deinstitutionalization was not a policy of moving patients from wards to cells. It was a messy, often failed attempt to shift care from large state hospitals to community settings, enabled by antipsychotics, advocacy against institutional abuse, and the desire to stop using state hospitals as cheap dumping grounds for people who were not all acutely mentally ill. At the same time, the prison population grew because of drug-law enforcement, mandatory minimums, policing, and sentencing choices. The two trends happened in the same country and the same decades, but one did not mechanically produce the other.

If prisons were simply the new psychiatric hospitals, we would expect the incarcerated mentally ill to be there for the same reasons and for the same length of stay as former hospital patients. We do not see that. We see short jail stays for misdemeanors, drug possession, disorderly conduct, and homelessness, alongside long prison sentences for violent or repeat offenses. That is a criminal justice population with high rates of mental disorder, not a psychiatric census.

A man with opioid use disorder and depression who sells heroin is not a state hospital patient. A woman with PTSD and alcohol use disorder who gets into a bar fight is not a state hospital patient. A young man with first-episode psychosis who panics and is restrained by police is, and in a functioning system should be diverted to a crisis unit, not booked. Substance use disorders are classified as mental disorders, but treating them as psychiatric hospital material inflates the ratio. Addiction treatment is its own field, with its own settings: medication-assisted treatment, residential programs, outpatient counseling, jail-based early intervention.

The hardest case is the one the Vox piece is really pointing at. A person with untreated schizophrenia is found sleeping on a bench, steals food, is arrested, spends a week in a cell, receives a dose of an antipsychotic, is released without a warm handoff, and returns to the street. Or a person in acute mania is brought to an ER, boards for two days because no psychiatric bed is available, is arrested for being disruptive, and ends up in a jail medical unit. In those cases, incarceration is doing something that a medical system should be doing: containing a sick person and stabilizing symptoms. That is a genuine failure, and I see the downstream damage—interrupted treatment, stigma, lost housing, worse prognosis.

But the failure is not best named by calling prison the substitute. The substitute framing suggests the system is complete, just in the wrong building. It is not complete. The missing pieces are crisis response that can handle a 2 a.m. psychotic episode without police as default, medication access, housing, benefits navigation, substance use treatment, and legal diversion for people whose offense is essentially a symptom. In many places those pieces exist in fragments. In others they do not. The result is that the mentally ill end up in multiple places: ERs, shelters, streets, nursing homes, group homes, outpatient clinics, and prisons. Prison is the most visible and morally shocking of those places because it is locked and because the state is punishing as well as failing.

As a psychiatrist, I do not want to defend prisons as mental health infrastructure. They are bad for mental illness. Crowding, noise, lack of privacy, violence, restraints, and continuity gaps make recovery harder. But the policy lesson of the ten-to-one ratio is not “we have already built the system; we just need to admit it is a psychiatric one.” The lesson is that we have not built the community system we promised when we closed the state hospitals, and we have filled the gap with legal custody.

The right statistic is not how many mentally ill people outnumber state hospital patients. It is how many people with treatable illness are being arrested, held, and released without care because no better option was available.

"The Vox piece gets the emotional fact right: jails and prisons are full of people with mental illness, and the care they get is often poor. It gets the arithmetic and the history wrong.

The ten-to-one figure is a ratio, not a diagnosis. In recent years the state psychiatric hospitals have held roughly 50,000 patients. Jails and prisons hold roughly two million people. If you ask a broad screening question—do you have depression, anxiety, ADHD, PTSD, a substance use disorder, or some other DSM disorder?—a large share of the prison population will answer yes. Multiply that by two million and you can get a half-million or more. Divide by 50,000 and you get ten. But the denominator is not the whole mental health system. It is one kind of public inpatient bed. It excludes private psychiatric hospitals, freestanding crisis units, psychiatric wings of general hospitals, residential treatment, intensive outpatient programs, assertive community treatment teams, and the many people being managed in primary care or by a psychiatrist's office. It also excludes the fact that the old state-hospital population was not the same category as today's 'mentally ill prisoner.' In the 1950s, state hospitals held people with intellectual disabilities, dementia, chronic alcoholism, poverty, and deviant behavior—categories we now house in nursing homes, developmental centers, addiction programs, or, yes, jails. Comparing 2020s prison screens to 1950s state hospital censuses is comparing two different universes.

If you use the narrower category that actually matches a state hospital population—serious, persistent mental illness with functional impairment—the ratio shrinks. Estimates vary, but the number of people with serious mental illness in jails and prisons is commonly put in the low hundreds of thousands at most, and in some BJS tabulations much lower. Against 50,000 state hospital patients, that is not a tenfold replacement; it is an overlap. Some of those people would have been hospital candidates. Many would not. A man with opioid use disorder and depression who sells heroin is not a state hospital patient. A woman with PTSD and alcohol use disorder who gets into a bar fight is not a state hospital patient. A young man with first-episode psychosis who panics and is restrained by police is, and in a functioning system should be diverted to a crisis unit, not booked.

The historical story also does not support 'substitute.' Deinstitutionalization was not a policy of moving patients from wards to cells. It was a messy, often failed attempt to shift care from large state hospitals to community settings, enabled by antipsychotics, advocacy against institutional abuse, and the desire to stop using state hospitals as cheap dumping grounds for people who were not all acutely mentally ill. At the same time, the prison population grew because of drug-law enforcement, mandatory minimums, policing, and sentencing choices. The two trends happened in the same country and the same decades, but one did not mechanically produce the other. If prisons were simply the new psychiatric hospitals, we would expect the incarcerated mentally ill to be there for the same reasons and for the same length of stay as former hospital patients. We do not see that. We see short jail stays for misdemeanors, drug possession, disorderly conduct, and homelessness, alongside long prison sentences for violent or repeat offenses. That is a criminal justice population with high rates of mental disorder, not a psychiatric census.

The hardest case is the one the Vox piece is really pointing at. A person with untreated schizophrenia is found sleeping on a bench, steals food, is arrested, spends a week in a cell, receives a dose of an antipsychotic, is released without a warm handoff, and returns to the street. Or a person in acute mania is brought to an ER, boards for two days because no psychiatric bed is available, is arrested for being disruptive, and ends up in a jail medical unit. In those cases, incarceration is doing something that a medical system should be doing: containing a sick person and stabilizing symptoms. That is a genuine failure, and I see the downstream damage—interrupted treatment, stigma, lost housing, worse prognosis.

But the failure is not best named by calling prison the substitute. The substitute framing suggests the system is complete, just in the wrong building. It is not complete. The missing pieces are crisis response that can handle a 2 a.m. psychotic episode without police as default, medication access, housing, benefits navigation, substance use treatment, and legal diversion for people whose offense is essentially a symptom. In many places those pieces exist in fragments. In others they do not. The result is that the mentally ill end up in multiple places: ERs, shelters, streets, nursing homes, group homes, outpatient clinics, and prisons. Prison is the most visible and morally shocking of those places because it is locked and because the state is punishing as well as failing.

As a psychiatrist, I do not want to defend prisons as mental health infrastructure. They are bad for mental illness. Crowding, noise, lack of privacy, violence, restraints, and continuity gaps make recovery harder. But the policy lesson of the ten-to-one ratio is not 'we have already built the system; we just need to admit it is a psychiatric one.' The lesson is that we have not built the community system we promised when we closed the state hospitals, and we have filled the gap with legal custody. The right statistic is not how many mentally ill people outnumber state hospital patients. It is how many people with treatable illness are being arrested, held, and released without care because no better option was available."

prompt: Write a movie review of Don't Look Up, but not the usual one about existential risk. I want to know what it says about politics and trust in experts, and whether the film actually holds together.
response:
Don’t Look Up is usually discussed as a climate film with a rock, but that is the wrong level. The comet is a stress test. The film is about what happens when a fact enters public life: it is formatted, scheduled, branded, and finally discarded. Its real subject is not extinction but the channels through which warnings travel, and the film is much sharper about those channels than it is about the people who use them.

The opening television interview sets the terms. Myles and Kate have done the calculation. They know the comet will hit in seven months. The show does not ask them to explain the orbit; it asks them to quantify their own fear. “Are we going to die?” becomes a segment. Kate’s careful probability is treated as a joke; Myles’s certainty is treated as a performance. The scientists are not wrong. They are made unusable. The film’s first political claim is that expertise cannot survive contact with the entertainment format, because the format needs conflict, personality, and a next episode, not a date.

The White House scenes develop this. President Orlean and her vice president do not need to deny the comet. Denial would be clumsy and would give the opposition a story. Instead, they manage the tone. The comet is a scheduling problem, a photo opportunity, a way to look decisive, and eventually a second-term asset. The film is not making a partisan point here; it is making a structural one. In a system where leadership is judged by poll numbers and news cycles, the rational response to a long-term catastrophe is to pretend it is short-term. The president’s sin is not that she lies about the rock; it is that she teaches the public the correct emotional response. If the person in charge treats the warning as an inconvenience to be handled, the public learns that it is an inconvenience.

This is where the film’s idea about trust in experts becomes interesting. Myles is not untrustworthy because he is a bad scientist. He is untrustworthy because the only way to keep him visible is to turn him into a celebrity. He dances, makes faces, becomes a meme, gets a following. The audience inside the film stops caring about his data and starts caring about his brand. Kate, who remains closer to the work, is less watchable. The system does not reward the person who can do the calculation; it rewards the person who can be consumed. Trust, in the film, is not a judgment about competence. It is a byproduct of familiarity, access, and narrative. The billionaire Bruce is the mirror image of this: he is a fraud, but he is trusted because he offers a solution, has money, and speaks with confidence. Even the proposed fix becomes political: the comet turns into a contract, and the contract goes to the man who can promise the most while remaining least accountable. The public does not say, “I don’t believe science.” It says, “I don’t believe this person on this show.” The distinction matters.

The politics of the film are broadest and weakest here. It mocks the president, the media, the billionaire, the alternative-energy crowd, the socialite who turns the comet into a spiritual awakening, and the crowds dancing in the street. The satire is fun, but it is also undifferentiated. Every institution is captured by the same logic: convert the threat into something that can be sold, watched, or used. That is a true description of the film’s world, but it is not a theory of politics. It does not show how a warning could be made politically possible, because it does not identify any actor with both the motive and the capacity to say, “this is serious, it is boring, and it must be done before the next poll.” Everyone is a caricature, and the structure that makes the caricatures necessary is left invisible.

Does it hold together? As a sequence of missed connections, yes. Each character acts rationally within a narrow incentive. The scientist wants to be heard. The politician wants to be re-elected. The media wants ratings. The businessman needs cash flow. The socialite wants meaning. The comet does not create new motives; it exposes the existing ones. The tragedy is not stupidity. It is alignment failure. The film’s form helps: the rapid cuts, the pop songs, the celebrity walk-ons, and the tonal whiplash make the audience feel the attention economy from the inside. You cannot sit still with the fact of the comet, because the film will not let you. That is a real point, and it is the film’s best argument. Its tonal instability is not merely a style; it is the thesis. But it also prevents the film from accumulating moral weight. The laugh becomes a way of not feeling, and the film is complicit in the very avoidance it describes.

The hardest objection is that the film asks the audience to trust the one perspective it does not satirize: the perspective of the audience itself. McKay’s satire works only if you can step outside the spectacle and see the joke. If the problem is that public life has become a machine for turning warnings into content, the film is itself a piece of content, made with famous actors and a big studio, and it expects you to be the clearheaded one. It does not explain how a warning would land with people who do not already share its assumptions. It blames everyone, which is a comfortable position for a satire: nobody has to be responsible, so the system never has to be named. The film is centrist in the way that a lot of American satire is centrist, and its moral center is the audience’s temporary feeling of superior comprehension.

You cannot sit still with the fact of the comet, because the film will not let you. That is a real point, and it is the film’s best argument. Its tonal instability is not merely a style; it is the thesis. But it also prevents the film from accumulating moral weight. The laugh becomes a way of not feeling, and the film is complicit in the very avoidance it describes.

The hardest objection is that the film asks the audience to trust the one perspective it does not satirize: the perspective of the audience itself. McKay’s satire works only if you can step outside the spectacle and see the joke. If the problem is that public life has become a machine for turning warnings into content, the film is itself a piece of content, made with famous actors and a big studio, and it expects you to be the clearheaded one. It does not explain how a warning would land with people who do not already share its assumptions. It blames everyone, which is a comfortable position for a satire: nobody has to be responsible, so the system never has to be named. The film is centrist in the way that a lot of American satire is centrist, and its moral center is the audience’s temporary feeling of superior comprehension.

What remains is a diagnosis, not a remedy. The film says trust in experts is not a civic virtue that can be restored by better communication. It is an institutional product. Experts are trusted when they are embedded in structures that protect their warnings from the market: independent review, legal accountability, professional norms, and a public media that is not forced to chase the next clip. When those structures are absent, expertise becomes personality, and personality loses to money and power. Don’t Look Up holds together as a portrait of that loss. It does not hold together as an argument for what should be done, because it refuses to choose a target. It is a useful map of how a warning dies, and a frustratingly vague map of how one might be kept alive.

prompt: Write a personal essay, with a metaphor if it helps, about that restless, uncomfortable stretch when you've changed as a person but your old identity and the way others see you haven't caught up.
response:
The first time I stopped smiling when someone told me I was “so easy to get along with,” I felt like I had dropped a coin into a deep well. The compliment was meant to land on the old me, the one who laughed first, who smoothed over the awkward pause, who said, “Tell me about it,” as if other people’s problems were rooms she had furnished. But the new me heard the sentence and thought: easy for whom? Easy as a surface? Easy because I didn’t ask for much? I didn’t say any of that. I said, “Thanks,” and the word sat in the air like a stone.

That was the beginning of the stretch. I had changed, or I was changing, but the change had no name yet. For three years I had been the person who made things easier: the one who remembered birthdays, who could talk to the difficult boss, who knew how to keep a dinner party from turning into a test. Then, without a single dramatic scene, I stopped being able to perform that ease. I didn’t stop caring. I stopped having the energy to be the room’s mediator. I said no to weekend plans. I let conversations go quiet. I stopped filling every silence with a joke.

People noticed. That was the first strange part. You would think that if you become less available, less agreeable, less useful, the effect would be invisible. It is not. The old identity had a function, and when the function falters, people feel the loss before they can explain it. My brother said I had gotten “intense.” A friend asked if I was sleeping. A colleague looked at me across a meeting as if I had failed to take notes on the emotional weather. None of them was being cruel. They were using the only diagnostic tools they had. When someone behaves outside the pattern, and the change has no story—no illness, no breakup, no obvious crisis—the default explanation is that something is wrong.

That is where the discomfort starts to live. You become a problem to be solved. Your new boundaries sound like coldness. Your new seriousness sounds like resentment. Your refusal to make everyone comfortable sounds like you have stopped caring about the group. The old you was legible. You knew where you stood. People knew where they stood. Now you are a stranger in a familiar body, and the familiar people keep handing you the old script, waiting for you to say your lines.

There is a metaphor I have used too often to dismiss: you move, but the mail keeps coming to the old address. Except identity is not a mailing address. You cannot simply wait for the letters to stop. The letters are conversations. They ask for the old tenant by name. They expect the old furniture in the old places. If you answer from the new house, in the new voice, they may decide the new tenant is rude, ungrateful, or lost. If you answer in the old voice, you are back in the old house, and the move never happened.

At a family gathering, my aunt asked why I didn’t call more. I wanted to say, “Because calling means I have to perform a version of myself that no longer fits,” but that would have sounded like a speech. Instead I said, “I’ve been busy.” She accepted it, but her face said she did not believe it. Busy with what? The new life had no visible shape yet. It was mostly absence: fewer parties, fewer obligations, fewer moments where I was useful to other people. Absence is hard to celebrate. It looks like withdrawal until you have filled it with something concrete.

The hardest objection to all this is that maybe I am making the lag about other people when I have not actually changed enough. The new self is still half rehearsal. I still want the old approval. When someone says, “You’ve changed,” part of me is relieved: they see it. Another part is ashamed: I was pretending for so long that the pretending is all they knew. The desire to be recognized as new can be a kind of vanity. It wants a new costume, not the slow work of being known. It wants the room to applaud the transformation, because then the transformation is safe. If no one notices, how do I know it is real? If everyone notices and disapproves, how do I know I should keep going?

And yet there is something real in the frustration, too. A person is not a secret to be guessed. If every change has to be explained as emergency—illness, heartbreak, a bad year—then ordinary growth has no language. “I’m becoming less available” is not a confession. “I no longer find that joke funny” is not betrayal. “I need to think before I say yes” is not a character flaw. But we often have to translate internal change into external crisis before others will take it seriously. We have to make the new self dramatic enough to be believed.

What helps is not announcing. You cannot make people update you by telling them. You can only repeat, over time, the new behavior in low-stakes ways. Let them be surprised. Let them call you cold and not defend yourself. Let the old identity stand there, awkward and outdated, while you do the next small thing differently. Some people will adjust. Some will not. The ones who cannot adjust may have been loving a version of you that was mostly performance. That is not a reason to hate them. It is a reason to stop performing.

Last month at a dinner, a friend said, “You used to be so much fun.” The old me rose in my body like a reflex, ready to make a joke, to soften the edge, to prove I was still the one who made rooms easier. I let the reflex finish. “Yeah,” I said. “I’ve been quiet.” He looked at me as if I had answered a different question. I had. The old identity was still sitting across from me, wearing my face. But it no longer had the keys.

prompt: After a talk in London where you said startups would do better in Silicon Valley, an organizer got up to rebut you. Write an essay making the case properly: should startups move to a startup hub, and when shouldn't they?
response:
The organizer was right to object. “Startups would do better in Silicon Valley” sounds like a universal law, and it is not. It is a conditional statement with the condition left out. A startup should move to a hub when the network it needs is denser there than anywhere else and when the cost of getting that network remotely is higher than the cost of moving. It should not move when its advantage is local, when its market is somewhere else, or when the move is mostly about the founder’s image.

I am using “startup” in the venture sense: a company trying to grow beyond its home market, often with outside capital, into a business large enough to matter globally. If you are opening a café, a local agency, or a small software house that serves regional clients, the question is different. For those businesses, a hub is usually a cost center. The hub question only becomes urgent when the company is chasing a large market and needs to scale faster than its local environment can support.

A hub is a place where the inputs of a company are close together: customers, investors, employees, suppliers, lawyers, accountants, competitors, and other founders. The value is not that the people are smarter. It is that the distance between decisions is shorter. A founder can meet a potential customer for lunch, call a specialist contractor, hire an engineer who just left a comparable company, and talk to an investor without a flight. In a thin market, each of those steps takes weeks. In a dense one, they can take days. That difference matters most when the company is trying to learn what works and then pour fuel on it.

Silicon Valley is the strongest hub for a particular class of company: venture-backed software and internet businesses aiming at the US market or a global market in which US investors set terms. It has the deepest pool of experienced operators, the most venture capital, and a habit of building companies as global platforms. Stripe, Airbnb, and Uber are examples of companies that started there and became global. But London is also a hub, with its own strengths in fintech, professional services, and English-language global reach. Revolut, Monzo, and Deliveroo show that a London-based company can become global without making San Francisco its home. If the company in question was a London fintech, my sentence was not just imprecise; it was wrong. London’s fintech ecosystem is not a consolation prize. For some businesses, it is the better fit.

The strongest objection to the hub argument is that the effect is mostly selection. Ambitious founders go to San Francisco, so companies there succeed because the founders were already likely to succeed. Some of this is true. Hubs are sorting machines. But even if the causal effect is smaller than the stories suggest, the practical question is access. A founder can read about network effects; importing them is harder. If the founder can get the same introductions, hires, and commercial terms remotely, the hub does not matter. For many companies, especially early ones, that is not true.

Remote work changed the office question more than the network question. A company can employ people in three countries and still need its founders to be where the deal happens. Investors still prefer to be able to visit. Customers still often prefer a vendor in their time zone. A company selling to New York can do morning calls from London, but it is still four hours away; from San Francisco it is seven or eight hours away, and same-day follow-through becomes harder. A hub is no longer just a floor plan. It is a social and commercial density.

The case for moving is strongest when a company is building a product that can be sold globally from one codebase, needs venture-scale capital, and is trying to enter a market whose center of gravity is elsewhere. A developer-tools company selling to American enterprises, a consumer platform aiming at North America, a fintech that needs US banking partnerships: for these, being in or near the relevant US hub reduces friction at the exact moment when speed matters. The move is worth it if the next ten customers, the next fifty hires, and the next round of investors are mostly in that hub.

It is also most defensible before the company has become too large to move. A three-person team can relocate in a month; a 300-person company cannot. But it is also too early if the product is untested. Moving before you know what you are selling turns a search for product-market fit into a search for an office. A team with a prototype and no recurring revenue should not spend a quarter on leases, payroll systems, visas, and broken commutes. It should find customers where it is, or talk to them daily, and move only when the next milestone requires it.

A startup should not move to a hub when its moat is local. A delivery platform, a property-tech company, a logistics network, a healthcare service, or a local marketplace wins by being embedded in a city or country: couriers, landlords, doctors, suppliers, regulators, and customer trust are all local. London density does not help a company whose customers are plumbers in Manchester or pharmacies in Lyon. The relevant network is not in the famous hub; it is on the street.

Nor should it move to the wrong hub. Biotechnology clusters in Boston and Cambridge, Massachusetts, because of universities, labs, and pharma partners. Hardware supply chains are in Shenzhen. Enterprise software has long had a New York presence. Southeast Asian fintech may be best served from Singapore. The question is not “where is the most famous hub?” but “where are the people who can say yes to me?” A biotech in Cambridge, Massachusetts should not move to Silicon Valley just because of prestige. A hardware company in Shenzhen should not move to London just to look venture-scale.

If the company already has product-market fit and a defensible local position, moving can destroy more than it creates. It raises costs, disrupts customers, complicates employment contracts, and can look like a loss of focus. In that case the right move is usually a satellite office: put the sales lead in New York, the engineering manager in Berlin, the founder in London, and keep the legal and operational center where the market is. Slack started in Denver, a strong tech city but not the densest hub, and grew into a major company. It later moved its headquarters to San Francisco as it scaled. That sequence shows both sides: a company can find fit outside the top hub, but when it needs the largest pool of talent and capital, it may still drift toward the center.

If the team cannot move, do not force it. A co-founder who stays because of a child, a health issue, or a local business can still contribute, but the plan must be honest about who needs to be in the hub. Usually it is the CEO or the person raising money and selling, not the whole company. Moving a company is not just changing a mailing address. It can mean new incorporation, payroll, benefits, visas, and tax advice. That cost is real and should be put on the same side of the ledger as the expected benefit.

A company should not move just because an investor hinted at it. US venture investors often prefer a US base because it makes follow-on rounds, hiring, and exit easier. That preference is real, but it is a demand-side effect, not a law of nature. The founder’s job is to choose the base that creates value, not to satisfy the investor’s commute.

So the proper answer to the organizer is not “Silicon Valley wins.” Hubs matter because they compress the distance between a company and the people who can accelerate it. A startup should move to a hub when it is chasing a large market and the network it lacks is concentrated there. It should stay put when its advantage is local, when its domain has a different center, when it has already found fit, or when the move is a status gesture. The test is not where the startup looks most serious. It is whether the next milestone requires being there.

prompt: Tell me the story of learning an invented language as an adult: why you'd start, how far you'd go, and whether it was worth it. Be candid, including the parts that don't flatter you.
response:
You are thirty-eight, and a real language has been a slow humiliation. You took French in school, survived it with conjugation tables, and now you can say you are going to the bathroom but not what the waiter just said. An invented language looks like a way out. The grammar is often written down by one person or a small group, with fewer historical accidents in it. There is no native accent you will be graded on. If you learn the rules, you can be correct. That is the lure, and it is also the first unflattering fact: you want a language where competence is visible and where nobody can make you feel small by speaking faster.

Maybe it is Esperanto. Maybe it is toki pona, with its tiny vocabulary and puzzle-like grammar. Maybe it is Klingon, because you have wanted to belong to a world since you were fifteen. The first month feels like cheating. You learn the alphabet, the first hundred words, the way questions are formed. You write your name. You write “today I am learning this language.” You feel clever. Then the work begins. You make flashcards. You read a grammar explanation three times. You try to say “I would have liked to have gone” and discover that even a simple language has a place where your thought gets stuck.

After six months, a common stopping place is a few hundred words and the main verb forms or noun cases. You can read a slow text. You can write a paragraph if you keep a dictionary open. You can translate in your head, but not fast. You cannot dream in it. You cannot get angry in it. That is the border. To cross it you need use, and use is the part invented languages make difficult. Esperanto has a community: conversations, letters, meetings, people who use it as a first language. Toki pona has scattered speakers and a culture of minimal sentences. Klingon has enthusiasts who will correct your verb affixes with affection. If you find one or two people, the project changes. You prepare a page of sentences. You speak for twenty minutes. You are literal, slow, and often wrong. The other person does not look bored. That is strange and a little dangerous, because now the language has a reason to exist outside your notes.
